entries.summary: 'I will pray the Father, and He shall give you another Comforter (allon Paraklēton), that He may abide with you for ever' is for Cyril the principal Johannine text on the personal divinity of the Holy Spirit. 'Another' (allon — implying same-kind-as) Cyril stresses: the Spirit is the same KIND of divine Person as Christ is — not a different ontological category, not a lesser being, not merely impersonal divine power. 'Paraklēton' Cyril expounds as advocate/comforter/encourager/intercessor — all four functions belong to the Spirit because they all belong to the divine Person. 'Abide with you for ever' establishes the permanence of the post-Pentecost Spirit-indwelling (as distinct from the intermittent prophetic-inspiration of the Old Covenant economy).
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk X.16 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Even the Spirit of truth (to Pneuma tēs alētheias); whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth Him not, neither knoweth Him' Cyril takes as the pneumatological criterion of saving knowledge. The world's incapacity to receive the Spirit Cyril attributes not to ontological lack but to the cognitive condition of unbelief that blocks perception. 'Ye know Him' (gnōskete) Cyril emphasizes as the disciples' present-tense possession of pneumatic knowledge — even before Pentecost, in nascent form. The eschatological 'shall be in you' (en hymin estai) Cyril reads as the post-Pentecost completion of what is here proleptically begun. Cyril's pneumatology of progressive economy (already present in the verse) becomes systematic in his On the Holy Trinity dialogues.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk X.17 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'At that day ye shall know that I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you' Cyril takes as the perichoretic extension to the Church: just as the Son is in the Father (Trinitarian mutual indwelling), so the believer is in the Son (ecclesial-mystical incorporation) and the Son in the believer (sacramental-Spiritual indwelling). The order is crucial for Cyril: the Trinitarian indwelling grounds the ecclesial, which grounds the Christological-in-the-individual. 'At that day' Cyril reads as the post-Pentecost age in which the Spirit's indwelling makes this triple participation effective. The Tewahedo Anaphora's epiclesis prayers explicitly invoke this triple participation as the gift the eucharistic communion realizes in the worshipper.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk X.20 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, He shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you' is for Cyril the locus classicus for the apostolic-authority basis of Scripture and Tradition. The Spirit's twin functions (teach + remind) presuppose the prior content given by Christ; the Spirit does not invent new revelation but illuminates and consolidates what Christ has spoken. This grounds Cyril's argument against any sectarian claim to revelation beyond the apostolic deposit: the Spirit's teaching is bounded by what Christ taught. The Tewahedo doctrine of the inseparability of Scripture-and-Tradition (Mäṣḥafä Hēnok + Mäṣḥafä Qǝddase together with the Tanakh + NT) rests on this Cyrilline reading.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk X.26 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'My Father is greater than I' (ho Patēr meizōn mou estin) is THE most contested verse in Cyril's John commentary — the Arian polemical favorite throughout the 4th century, requiring careful orthodox exposition. Cyril resolves through the standard distinction: the verse predicates 'greater' of the Father with respect to the assumed humanity of the incarnate Son, NOT with respect to the eternal divine nature. Insofar as the Son is incarnate (took on human nature), the unincarnate Father is 'greater' in mode-of-existence; insofar as the Son is eternal Word, He is consubstantial-equal with the Father. The verse therefore confirms rather than denies the incarnation, and presupposes rather than undermines the consubstantiality. This careful exposition is one of Cyril's most-cited Johannine passages in later Greek theological tradition.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk X.28 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.summary: On 'the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters' Ephrem reads the threefold negation (tōhū wā-bōhū + darkness + deep) as the proper unfolded condition of created matter awaiting form. Against any reading that would treat the primal chaos as evil or co-eternal, Ephrem insists matter is created good but unformed; form is the divine speech-act that makes the unformed habitable. The Spirit's 'moving' (the Syriac merahhefa carries the sense of a bird brooding over its nest) Ephrem reads as the active warmth that prepares matter for the Word's subsequent commands. This pneumatological-cosmological reading is the Syriac tradition's most distinctive contribution to early creation theology.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis I.2 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: 'And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness' Ephrem takes as the establishment of the elemental moral framework that the entire Scripture presupposes. The dividing (the Syriac fres = to separate definitively) is not provisional but ordinative: light and darkness are henceforth bounded by divine decree. Ephrem reads the 'goodness' (the Syriac tabbutha) as not merely aesthetic approval but the recognition that the light corresponds to the divine intent — God names what He has done as fitting. This pattern (creation + recognition + naming) Ephrem extracts as the divine workflow that the believer is called to imitate: every legitimate work is done, recognized, and named for what it is.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis I.4 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: On 'Let there be a firmament (rāqīa') in the midst of the waters' Ephrem describes a tripartite cosmology that the medieval Tewahedo tradition continues to teach: the waters above (the celestial reservoirs from which rain descends), the firmament (the visible heaven, made of compacted water frozen by the divine command), and the waters below (the seas + the deep). Ephrem is careful against any reading that would make the firmament a fixed metallic dome (against pagan Babylonian cosmologies); rather, it is a flexible-but-stable boundary that holds the upper waters in place by divine sustaining act, not by inherent material property. The Andəmta homiletic tradition preserves Ephrem's tripartite cosmology in its liturgical hymnody on the first creation day.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis I.6 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind' Ephrem takes as the establishment of generative ordering: the divine speech-act is not the immediate creation of plants (which would be a continuous miracle) but the inscribing of seed-and-fruit cycles into the earth's productive nature. The 'after his kind' (lemīneh) Ephrem reads as a constitutive boundary: each created kind reproduces within its own categorical limits, not crossing them. This Ephremic reading provided the patristic-tradition framework within which medieval Tewahedo natural philosophy understood the species' fixity — a framework that subsequent Andəmta commentators preserved without modification through the early modern period.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis I.11 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: On 'Let there be lights in the firmament... for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years' Ephrem makes the foundational anti-astrological argument: the heavenly luminaries are SERVANTS for marking time, not GODS for determining destiny. The fourfold purpose (signs / seasons / days / years) Ephrem reads as exhausting the legitimate functions of the heavens; any further attribution (horoscopic prediction, fate, divinatory power) is human invention not divine grant. The Tewahedo liturgical calendar — which depends on careful astronomical observation for determining Easter (the Bahire Hassab computus tradition) — derives its theological legitimacy directly from this Ephremic reading: astronomy in service of liturgy is sacred; astrology in service of fate-prediction is forbidden.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis I.14 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life' Ephrem reads as the inauguration of animal life — a categorical distinction from plant life established on day three. The Syriac 'rahhash' (moving / creeping) Ephrem takes as the defining attribute: animal life is characterized by self-movement, which presupposes the kind of nephesh-soul that plant life lacks. Yet Ephrem is careful against any reading that would make animal life autonomous: the abundance is divinely commanded, not naturally emergent, and the soul of the animal is a divine breath given for animal-purposes (not transferable to humanity, which receives its own distinct divine inbreathing in 2:7).
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis I.20 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: On 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness' Ephrem provides the Syriac patristic reading of the plural: the speaking is internal to the Godhead, the Father addressing the Word and the Spirit in eternal counsel — not (against the Rabbinic reading) the angels, since the image is a divine image and angels are not creators. The 'image' (tzalem) and 'likeness' (demut) Ephrem distinguishes: the image is given fully at creation (rational soul + capacity for moral choice), the likeness is the EVENTUAL conformity-to-God that life-in-grace cultivates. The Tewahedo doctrine of theosis (deification) inherits this Ephremic distinction: humans are made AS image, called TO likeness, completed in the eschaton.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis I.26 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'And God saw every thing that He had made, and, behold, it was very good' Ephrem reads as the consummative divine judgment on the entire six-day creative work. 'Very good' (tab tab — the Syriac doubles the adjective for intensity) Ephrem takes as ontological assessment, not merely aesthetic: the cosmos as a whole, in its differentiated unity, perfectly fulfills the divine intention. Against any later Marcionite or gnostic reading that would treat matter or embodiment as defective, Ephrem insists Gen 1:31 is the theological foundation for the goodness of creation — including matter, body, sexuality, work, and time — all 'very good' in their proper places. The fall in Gen 3 corrupts but does not negate this primordial goodness.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis I.31 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: On 'God ended His work which He had made; and He rested on the seventh day' Ephrem reads the rest (the Syriac 'ettnih) not as cessation from activity (God's providential governance never pauses) but as the establishment of the Sabbath pattern — the divine ordering of time into work-and-rest. The seventh-day rest is therefore not God's exhaustion but God's instructional gift: humans are taught their own work-rhythm by divine example. Ephrem connects this with the eschatological Sabbath-rest awaited by the faithful (cf. Heb 4:9 sabbatismos): the weekly rest typifies the eternal rest, and the eternal rest fulfills the weekly. The Tewahedo Sabbath observance (preserving the Saturday observance alongside Sunday Eucharist) traces its theological warrant to this Ephremic reading.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis II.2 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: On the two trees of Eden — 'the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil' — Ephrem provides his characteristic Syriac reading: the tree of life is real (it would have conferred immortality on those who ate from it in obedience), and the tree of knowledge is real (its prohibition was the means by which moral obedience was tested). Against allegorizing readings that would dissolve both trees into mere metaphor, Ephrem insists on their referential reality while preserving their theological significance: physical eating mattered because the tree was the appointed sign of moral allegiance. The Tewahedo Andəmta tradition preserves this Ephremic concrete-and-symbolic reading.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis II.9 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him' Ephrem reads as the divine recognition of the relational nature of humanity. Adam's solitude is the first thing in creation called 'not good' (the only such utterance in the entire creation account); thus human relationality is not optional add-on but essential constitutive feature. The 'help meet' (the Syriac me'addranita meqabblanitha — a helper corresponding to him) Ephrem reads with care against any reading that would make Eve subordinate-in-essence: she is a helper precisely because she corresponds to him as equal and counterpart. This grounds the Tewahedo theological framing of marriage as a sacramental union of equals.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis II.18 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: On the creation of Eve from Adam's rib (the divine sleep + the taking of the rib + the building into woman) Ephrem provides the foundational Syriac patristic reading: Adam's deep sleep prefigures Christ's death-sleep on the cross, the rib taken prefigures the wound of Christ's side, and Eve formed from the rib prefigures the Church born from Christ's pierced side. This is the typological-sacramental Adam-Christ + Eve-Church parallel that becomes determinative for medieval Tewahedo ecclesiology: the Church is not externally added to Christ but proceeds from His own pierced side as Eve proceeded from Adam's rib. The Tewahedo Anaphora of Our Lord Jesus Christ explicitly echoes this typology.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis II.21 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: The serpent's counter-claim — 'Ye shall not surely die' — Ephrem identifies as the prototype of every subsequent satanic suggestion: the direct contradiction of the divine word, dressed in the form of liberation-from-prohibition. Ephrem notes the technique: the serpent does not deny God's existence (that would be too clearly false to the unfallen Eve), but denies the consequence God attached to disobedience. The lie is in the consequence, not in the premise. This pattern (true premise + false consequence) Ephrem identifies as the demonic-tempter signature throughout salvation history — recurring in the wilderness temptation of Christ (Mt 4) where Satan again quotes truly-but-misapplied Scripture.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis III.4 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked' Ephrem reads as the inverse of true illumination: the opening of the eyes that the serpent promised does occur, but it is opening TO shame rather than opening TO knowledge of God. The 'nakedness' Ephrem distinguishes from physical undress (Adam and Eve were physically unclothed before the fall without shame): post-fall nakedness is the felt absence of the divine glory that had covered them in their innocent state. Ephrem here grounds the patristic-Syriac tradition that Adam and Eve in Eden were clothed in light (the divine glory itself); the fall stripped them of that radiant covering, leaving the now-shameful bare flesh that needed fig leaves and then God-given skins.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis III.7 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: God's question — 'Where art thou?' — Ephrem takes as pastoral rather than informational: the omniscient God does not ask because He needs to know Adam's location, but because He gives Adam the opportunity to confess. The question opens a space for repentance that Adam tragically fills with deflection and blame-shifting (3:12: 'the woman whom thou gavest to be with me'). Ephrem reads this as the founding pattern of every subsequent pastoral encounter: God invites confession before pronouncing judgment; refusal of the invitation hardens the judgment. The Tewahedo sacrament of confession draws its theological frame from this Ephremic reading: the priest asks not to learn but to invite acknowledgment.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis III.9 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: Ephrem's reading of the protoevangelium ('it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel') is THE Syriac patristic basis for early Christological reading of Genesis. The 'seed of the woman' Ephrem takes as singular-Messianic (Christ born of the virgin) AND collectively-ecclesial (the Church suffering yet finally triumphant). The bruising of the head is the decisive wound (mortal) that the seed inflicts on the serpent; the bruising of the heel is the suffering wound (recoverable) that the serpent inflicts on the seed in the wounding of the cross. Ephrem's reading is one of the most-cited patristic precedents in the medieval Tewahedo Mariological tradition, which preserves the singular-Messianic reading without diluting it into the Western 'she shall bruise' Vulgate variant.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis III.15 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground' Ephrem reads as the imposition of mortality + the dignification of labor. Mortality enters as judgment ('thou shalt return'); but labor is given as both consequence-of-fall AND mercy-toward-fallen-humanity — work occupies the soul that would otherwise turn to deeper rebellion in idleness. The 'sweat of thy face' Ephrem reads as marking labor with the dignity of effort: post-fall human work is genuinely costly and genuinely productive. The Tewahedo monastic tradition's emphasis on manual labor (the Egyptian-Syriac desert father heritage) inherits this Ephremic reading: work is ascetic gift, not curse to be evaded.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis III.19 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'He placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way' Ephrem reads as the institution of the guarded sacred space that the entire Levitical and patristic liturgical tradition will subsequently elaborate. The Cherubim + flaming sword prefigure the veil of the Temple (which similarly guards the holy of holies), the icon screen of the Tewahedo and Eastern Orthodox church buildings (which guards the altar), and ultimately the eschatological gates of the heavenly Jerusalem. Ephrem reads the 'turning every way' (mithhappek) as denoting omnidirectional guarding: no approach from any angle can pierce the divine prohibition; only divine permission (Christ's opening of the way through His own flesh, per Heb 10:19-20) restores access.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis III.24 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: God's warning to Cain — 'sin lieth at the door' (chattat robets) — Ephrem reads with characteristic concrete-typological precision. The Syriac participle (rabea — crouching, like a beast of prey) is preserved; sin is figured as a hostile creature lying in wait outside the door of the soul, requiring active mastery from within. 'And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him' Ephrem takes as both warning and promise: sin's pressure is real but not insuperable; mastery is achievable through divine help. The Tewahedo monastic ascetic-theological tradition draws its anti-passion combat language directly from this Ephremic reading: the passions are recognized, then resisted, then subdued.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis IV.7 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: Cain's deflection — 'Am I my brother's keeper?' — Ephrem identifies as the prototype of every subsequent attempted evasion of relational responsibility. The rhetorical question is not innocent ignorance but calculated false-disclaim: Cain knows precisely where Abel is (in the ground he buried him in) but pretends ignorance. Ephrem notes the deep irony: Cain SHOULD have been his brother's keeper (the Hebrew shomer carries the sense of guardian-and-protector); his refusal to be so was the very act of fratricide. The Tewahedo communal-monastic tradition reads this verse as the textual foundation of mutual responsibility: each Christian is responsible for the spiritual welfare of his brothers and sisters, and the refusal of this responsibility is itself a form of fratricide.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis IV.9 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod' Ephrem reads as the geographical-spiritual figuration of every subsequent flight from divine presence. The 'land of Nod' (literally 'land of wandering' from the Hebrew nud) Ephrem takes as not merely place-name but condition: Cain's exile is into rootless wandering, the inverse of the agricultural settlement his rejected sacrifice had presupposed. The departure 'from the presence of the LORD' is not divine abandonment (God remains everywhere present) but Cain's chosen exit from the conscious-relational orientation that constitutes communion. Every subsequent biblical wandering (Abraham's call, Israel's wilderness, the prodigal son's far country) Ephrem reads against this Cainite prototype.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis IV.16 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him' Ephrem takes as central to the entire Tewahedo theological imagination, since Enoch is the canonical author of the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok (1 Enoch). The 'walking with God' Ephrem reads as the Syriac patristic ideal of continual conscious communion — the same standard upheld for Noah (6:9) and re-articulated for Abraham (17:1). The translation ('God took him') Ephrem takes literally: Enoch did not die in the ordinary mode but was assumed bodily into divine presence. Together with the parallel translation of Elijah (2 Kings 2:11), this establishes the Old Testament's witness to bodily glorification before the universal resurrection. Tewahedo eschatology preserves both translations with particular weight, since Enoch's translated state grounds the authority of the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok he composed.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis V.24 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: Lamech's naming of Noah — 'This same shall comfort us (yenahamenu) concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed' — Ephrem reads as prophetic anticipation grounded in pre-flood corruption. Noah's name (the Hebrew root n-w-h, to rest/comfort) Ephrem takes as etymologically programmatic: Noah will be the one through whom the post-flood relief is mediated, the cursed ground (Gen 3:17) being either washed clean or replaced by new earth in the renewal that follows the flood. Ephrem reads Lamech's hope as proleptically Christological: every Old Testament expectation of comfort-mediated-by-a-righteous-one ultimately points beyond itself to Christ as the true Comforter. The Tewahedo Synaxarium preserves Noah on the 10th of Magabit as a type of Christ.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis V.29 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'My Spirit shall not always strive (yadōn) with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years' Ephrem reads the 120-year span as the divine grant of additional time for repentance before the flood — not the post-flood human lifespan but the specific pre-judgment window during which Noah preached repentance. The 'striving' of the Spirit Ephrem takes as the ongoing convicting work of the Spirit in human conscience, eventually withdrawable when persistent rebellion makes further striving fruitless. The verse anchors the Syriac patristic doctrine that divine patience has limits not because of any weariness in God but because of the moral structure that requires consequence to follow on settled refusal.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis VI.3 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD' Ephrem reads as the textual locus classicus for grace (the Syriac taybutha) preceding-and-grounding human righteousness, not following on it. The 'found' (matsa') Ephrem notes carries the sense of discovery within an existing reality, not the achievement of something new: grace was already there in God's disposition; Noah encountered it. Yet the verse immediately follows (in v. 9) with 'Noah was a just man and perfect... and Noah walked with God' — so grace and human righteousness are not opposed but coordinated. Ephrem reads this as the seed of the Pauline doctrine of justifying grace that issues in genuine righteousness — neither merit-earning grace (against Pelagianism) nor grace-displacing-righteousness (against later antinomianism).
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis VI.8 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: On the divine command to build the ark — 'Make thee an ark (tēbat) of gopher wood' — Ephrem develops the canonical Syriac patristic typology: the ark prefigures the Church (the salvific vessel that carries the faithful through the waters of judgment), and the wood of the ark prefigures the wood of the cross (the material instrument of salvation). The dimensions Ephrem reads symbolically (length 300 / breadth 50 / height 30 cubits): the ark's proportions match the human body's, since the salvation of humanity required the assumption of human form. The Tewahedo Anaphora of Athanasius preserves this Noah-ark-Church-cross typological cluster prominently in its anamnesis prayer.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis VI.14 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: On the flood's onset — 'all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened' — Ephrem reads the dual-source flooding as the cosmic-symbolic reversal of the Day 2 separation of waters (Gen 1:6-7). The firmament that had held the upper waters in place is, as it were, unstoppered; the deep that had been bounded breaks its bounds. Creation un-creates itself by divine permission — order returning to chaos because of human moral disorder. This Ephremic reading establishes the deep theological principle that cosmic order and moral order are not independent: human sin has cosmic-environmental consequences, and the restoration of moral order is the precondition for the restoration of cosmic order. The Tewahedo doctrine of the new heavens and new earth (cf. Mäṣḥafä Hēnok 91) traces this principle forward.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis VII.11 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: After Noah's post-flood sacrifice — 'the LORD smelled a sweet savour; and the LORD said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake' — Ephrem reads as the inauguration of the Noahic covenant of cosmic stability. The 'sweet savour' (the Syriac rīhā d-nyahha) Ephrem takes as the prototype of every subsequent acceptable sacrifice — Abel's, Abraham's, the Mosaic sacrificial system, and ultimately the eucharistic sacrifice of Christ. God's interior speech ('said in his heart') Ephrem takes as decisive: the divine commitment is irrevocable not because of external pressure but because of intrinsic divine resolve. The Tewahedo liturgical reading of this verse on Noah's feast day (10th of Magabit) preserves this Ephremic emphasis on the interior divine commitment.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis VIII.21 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: On the rainbow as covenantal sign — 'I do set my bow (qashti) in the cloud' — Ephrem makes the most of the Hebrew qesheth's dual sense of 'bow' = both rainbow AND warrior's weapon. God sets His bow (war-weapon) in the cloud: His instrument of judgment is permanently sheathed as covenantal pledge that the universal-deluge mode of judgment will not recur. The bow is set with its string facing downward (toward earth) and its arc facing upward — figuratively, the weapon is laid aside, not aimed. Ephrem reads this as the textual root of the Syriac patristic teaching that divine wrath, while real, is never the final word: the rainbow stands over every subsequent storm as the visible reminder that mercy has the last word.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis IX.13 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: Noah's pronouncement after the Ham-incident — 'Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren' — Ephrem reads with careful precision against any reading that would extract a permanent racial-ethnic curse. The curse falls on CANAAN (Ham's son), not on Ham himself or on Ham's other descendants; the cursing is therefore localized and historical (fulfilled in the Canaanite-Israelite encounters of Joshua-Judges), not racially universal. Against the early-modern American mis-application of this verse to justify African slavery, Ephrem's text-bounded reading clearly precludes such extension: the curse is on a specific lineage (Canaan), for a specific reason (Canaan's prefigured idolatry and immorality), with a specific fulfillment (the dispossession of the Canaanite peoples by Israel). The Tewahedo reading inherits Ephrem's text-bounded precision.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis IX.25 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: The Babel-builders' resolution — 'let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name' — Ephrem reads as the prototype of every subsequent self-deifying human project. The 'tower whose top may reach unto heaven' Ephrem takes as the inversion of the rightful divine order: instead of God descending to dwell with humanity (as He will at Sinai, in the Temple, and ultimately in the Incarnation), humanity attempts to ascend to heaven by its own engineering. The 'let us make us a name' Ephrem identifies as the deepest motive: the desire for autonomous self-significance apart from divine naming. The Tewahedo theological reading of Babel maintains this Ephremic anti-Promethean frame: every human construct that aims at deity by self-effort is doomed to confusion.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis XI.4 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth' Ephrem reads as the etymological-theological hinge that interprets the entire Old Testament's subsequent encounter with multiple languages. The confusion of tongues (the Hebrew balal = to mix / confound) at Babel is divine judgment-as-mercy: the unified human project was unifiedly evil; fragmentation by language limits the scope of any single evil. The Pentecost (Acts 2) Ephrem reads as the inverse-recapitulation: not the abolition of linguistic diversity but the Spirit's gift of cross-linguistic intelligibility around the proclamation of Christ. The Tewahedo Pentecost liturgy explicitly cross-references Gen 11:9 in its hymns, preserving this Ephremic Babel-Pentecost typological pair.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis XI.9 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman' Cyril takes as the sixth of Christ's 'I AM' sayings and the foundational text for the doctrine of vital union between Christ and the Church. 'True' (alēthinē) Cyril emphasizes against any merely metaphorical or typological reading: Christ is not LIKE a vine, He IS the vine in the substantive sense — the source of life for the branches grafted into Him. The Father as 'husbandman' (geōrgos) Cyril reads as the Trinitarian operation in vine-tending: the Father's pruning and cultivating work is exercised through the Son in the Spirit. The Tewahedo Anaphora preserves this vine-husbandman language in its ecclesiological prayers.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk X.1 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'I am the vine, ye are the branches: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing' is for Cyril the Christological-ecclesiological pin against any reading that would make Christian life autonomous. The reciprocal abiding (en emoi / en autō — in me / in him) Cyril takes as extending the Johannine perichoresis (14:10-11) from the Trinity to the Christ-Church relation by participation. 'Without me ye can do nothing' (chōris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden) Cyril takes with full force: not 'less effectively' but 'nothing at all' — every fruit-bearing in the Christian life is participatory in Christ's own activity. The verse is the textual foundation for the Tewahedo doctrine of synergism-in-grace: human cooperation is real but always sourced in prior divine indwelling.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk X.5 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends' Cyril reads as Christ's self-disclosure of the love that the cross will enact within hours. The 'greater' (meizona) establishes the comparative absolute: no love exceeds self-laying-down-for-friends. Christ's love for the world (Jn 3:16) is enacted as this love in the cross; the cross is therefore the visible measure of the previously-invisible Trinitarian love. 'For his friends' (hyper tōn philōn autou) Cyril reads with care: the love is universal in offer (15:16 'I have chosen you'), particular in friendship-bond. This anticipates the eucharistic ethic that becomes determinative for the Tewahedo monastic-martyrological tradition: laying-down-of-life is the Christian's proper response to having been thus loved.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk X.13 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit' Cyril takes as the dominical doctrine of election as priority of divine initiative. The reversal of expected ordering (the human disciple-choice is preceded and constituted by divine choice) Cyril reads as eliminating any boast: apostleship is gift, not achievement. 'Ordained' (ethēka — set / placed / appointed) Cyril notes carries the sense of sacramental commission: the appointment is not merely informational but operatively confers what it commissions. The Tewahedo doctrine of holy orders draws its theological warrant from this Cyrilline reading: ordination is participation in Christ's own ordaining act.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk X.16 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, He shall testify of me' is THE pneumatological text Cyril cites most heavily in his Trinitarian theology. The Greek ekporeuetai (proceedeth) Cyril reads as the eternal procession of the Spirit from the Father (the Eastern Orthodox foundation for the original Nicene formulation, against the later Western Filioque). Yet 'whom I will send' (pempsō egō) preserves the Son's role in the temporal mission of the Spirit. Cyril distinguishes carefully: the ETERNAL procession is from-the-Father-alone; the TEMPORAL mission is through-the-Son. This distinction becomes determinative for Eastern + Oriental Orthodox pneumatology, including Tewahedo.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk X.26 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'And ye also shall bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning' Cyril takes as the apostolic-foundation text grounding the historical-witness character of the Christian message. 'From the beginning' (ap' archēs) Cyril reads as the public-ministry beginning (from the Baptist's witness onward) — the apostles' qualification to bear witness rests on direct historical eyewitness, not on personal religious experience alone. This grounds the patristic-Tewahedo doctrine of apostolic succession: the Church's authoritative teaching traces back through a continuous chain to the eyewitness apostles, who saw with their own eyes what they then proclaimed.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk X.27 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'It is expedient (sympherei) for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send Him unto you' Cyril takes as the dominical pneumatology of progressive economy. Christ's bodily departure is necessary for the Spirit's coming because the modes of presence are different: Christ in the flesh was geographically limited (could be in one place at a time); the Spirit indwelling the Church is universally present everywhere His people gather. The 'expedient' (sympherei — beneficial / advantageous) Cyril emphasizes as not consolation-prize but actual upgrade: ascension + Spirit-coming is a richer mode of presence than incarnate proximity. The Tewahedo Anaphora's epiclesis prayers explicitly invoke this Cyrilline reading.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.7 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'When He, the Spirit of truth, is come, He will guide you into all truth: for He shall not speak of Himself; but whatsoever He shall hear, that shall He speak' Cyril unpacks against any reading that would make the Spirit a separate or supplementary teaching source. 'He shall not speak of Himself' Cyril reads as expressing perfect Trinitarian harmony: the Spirit's teaching IS the Father's + Son's teaching, mediated through the Spirit's distinctive operation, not a separate revelation. 'All truth' (eis tēn alētheian pasan) Cyril limits to the Christological-soteriological deposit: the Spirit guides into ALL the truth Christ has given, not into endless new revelations. This grounds patristic-Tewahedo apostolic-deposit doctrine.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.13 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy' Cyril reads as the eschatological pattern of Christian experience: present suffering is not negated but transmuted by the resurrection. 'Turned' (genēsetai eis charan — shall be made into joy) Cyril takes literally: not 'replaced by' joy after sorrow ends, but TRANSFORMED INTO joy. The Easter pattern (Friday's sorrow becomes Sunday's joy through the cross-resurrection event) is the paradigm. Cyril applies this to every subsequent Christian experience of suffering: nothing in the Christian life is finally lost; every present sorrow is the seed of a future joy by participation in the paschal pattern. The Tewahedo Easter Anaphora preserves this transformative reading.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.20 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again, I leave the world, and go to the Father' Cyril takes as the compressed Johannine summary of the entire incarnational economy. The four-fold movement (procession from Father / incarnation into world / departure from world / return to Father) Cyril reads as the dogmatic structure that the entire Gospel of John traces verse-by-verse. The 'came forth' (exēlthon) preserves the eternal procession; the 'come into the world' (elēlytha eis ton kosmon) marks the historical incarnation; the 'leave the world' (aphiēmi ton kosmon) anticipates the cross-and-ascension; the 'go to the Father' (poreuomai pros ton Patera) marks the consummation in glory. The Tewahedo Christmas Anaphora explicitly echoes all four movements.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.28 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome (nenikēka) the world' is for Cyril the closing dominical pin of the Farewell Discourses. The perfect tense 'have overcome' (nenikēka — completed action with continuing result) Cyril takes proleptically: the victory is spoken of as already accomplished from the perspective of the eternal Word, even though the cross-and-resurrection still lay ahead historically. 'Be of good cheer' (tharseite — take courage, be confident) is therefore not consolation despite-defeat but participatory rejoicing-in-victory: the disciples are invited to share Christ's confidence that the outcome is settled. This grounds the Tewahedo martyrological tradition's characteristic theological confidence.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.33 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee' opens the High-Priestly Prayer that Cyril treats with particular reverence — calling it 'the prayer the Church prays back to the Father along with Christ.' The 'hour' (hōra) Cyril reads as the kairos-hour of the entire incarnational economy: the appointed time toward which all prior events of Christ's life have been ordered. The mutual glorification (Son-glorified-by-Father and Father-glorified-by-Son) Cyril reads as preserving the Trinitarian symmetry: glory belongs to all three Persons, communicated reciprocally, never possessed monopolistically. This is the textual frame for the entire Tewahedo doxological tradition.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.1 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent' Cyril unpacks as the dominical definition of eternal life: not merely endless duration but cognitive-relational participation in the divine knowledge. The infinitive 'might know' (ginōskōsi — continuous action) Cyril takes as denoting ongoing personal knowing, not single intellectual grasp. The pairing (the Father AS only true God AND Jesus Christ AS sent) Cyril carefully reads to preserve both monotheism (against pagan polytheism) and Christological inclusion in deity (against Arian subordination): both clauses together constitute the saving knowledge. This verse anchors the Tewahedo catechetical tradition's definition of theosis as participation-by-knowing.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.3 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was' (para seautō tē doxē hē eichon pro tou ton kosmon einai para soi) is Cyril's strongest single-verse text for the eternal pre-existence of the Son. 'Before the world was' Cyril takes against any Arian reading: the Son had glory WITH the Father before creation existed — therefore the Son's existence is not within creation's scope but eternal, alongside the Father from the very beginning. 'Thine own self' (para seautō) preserves the Personal distinction even within the consubstantial unity: the glory is shared between distinct Persons, not collapsed into Sabellian identity. This verse is among Cyril's most-cited prooftexts in the Twelve Anathemas against Nestorius.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.5 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth' Cyril takes as the dominical pin for the Word-mediated character of sanctification. 'Sanctify' (hagiason — set apart, make holy) Cyril reads as not merely declarative (treated as holy) but operatively transformative (actually made holy). The instrument of sanctification ('through thy truth') Cyril identifies as the apostolic Word given by Christ to the Church — the deposit that the Spirit teaches into all truth (16:13). The closing 'thy word is truth' Cyril takes with full force: the Word (the eternal Logos) IS the truth, and the spoken word (the apostolic Scripture) participates in that truth. This grounds the patristic-Tewahedo doctrine of Scripture's truth as Christ's own truth mediated.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.17 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us' is for Cyril THE ecclesiological text of the entire Gospel. The unity asked for is participatory: ecclesial unity is grounded in and patterned after Trinitarian unity. 'As' (kathōs) Cyril reads as analogical (a real likeness preserved across the ontological difference between Trinitarian-unity-by-nature and ecclesial-unity-by-grace). 'That the world may believe' (hina ho kosmos pisteusē — closing the verse) Cyril takes as missiological warrant: the visible unity of the Church is the primary evidential basis for the Gospel's credibility. The Tewahedo communion's preserved liturgical unity across 1700 years draws its theological warrant from this verse.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.21 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory' Cyril takes as the dominical eschatological prayer. 'Be with me where I am' (hina hopou eimi egō kakeinoi ōsi met' emou) Cyril reads as the consummation of the entire salvific economy: the goal is not merely forgiveness or moral renewal but ETERNAL CO-PRESENCE with the incarnate Word. 'Behold my glory' (theōrōsi tēn doxan tēn emēn) Cyril takes as the visio Dei — the eternal vision of God in the glorified flesh of Christ. This grounds the Tewahedo eschatological tradition that pictures heaven as eternal participatory contemplation of Christ's glory, not as static reward.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.24 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: Christ's self-identification at the arrest — 'I am he' (egō eimi) followed by the arresting party going backward and falling to the ground — Cyril reads as the deliberate Johannine theophanic intrusion into the Passion narrative. The 'I AM' Cyril links to the divine self-disclosure (Ex 3:14 ego eimi ho ōn); the falling-back is the standard biblical reaction of the unholy when confronted with theophany (cf. Ezek 1:28, Rev 1:17). Cyril's theological point: even at the moment of voluntary self-surrender, Christ's divinity is manifested visibly. The arrest happens only because Christ permits it, not because the arresting party has the power to take Him.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.6 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: Christ's rebuke of Peter — 'The cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?' — Cyril takes as the deliberate Johannine inversion of the Synoptic Gethsemane prayer ('let this cup pass from me'). John omits the Gethsemane agony entirely; instead, Christ at the moment of arrest already speaks the conformed-will resolution: the cup will be drunk. The 'shall I not drink' (ou mē piō auto) is rhetorical question expecting affirmative answer: of course He will drink, because the Father has given it. Cyril reads this as confirming the perfect alignment of the Son's incarnate will with the Father's eternal will, even at the moment of greatest stress. This grounds Cyril's later argument for the integrity of Christ's human will (against Apollinarian denial).
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.11 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'My kingdom is not of this world (ek tou kosmou toutou): if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence' Cyril takes as the dominical pin against any theocratic or revolutionary reading of Christ's mission. The kingdom's NOT-FROM-HENCE (ek — out of, sourced in) does not mean NOT-FOR-HERE: it means not deriving its character from this-world's power structures (force, military conquest, political dominance). The kingdom IS for the world, but it operates by different means (suffering love, persuasive truth, sacramental presence). Cyril's reading establishes the theological frame for the Tewahedo monastic tradition's withdrawal-from-political-power as the proper kingdom-ethic, while still affirming the kingdom's universal scope.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.36 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: Pilate's question — 'What is truth?' (ti estin alētheia) — Cyril treats with characteristic theological tragedy. Truth Himself stands before Pilate (Christ is the truth per 14:6); Pilate fails to recognize what is right in front of him. Cyril notes the absence of any answer from Christ: the only proper response to a question that misses what is already self-evidently present is silence. Pilate's tragic moment becomes the prototype of every subsequent encounter with Christ where the questioner cannot or will not see what is before them. The Tewahedo Good Friday liturgy preserves this moment with particular weight; the question and the silence stand as the textual icon of unbelief.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.38 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: Christ's reply to Pilate — 'Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above' — Cyril takes as the comprehensive doctrine of divine sovereignty over even the Passion's executioners. Pilate's authority is real (not denied) but derivative (not autonomous): every act of the powerful is bounded by divine permission. 'Therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin' (continuing the verse) Cyril takes as establishing graduated responsibility within the system: the Sanhedrin who delivered Christ to Pilate bear greater responsibility than Pilate, who merely executes their judgment within the bounds of his secondary authority. This nuanced reading shapes the Tewahedo Holy Week liturgy's careful theological framing.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.11 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: Christ's words from the cross to His mother and the beloved disciple — 'Woman, behold thy son! ... Behold thy mother!' — Cyril reads at multiple levels. Literally, Christ provides for Mary's continued care after His death (the eldest son's filial obligation discharged even from the cross). Typologically, Cyril takes Mary as figure of the Church and John as figure of every disciple: in establishing John as Mary's son, Christ establishes the Church as the Mother of every believer + every believer as the Church's son. The Tewahedo Marian veneration (which is particularly developed compared to other Christian traditions) draws its theological warrant from this Cyrilline reading.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.26 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: Christ's dying word — 'It is finished' (tetelestai) — Cyril takes as the dominical declaration of completed accomplishment. The perfect tense (tetelestai — completed action with continuing result) Cyril emphasizes: the work IS finished, definitively and abidingly. NOT 'I am dying' or 'I have failed' but 'the work is complete.' Cyril reads this as encompassing: the entire prophetic-typological economy of the Old Testament now fulfilled; the redemptive work for which the Word became flesh now consummated; the price for sin now paid in full. 'He bowed His head, and gave up the ghost' Cyril notes the order: Christ acts (bows head, gives spirit) — He is not passively overtaken by death but actively releases His life. The cross is sovereign self-offering, not victim's defeat.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.30 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: John's interpretive comment — 'For these things were done, that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken' (citing Ex 12:46 / Num 9:12 / Ps 34:20) — Cyril takes as decisive paschal typology. The Passover lamb's prohibition on broken bones is fulfilled in the crucifixion's NOT-broken-bones (against the standard practice of breaking the legs to hasten death — done to the two thieves but providentially omitted for Christ). Cyril reads this as the divine providential ordering of even the smallest details of the Passion to display the Christ-as-Paschal-Lamb typology. The Tewahedo Passover-Easter liturgical complex preserves this typological reading prominently in its hymnody.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.36 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: The Risen Christ's words to Mary Magdalene — 'Touch me not (mē mou haptou); for I am not yet ascended to my Father' — Cyril treats with care. The 'touch me not' Cyril reads not as ritual-purity concern (the resurrection-flesh is not unclean) but as redirecting Mary's grasping affection: the post-resurrection relationship will be different in mode, mediated through the ascension and the Spirit's coming. 'I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God' Cyril reads with careful Trinitarian precision: the distinction (MY Father / YOUR Father) preserves the Son's unique-by-nature sonship as distinct from the believers' adoptive-by-grace sonship. The verse establishes the theological basis for the Tewahedo doctrine of adoptive theosis.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.17 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'And when He had said this, He breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost' Cyril treats as a Trinitarian-pneumatological text of extraordinary density. The breathing (enephysēsen — the same verb as in Gen 2:7 LXX, where God breathes life into Adam) Cyril reads as the deliberate new-creation parallel: the Risen Christ inaugurates the eschatological new creation by breathing the Spirit into the new humanity. The 'Receive ye the Holy Ghost' (labete Pneuma Hagion) Cyril carefully distinguishes from Pentecost: this is the Spirit-gift FOR the apostolic commission (immediately followed by 'Whose soever sins ye remit'), Pentecost is the Spirit-gift for universal indwelling. Both are real; both are sourced in Christ. The Tewahedo holy-orders prayer at episcopal consecration echoes this verse explicitly.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.22 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed' Cyril takes as the dominical pin for faith-without-direct-evidence as the normative Christian condition. The Risen Christ does NOT rebuke Thomas's prior demand for evidence (the wounds are shown, the touch is offered); but He does proleptically commend the future generations whose faith will rest on apostolic testimony rather than direct sensory verification. The 'blessed' (makarioi) Cyril reads as ranking apostolic-testimony-based faith on the same scale as direct-sight faith — perhaps even higher, since it operates with less crutch. This grounds the entire Tewahedo catechetical-apologetic tradition that proclaims the Gospel as worthy of faith based on apostolic testimony.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.29 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: The threefold question — 'Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these?' — Cyril reads as the deliberate counterpart to Peter's threefold denial. Christ's repetition is restorative, not accusatory: each affirmation of love undoes one denial. 'More than these' (pleon toutōn) Cyril reads as referring to the other disciples (Peter had boasted in 13:37 that he would die for Christ even if all others fell away — Christ now tests the boast). The Greek verbal play (agapē / phileō) Cyril notes but treats with characteristic restraint: both verbs in John often function as synonyms; the deeper distinction is in the questioning-and-answering pattern itself, not in word-choice subtleties.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.15 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Feed my sheep' (boske ta probata mou) — the third and culminating commission to Peter — Cyril takes as the dominical institution of the pastoral office. The shift from 'lambs' (arnia, in v. 15) to 'sheep' (probata, in v. 17) Cyril reads as moving from the inexperienced new converts to the mature flock — the entire spectrum of pastoral responsibility is committed to Peter and through him to every subsequent pastor. The repetition Cyril sees as marking the deliberate sacramental-commissioning weight: this is not casual exhortation but solemn appointment. The Tewahedo ordination of bishops and priests preserves this verse's institutional weight in its consecration prayers.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.17 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.summary: 1 Enoch opens with a programmatic blessing 'which Enoch blessed the elect and righteous, who will be living in the day of tribulation, when all the wicked and godless are to be removed' (Charles 1912 trans.). The opening immediately establishes the book's apocalyptic-eschatological orientation: it is written for the persecuted righteous of a future tribulation, not as historical narrative but as prophetic vision. The Tewahedo canonical reception locates this opening alongside the Pentateuchal openings as setting the entire revelatory horizon — the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok is read liturgically in Tewahedo Lenten cycles precisely for this eschatological orientation.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 1:1-3, trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (Oxford: Clarendon, 1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Behold, He cometh with ten thousands of His saints to execute judgment upon all, and to destroy all the ungodly' is the verse the New Testament Jude 1:14-15 quotes VERBATIM, attributing it to 'Enoch, the seventh from Adam'. Jude's canonical-NT quotation of 1 Enoch as inspired prophecy is the strongest textual basis for the Tewahedo canon's reception of 1 Enoch as Scripture — if Jude treats 1 Enoch as prophetic Word, the Tewahedo argues, the rest of the Church should at least not deny what an apostle affirmed. This verse is therefore THE textual bridge between 1 Enoch and the canonical New Testament.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 1:9, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Jude 1:14-15 quoting this verse verbatim.

entries.summary: 'It came to pass when the children of men had multiplied that in those days were born unto them beautiful and comely daughters. And the angels, the children of the heaven, saw and lusted after them' — the foundational Watcher narrative that expands Genesis 6:1-4. Two hundred angels under Semjâzâ descend on Mount Hermon and bind themselves by oath to take human wives, knowing the act is forbidden. The Tewahedo reading takes this not as mythological folklore but as actual cosmic-historical rebellion: the disordering of the angelic order is the proximate cause of the disordering of the human order that necessitates the Flood. This is the Tewahedo canonical anchor that distinguishes its angelology from those of other Christian traditions.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 6:1-2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Tewahedo canonical text (Mäṣḥafä Hēnok).

entries.summary: 'And they were in all two hundred; who descended in the days of Jared on the summit of Mount Hermon' — the precise location and numbering of the Watchers' descent. Mount Hermon in northern Israel (the headwaters of the Jordan) becomes for the Tewahedo tradition the geographical inverse of Mount Sinai: Sinai is where God descends to give the Law; Hermon is where the rebellious angels descend to disorder creation. The Mäṣḥafä Hēnok dating in the days of Jared (Enoch's father) places the rebellion seven generations after Adam — the moral entropy of the post-fall world accelerating until Noah.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 6:6, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And they became pregnant, and they bare great giants, whose height was three thousand ells' — the Nephilim of Genesis 6:4 here named explicitly as the half-angelic offspring of the Watchers' union with human women. The 'three thousand ells' (vastly hyperbolic — Charles notes the Greek tradition has lower numbers) signals the disordered scale of the offspring: not merely large humans but a different ontological category, neither fully angelic nor fully human. The Tewahedo theological reading takes this as the prototype of every subsequent demonic infestation: the half-creatures that issue from forbidden union belong to no created order and find their proper place only in destruction.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 7:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'Azâzêl taught men to make swords, and knives, and shields, and breastplates' — the Watchers' second crime: teaching humans forbidden technologies that enable violence and seduction. The catalog continues with metallurgy, cosmetics, sorcery, astrology, weather magic, root-cutting, and astronomical secrets. The Tewahedo reading takes this as the prototype of every subsequent technology-corrupted-by-fallen-knowledge: the technologies themselves are not evil, but their introduction by rebel angels (rather than by the proper covenantal tradition) makes them weapons of disorder rather than tools of stewardship. This is the textual root of the Tewahedo monastic ascetic suspicion of certain technological luxuries.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 8:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: God's command to the archangel Raphael — 'Bind Azâzêl hand and foot, and cast him into the darkness... and cover him with darkness, and let him abide there forever' — establishes the cosmic-judicial pattern for the punishment of rebellious angels. Azâzêl is bound (not destroyed) and confined to the darkness 'till the day of the great judgment' (10:6). This is the Tewahedo theological warrant for the doctrine of pre-final-judgment angelic imprisonment (cf. 2 Pet 2:4 'God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment'). The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors the archangel Raphael on the 3rd of Pagumē with explicit cross-reference to this binding.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 10:4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. 2 Pet 2:4 + Jude 1:6.

entries.summary: Enoch's ascent vision begins: 'I was borne aloft in the clouds, and they raised me upward... and the winds in the vision made me fly and lifted me upward.' This is the foundational Jewish-apocalyptic throne-vision pattern that Ezekiel's chariot, Daniel's Ancient of Days, and Revelation's heavenly throne room all develop. Enoch's vision precedes the prophetic and apocalyptic literature it patterns. The Tewahedo liturgical tradition draws explicit cross-reference between Enoch's ascent and the eucharistic anaphora's heavenly-court invocations: the worshipper at the altar is ushered into the same throne-room Enoch beheld.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 14:8-9, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I beheld a lofty throne: its appearance was as crystal, and the wheels thereof as the shining sun, and there was the vision of cherubim. And from underneath the throne came streams of flaming fire so that I could not look thereon' — the central throne-vision of 1 Enoch's first half. The throne with wheels, crystal appearance, cherubim, and streaming fire combines Ezekiel 1's chariot, Daniel 7's Ancient of Days throne, and the Sinai theophany. Enoch's vision becomes the canonical Tewahedo template for every subsequent throne-vision in Christian apocalyptic literature, and the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok's liturgical reading on the Feast of the Transfiguration explicitly connects Enoch's beholding with Peter, James, and John's beholding on Tabor.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 14:18-22, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: The Most High addresses Enoch directly: 'Fear not, Enoch, thou righteous man and scribe of righteousness: approach hither and hear my voice.' This is the dominical commissioning of Enoch as 'the scribe of righteousness' — the title that becomes Enoch's canonical Tewahedo designation. The address establishes Enoch as the prototype of the prophetic scribe: not an autonomous voice but an inspired recorder, and not a recorder of human history but of divine self-revelation. The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors Enoch on the 27th of Hidar specifically as scribe-of-righteousness, with this verse appointed for liturgical reading.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 15:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: Enoch's vision of Sheol describes four 'hollow places' for the dead awaiting judgment, distinguished by moral status. 'There I saw the spirits of the children of men dead' — including a special place where Abel's soul cries out for vengeance against Cain. This text is one of the most developed pre-Christian Jewish accounts of the intermediate state of the dead, prefiguring the Lukan rich-man-and-Lazarus distinction (Lk 16:19-31). The Tewahedo eschatological tradition draws explicit cross-reference: the intermediate state is real (souls preserve their identity and moral status between bodily death and final resurrection), differentiated (the righteous and wicked are separated), and provisional (awaiting the final judgment).
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 22:5-9, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'The second vision which he saw, the vision of wisdom — which Enoch the son of Jared, the son of Mahalalel...' opens the Book of Parables, the most theologically dense section of 1 Enoch. Where the Watchers material is mythological-historical, the Parables are visionary-eschatological, centering on the figure of the Son of Man as cosmic judge. The opening dating in 'the days of Jared' (consistent with 6:6) anchors the Parables historically while the visionary content opens onto the eschaton. The Tewahedo reception of the Parables as canonical Scripture gives the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok its distinctive Christological-eschatological weight.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 37:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'When the congregation of the righteous shall appear, and sinners shall be judged for their sins, and shall be driven from the face of the earth' opens the eschatological program of the Parables: the visible appearing of the elect community + the judgment + the removal of the wicked. The 'congregation of the righteous' (the Ethiopian-Geez term ṣabā ṣādeqān) becomes for Tewahedo ecclesiology a key term for the eschatological Church gathered for the final judgment. The verse establishes that judgment is not destruction-for-its-own-sake but vindication-of-the-righteous: the wicked are removed precisely to clear the earth for the elect's full inheritance.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 38:1-2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And there I saw One who had a head of days, and His head was white like wool, and with Him was another being whose countenance had the appearance of a man' — the foundational Son of Man vision. The 'head of days' clearly echoes Daniel 7:9 'Ancient of Days'; the 'another being whose countenance had the appearance of a man' echoes Daniel 7:13 'one like the Son of Man'. 1 Enoch develops the Danielic figure into a sustained pre-Christian Jewish messianic-cosmic-judge figure. The New Testament's use of 'Son of Man' as Christ's self-designation (84 times in the Synoptics + 13 in John) presupposes this Enochic development; the Tewahedo reception of the Parables as canonical Scripture preserves the inter-textual continuity that other Christian canons obscure by omitting 1 Enoch.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 46:1-3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Dan 7:9-14 + the NT 'Son of Man' Christology.

entries.summary: The angel-interpreter tells Enoch about the Son of Man: 'This is the Son of Man who hath righteousness, with whom dwelleth righteousness, and who revealeth all the treasures of that which is hidden... because the Lord of Spirits hath chosen him' — establishing the pre-existent, divinely-elected character of the Son of Man. He IS righteousness (not merely possesses it), He reveals hidden things (the apocalyptic-revelatory role), and He is chosen by the Lord of Spirits (the Enochic title for God). This is the most developed pre-Christian Jewish text on the heavenly messianic-Son-of-Man figure; Tewahedo Christology reads it as proto-Christological prophecy that the New Testament's Son-of-Man Christology fulfills.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 46:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'At that hour that Son of Man was named in the presence of the Lord of Spirits, and His name before the Head of Days' — the eternal naming of the Son of Man before God. This is one of the strongest pre-existence texts in 1 Enoch: the Son of Man is NAMED (constituted as the named person) before the Lord of Spirits, in a moment that precedes the creation events (48:3 'Yea, before the sun and the signs were created, before the stars of the heaven were made'). Tewahedo Christology reads this as pre-Christian Jewish prophetic anticipation of the eternal generation of the Son — a verse no Western patristic tradition could engage with at this depth because Western Christianity lost the 1 Enoch text after the early centuries.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 48:2-3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'For this reason hath He been chosen and hidden before Him, before the creation of the world and for evermore' — the pre-existent Son of Man is described as 'hidden' (sambə'a) before God until the eschatological revealing. The hiddenness-followed-by-revealing pattern Tewahedo reads as the proto-form of the New Testament's mystery-revealed pattern (cf. Col 1:26, Eph 3:9): what was hidden in God before all ages is now revealed in Christ. The Mäṣḥafä Hēnok preserves what other canons lose: the explicit pre-Christian Jewish development of the hidden-then-revealed cosmic Son of Man.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 48:6, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in those days shall the earth also give back that which has been entrusted to it, and Sheol also shall give back that which it has received, and hell shall give back that which it owes' — the resurrection of the dead in Enochic apocalyptic. The three-way restitution (earth gives back bodies; Sheol gives back righteous spirits; hell gives back the wicked) anticipates the New Testament resurrection accounts. The Tewahedo eschatological tradition draws explicit cross-reference: 1 Enoch's resurrection vision pre-dates the Pharisaic-Pauline development and provides the canonical Jewish textual basis for the doctrine. The Mäṣḥafä Hēnok is read liturgically in Tewahedo funeral rites for precisely this verse's hope.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 51:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And one portion of them shall look on the other, and they shall be terrified, and they shall be downcast of countenance, and pain shall seize them, when they see that Son of Man sitting on the throne of his glory' — the eschatological enthronement of the Son of Man with the kings of the earth before him in judgment. The verse provides the canonical Jewish basis for Matthew 25:31 ('When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory'). Tewahedo Christology preserves this inter-textual continuity: Matthew's enthroned Son of Man is the same as 1 Enoch's; the Gospels presuppose the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok's developed figure.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 62:5, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Mt 25:31.

entries.summary: 'Thou art the Son of Man who art born unto righteousness, and righteousness abides over thee, and the righteousness of the Head of Days forsakes thee not' — the controversial closing of the Parables where Enoch himself is identified WITH the Son of Man. Charles' translation preserves this identification; some scholars argue for an alternative reading. The Tewahedo reception holds the text as it stands: Enoch's eschatological exaltation to the role of Son of Man does NOT compete with later Christological identification but anticipates it — Enoch is a TYPE of the Son of Man whose fullness is Christ. This typological reading is preserved in the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok's catechetical use within the Tewahedo monastic tradition.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 71:14, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'The book of the courses of the luminaries of the heaven, the relations of each, according to their classes, their dominion and their seasons, according to their names and places of origin, and according to their months' opens the Astronomical Book — the oldest section of 1 Enoch (dated by Charles to ~3rd century BC). The book establishes a 364-day solar calendar that the Tewahedo liturgical tradition partly preserves alongside the lunar calendar of the rest of Christianity. The verse establishes Enoch's astronomical authority as derived from angelic instruction (Uriel reveals the celestial mechanics to Enoch), placing astronomy within the legitimate prophetic-revelatory tradition rather than the forbidden Watcher-teaching of 8:1.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 72:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: The angels who escort Enoch tell him: 'Declare everything to thy son Methuselah, and show to all thy children that no flesh is righteous in the sight of the Lord, for He is their Creator' — the foundational anthropological pessimism that anticipates Pauline 'all have sinned' (Rom 3:23). The Tewahedo reading connects this verse to the Romans passage explicitly: the apostolic doctrine of universal sinfulness has its Jewish-canonical basis in the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok, not introduced by Paul ex nihilo but inherited from the prophetic-apocalyptic tradition. The pessimism is grounded ontologically ('for He is their Creator' — only the Creator is finally righteous) rather than merely empirically.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 81:5, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Rom 3:23.

entries.summary: 'I saw in a vision how the heaven collapsed and was borne off and fell to the earth' opens the first Dream Vision — Enoch's vision of the Flood as cosmic-symbolic event. The collapse of heaven (the firmament un-stoppered) and its fall onto earth pictures the de-creative reversal of the Genesis 1 separation. This visionary mode of recording the Flood prefigures the apocalyptic visionary mode of Daniel and Revelation: history is shown to the prophet in symbolic-cosmic dream form, not merely narrated. The Tewahedo Synaxarium's Noah liturgy on 10 Magabit explicitly includes Enochic dream-vision elements alongside the Genesis narrative.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 83:3-5, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: The Animal Apocalypse opens with Enoch's vision of human history under the symbolism of animals: 'I saw in my vision how a bull came forth from the earth, and that bull was white' — Adam as the white bull. The entire patriarchal-Mosaic-monarchic-exilic-Hasmonean history is then narrated in animal allegory (humans as animals, angels as men, the elect as sheep, the wicked as wolves and other predators). This is the most extensive surviving pre-Christian Jewish historical-prophetic allegory; its inclusion in the Tewahedo canon gives the Ethiopian Christian historical imagination a unique typological grammar that Western Christianity (lacking the text) cannot access.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 85:1-3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I saw till that horns grew upon those lambs, and the ravens cast down their horns; and I saw till there sprouted a great horn of one of those sheep' — the rise of Judas Maccabeus as the 'great horn' in the Animal Apocalypse's symbolic history. Charles dates the composition of this section to the Maccabean revolt (~165 BC), making it nearly-contemporary historical commentary in apocalyptic form. The verse establishes the Animal Apocalypse's prophetic-now character: it reads contemporary events as the unfolding of the cosmic drama. The Tewahedo reception preserves this prophetic-historical reading mode, applied throughout the medieval period to Ethiopian historical events.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 90:9, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I saw that a white bull was born, with large horns, and all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the air feared him and made petition to him all the time' — the climactic appearance of the messianic White Bull at the end of the Animal Apocalypse. The white bull echoes Adam (85:3 — Adam was the original white bull); the Messiah is therefore the eschatological New Adam, restoring the original Adamic kingship over creation. All beasts and birds fearing him + making petition to him is the universal recognition of his cosmic authority. The Tewahedo Christological reading takes this as proto-Christological prophecy fulfilled in Christ as the Last Adam (1 Cor 15:45) and the Lamb (Rev) who receives universal worship.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 90:37, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. 1 Cor 15:45 + Rev 5:13.
