This grounds the Tewahedo conviction that present demonic affliction operates through the spirits of the Watchers' DEAD offspring (Jub 10), not through the bound Watchers themselves.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 5:6 (Watchers + Flood judgment), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the day of the great judgment there shall be a great chastisement from before the Lord upon the earth, and he shall destroy them all and shall hate them as they have hated their lives, and from before His face shall pass away all flesh.' The flood is not the final judgment — it is a TYPE of the great judgment to come. **Tewahedo eschatological reading**: the doubled-judgment pattern (historic flood + eschatological consummation) is central to Tewahedo apocalyptic preaching; the homiletic application is that present evil is bounded by both witnesses.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 5:10 (Watchers + Flood judgment), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And He made for all His works a new and righteous nature, so that they should not sin in their whole nature for ever, but should be all righteous each in his kind always.' Post-flood creation receives a renewed-nature gift — sin is bounded in the new dispensation rather than merely judged in the old. **Tewahedo reading**: this 'new nature' is read as a partial restoration anticipating the Christological full restoration (2 Cor 5:17); the post-flood world is already under grace, not merely under judgment.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 5:12 (Watchers + Flood judgment), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the judgment of all is ordained and written on the heavenly tablets in righteousness — even (the judgment of) all who depart from the path which is ordained for them to walk in; and if they walk not therein, judgment is written down for every creature and for every kind.' **Tewahedo heavenly-tablets motif**: the divine judgment is pre-inscribed on heavenly tablets — a recurring Jubilees device that grounds Tewahedo theological certainty (the divine order is fixed, knowable, and unalterable). The same motif undergirds the Tewahedo reverence for written canonical text as participating in the heavenly archetype.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 5:13 (Watchers + Flood judgment), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And as for the children of Israel, it has been written and ordained: If they turn to Him in righteousness, He will forgive all their transgressions and pardon all their sins.' This verse, set in the Watchers-judgment context, establishes the principle that GENUINE REPENTANCE evokes mercy even against the backdrop of cosmic-scale judgment. **Tewahedo soteriology anchor**: the Tewahedo penitential tradition (Səb'atu Sǝfa'e — seven appointed days of fasting and confession) draws this verse as canonical warrant that no sin, however cosmic in implication, lies beyond repentance for those who turn.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 5:17 (Watchers + Flood judgment), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'It is written and ordained that He will show mercy to all who turn from all their guilt once each year.' The atonement is structured as ANNUAL — a yearly turning-point coincides with the Day of Atonement (Lev 16). **Tewahedo liturgical anchor**: the Tewahedo Astereyo (Day of Atonement, observed on the 10th of the seventh month) draws Jubilees 5:17-18 as canonical warrant — the Watcher-judgment context grounds the Day's solemnity as a participation in the cosmic-judgment economy, not merely a Mosaic cultic prescription.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 5:18 (Watchers + Flood judgment), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he made atonement for the land, and took a kid and made atonement by its blood for all the sins of the earth; for everything that had been on it had been destroyed, save those that were in the ark with Noah.' Noah's post-flood sacrifice is read as ATONEMENT FOR THE LAND ITSELF — not merely thanksgiving but cosmic cleansing. **Tewahedo reading**: the Tewahedo Səray Mənfäsawit (priestly aspersion) liturgies treat the land as a creature requiring atonement; Jubilees 6:2 is the canonical antecedent for this priestly cosmology.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 6:2 (Noahide covenant + Calendar), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the Lord smelt the goodly savour, and He made a covenant with him that there should not be any more a flood to destroy the earth.' The covenant is OCCASIONED by Noah's sacrifice — divine response to priestly action, not mere unilateral declaration. **Tewahedo reading** preserves the synergistic structure: God's covenant is real divine commitment but is responsively bound up with creaturely worship. The Tewahedo Qǝddase (Divine Liturgy) reads the post-Communion peace as participation in this Noahide-covenant pattern of God-responding-to-priestly-offering.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 6:4 (Noahide covenant + Calendar), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'But flesh, with the life thereof, with the blood, ye shall not eat; for the life of all flesh is in the blood, lest your blood of your lives be required.' Pre-Mosaic prohibition of blood consumption — universal Noahide ethics. **Tewahedo dietary anchor**: the Tewahedo Church's strict and ongoing observance of blood-abstention (animals must be drained at slaughter; blood-containing foods are formally proscribed) appeals directly to Jubilees 6:7 — pre-Mosaic, pre-Sinaitic, and therefore binding on all the children of Noah, not merely the children of Abraham. This is a sharp Tewahedo distinctive against Western Christian practice.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 6:7 (Noahide covenant + Calendar), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And ye shall make a covenant with the children of Israel for ever, in this month, upon the mountain with an oath, and ye shall sprinkle blood upon them because of all the words of the covenant which the Lord made with them for ever.' The blood-pact pattern is THE pattern of all divine-human covenanting — instituted with Noah, renewed at Sinai, fulfilled in Christ. **Tewahedo Christological reading**: the blood sprinkled on the Noahide remnant prefigures the Eucharistic blood of the new covenant; Tewahedo Eucharistic theology reads Jubilees 6:10 as the canonical antecedent that secures the universal scope of the Atonement.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 6:10 (Noahide covenant + Calendar), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And do thou command the children of Israel to observe this festival in all their generations for a commandment unto them: one day in the year in this month they shall celebrate the festival.' The annual atonement structure is COMMANDED, not optional — binding on the children of Israel as the priestly portion of all the children of Noah. **Tewahedo reading**: the Tewahedo Astereyo is observed with maximal seriousness (full fast, communal confession, priestly atonement liturgy) precisely because Jubilees 6:14 establishes it as a perpetual Noahide-Mosaic continuity, not a Mosaic-only cultic prescription.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 6:14 (Noahide covenant + Calendar), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'For this reason it is ordained and written on the heavenly tablets, that they should celebrate the feast of weeks in this month once a year, to renew the covenant every year.' **Tewahedo Pentecost anchor**: the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot / Pentecost) is canonically pre-Mosaic — established with Noah, not with Moses — and is the perpetual annual covenant-renewal feast. Tewahedo Pärräqlēṭos (Pentecost) is celebrated as the fulfilment of this Noahide-pattern feast in the descent of the Holy Spirit: the same annual covenant-renewal but now in the Spirit.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 6:17 (Noahide covenant + Calendar), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'On the first of the first month, and on the first of the fourth month, and on the first of the seventh month, and on the first of the tenth month — these are the days of memorial and the days of the seasons in the four divisions of the year; they are written and ordained as a testimony for ever.' Four quarterly memorial days fix the cardinal divisions of the year. **Tewahedo liturgical-calendar anchor**: the Tewahedo computus (Bāḥrä Ḥasab) places its four major fixed-date observances at structural cardinal points that descend from Jubilees 6:23 — the cosmos itself is liturgically marked, not just the priestly cycle.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 6:23 (Noahide covenant + Calendar), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'For there will be those who will assuredly make observations of the moon — how (it) disturbs the seasons and comes in from year to year ten days too soon.' The solar 364-day calendar is DEFENDED against lunar reckoning — those who follow the moon will drift ten days per year. **Tewahedo Bāḥrä Ḥasab defense**: the Tewahedo computus is a sophisticated solar-luni-harmonisation that explicitly retains a 364-day solar skeleton with computational corrections for the lunar cycle; Jubilees 6:35 is read as canonical warrant that the solar reckoning is primary and the lunar is subordinate.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 6:35 (Noahide covenant + Calendar), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And all the children of Israel will forget and will not find the path of the years, and will forget the new moons, and seasons, and Sabbaths, and they will go wrong as to all the order of the years.' **Tewahedo preservation anchor**: Jubilees 6:38 prophesies calendrical apostasy — and the Tewahedo Church reads its OWN computational preservation of the Bāḥrä Ḥasab through fifteen centuries as canonical-prophetic vindication. Tewahedo theological self-understanding is that the Ethiopian Church alone has not 'gone wrong as to all the order of the years.'
entries.attribution: Jubilees 6:38 (Noahide covenant + Calendar), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the seventh week in the first year thereof, in this jubilee, Noah planted vines on the mountain on which the ark had rested, named Lubar, one of the Ararat Mountains, and they produced fruit in the fourth year, and he guarded their fruit, and gathered it in this year in the seventh month.' Noah as first vintner — the post-flood new order includes WINE, a creaturely good destined for Eucharistic transposition. **Tewahedo reading**: Tewahedo eucharistic practice retains the Noahic-creaturely register through use of locally-produced wine; the vine's appearance in Jub 7:1 grounds the Tewahedo treatment of viticulture as part of the priestly economy.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 7:1 (Noah's commandments), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Canaan saw the nakedness of his father Ham, and he went out and told his two brethren who were without.' Canaan, not Ham himself, is the verse's actor — Jubilees clarifies the narrative ambiguity of Gen 9:22. **Tewahedo Hamitic-identity anchor (paired with Jub 9:13)**: the curse falls on Canaan (a specific bloodline) not on Ham (the broader descent). The Tewahedo reading is explicit: there is NO racial curse on the Hamitic descendants generally; the curse is bounded, juridical, and limited to Canaan's line. This is a sharp Tewahedo distinctive against the Western 'curse of Ham' racialisation.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 7:13 (Noah's commandments), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the twenty-eighth jubilee Noah began to enjoin upon his sons' sons the ordinances and commandments, and all the judgments that he knew, and he exhorted his sons to observe righteousness.' Noah teaches a comprehensive Noahide law to his grandchildren. **Tewahedo pre-Mosaic ethics anchor**: the Noahide commandments (enumerated 7:20-25 in Jubilees) are pre-Sinaitic universal natural law; Tewahedo missiology reads these as the substrate of pagan-religious convergence with biblical revelation, against which the Mosaic and Christic revelations are specifications, not negations.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 7:20 (Noah's commandments), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'For owing to these three things came the flood upon the earth, namely, owing to the fornication wherein the Watchers against the law of their ordinances went a whoring after the daughters of men, and took themselves wives of all which they chose; and they made the beginning of uncleanness.' The flood's cause is identified as a TRINITY of sins — fornication, uncleanness, and (by 7:24) bloodshed. **Tewahedo moral-theology anchor**: the Tewahedo confessional manual treats these three as the cardinal pre-flood sins recapitulated in every personal pre-baptismal confession; the flood-Watchers narrative becomes catechetical, not merely historical.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 7:23 (Noah's commandments), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'For I see, and behold the demons have begun (their) seductions against you and against your children — and now I fear on your behalf, that after my death ye will shed the blood of men upon the earth, and that ye, too, will be destroyed from the face of the earth.' Noah PROPHETICALLY warns of demonic seduction to come — the link between the bound Watchers' offspring (giants who died in the flood, now disembodied) and ongoing demonic harassment is established. **Tewahedo demonology bridge**: this verse links the Watchers-judgment narrative (Jub 5) with the Mastema-permission narrative (Jub 10) — the demons of present harassment are the disembodied spirits of pre-flood giants, bounded by Mastema's permission.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 7:27 (Noah's commandments), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And ye also, my children, observe the commandments of your father Enoch, and eat no blood, and observe the path of righteousness.' Noah cites his great-grandfather ENOCH as a normative source for his sons — Enoch is preached as PRE-MOSAIC patristic authority. **Tewahedo inter-canonical witness**: Jubilees and 1 Enoch mutually authorise each other within the Tewahedo canon — Jubilees cites Enoch (here and at 21:10), and 1 Enoch grounds the cosmology Jubilees presupposes. This mutual citation is unique to the Tewahedo/Eritrean Orthodox biblical structure.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 7:34 (Noah's commandments), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'For thus Enoch, the father of your father, commanded Methuselah, his son, and Methuselah his son Lamech, and Lamech commanded me all the things which his fathers commanded him.' Noah preserves a CHAIN OF TRANSMISSION — Enoch → Methuselah → Lamech → Noah — for the pre-Mosaic priestly halakhah. **Tewahedo apostolic-succession antecedent**: the chain-of-transmission motif (commandment passed from father to son across the generations) is a structural Tewahedo motif applied to the apostolic succession of the priesthood — bishops trace authority through unbroken succession that mirrors the Enoch-to-Noah pattern.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 7:39 (Noah's commandments), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'In the twenty-ninth jubilee, in the first week, in the beginning thereof, Arpachshad took to himself a wife and her name was Rasu'eja, the daughter of Susan, the daughter of Elam, and she bare him a son in the third year in this week, and he called his name Kainam.' Post-flood genealogical reconstruction — Arpachshad's son Kainam (Cainan) is included, matching the Septuagint and Tewahedo Bible against the Masoretic. **Tewahedo textual anchor**: the inclusion of Cainan between Arpachshad and Shelah (also Lk 3:36) is preserved in Jubilees, the LXX, and the Tewahedo Bible — a triple canonical witness against the Masoretic abridgement.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 8:1 (Geographic division), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he took to himself a wife and her name was Melka, the daughter of Madai, the son of Japheth, and in the fourth year he begat a son, and called his name Shelah, for, he said: Truly I have been sent.' Shelah's name etymologised as 'sent' — naming is theologically charged. **Tewahedo onomastic anchor**: Tewahedo baptismal-naming tradition draws on the Jubilees pattern of theologically-significant names assigned at birth; the practice of giving a Christian (often patristic or Marian) name at baptism participates in this Jubilees onomastic register.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 8:12 (Geographic division), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Noah rejoiced that this portion came forth for Shem and for his sons, and he remembered all that he had spoken with his mouth in prophecy; for he had said: "Blessed be the Lord God of Shem, and may the Lord dwell in the dwelling of Shem."' The Shem-blessing of Gen 9:26 is re-read as PROPHETIC ELECTION of Shem's line for divine indwelling — culminating in Christ's incarnation in the Shemitic line. **Tewahedo Christological reading**: the Shem-blessing is the FIRST Christological prophecy — divine indwelling promised generations before Abraham.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 8:18 (Geographic division), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he knew that a blessed portion and a blessing had come to Shem and his sons unto the generations for ever — the whole land of Eden, and the whole land of the Red Sea, and the whole land of the East, and India, and on the Red Sea and the mountains thereof, and all the land of Bashan.' Shem's portion is enumerated geographically — and INCLUDES the Red Sea region (i.e., the Horn of Africa coast). **Tewahedo geographic-providence anchor**: the Tewahedo reading identifies its own homeland as falling within the Shemitic portion — the Ethiopian highlands lie astride the Red Sea coast — and reads this as canonical warrant for the divine-indwelling-of-Shem prophecy reaching Ethiopia.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 8:21 (Geographic division), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And for Ham came forth the second portion, beyond the Gihon towards the south to the right of the Garden, and it extends towards the south and it extends to all the mountains of fire, and it extends towards the west to the sea of Atel and it extends towards the west till it reaches the sea of Mauq.' Ham's portion is described as fertile and SUBSTANTIAL — covering Africa southward. **Tewahedo Hamitic-identity anchor (paired with Jub 9:13 and 7:13)**: Ham's portion is DIVINELY ALLOTTED, not cursed. The Tewahedo reading celebrates Ham's African inheritance as canonical inheritance, not racial curse; the Gihon (read by Jubilees as the Blue Nile / Nile) flows through Ham's portion as divine watering of the land.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 8:25 (Geographic division), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And there came forth on the writing of Shem for Elam and his sons, the land of Elam from the heights of Tina to the East, until the borders of Assyria, the great river Tigris, and the borders of Media, and the inheritance of Lud.' The sub-allotment of Shem's portion to Elam preserves the geographical-juridical precision of the patriarchal division. **Tewahedo legal-anthropology anchor**: the Jubilees pattern of MAP-MAKING by divine sortition undergirds Tewahedo land-tenure theology — the rist (hereditary land right) system reads land-as-divine-portion through the Jubilees prism, against any conquest-based legitimation.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 9:2 (Subdivisions), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And for Cush came forth the second portion beyond the Gihon towards the east of the Red Sea and till the borders of India.' **Tewahedo Cushitic self-identification anchor**: the Tewahedo Church reads Cush's portion as canonically including Ethiopia — Cush, son of Ham, son of Noah, is the eponymous ancestor of the Cushitic peoples whose inheritance is here enumerated. This verse, alongside the Queen of Sheba narrative (1 Kings 10) and Acts 8 (the Ethiopian eunuch), grounds the canonical-genealogical anchor of Ethiopian Christianity.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 9:5 (Subdivisions), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And thus the sons of Noah divided unto their sons in the presence of Noah their father, and he bound them all by an oath, imprecating a curse on every one that sought to seize the portion which had not fallen (to him) by his lot.' The lot-casting is sealed with an OATH AND CURSE against future conquest. **Tewahedo anti-conquest-theology anchor**: the Tewahedo reading deploys Jubilees 9:14 as canonical warrant against colonial seizure — the inviolability of national-tribal inheritance is grounded in pre-Mosaic divine ordinance, not merely in modern political theory.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 9:14 (Subdivisions), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And they all said, "So be it; so be it" for themselves and their sons for ever throughout their generations till the day of judgment, on which the Lord God shall judge them with a sword and with fire, for all the unclean wickedness of their errors, wherewith they have filled the earth with transgression and uncleanness and fornication and sin.' The Noahide oath is binding UNTIL THE DAY OF JUDGMENT — eschatological enforcement of geographic inheritance. **Tewahedo eschatology anchor**: the Tewahedo apocalyptic preaching reads conquest and dispossession as sins to be answered at the great judgment by the same fire-and-sword pattern that ended the pre-flood violence.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 9:15 (Subdivisions), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the third week of this jubilee the unclean demons began to lead astray the children of the sons of Noah; and to make to err and destroy them.' The post-flood era opens with DEMONIC HARASSMENT — the disembodied spirits of the pre-flood giants now afflict humanity. **Tewahedo demonology anchor**: the Tewahedo understanding of demonic affliction operates through this Jubilees-Enochic frame: present demonic activity is conducted by the spirits of the Watchers' dead offspring (not the bound Watchers themselves), and is bounded by divine permission (Jub 10:8-9).
entries.attribution: Jubilees 10:1 (Demons + Mastema + Babel), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Noah prayed before the Lord his God, and said, "God of the spirits of all flesh, who hast shown mercy unto me and hast saved me and my sons from the waters of the flood, and hast not caused me to perish as Thou didst the sons of perdition; for Thy grace has been great towards me, and great has been Thy mercy to my soul."' Noah PRAYS — the pattern of priestly intercession against demonic affliction is established. **Tewahedo intercessory-prayer anchor**: the Tewahedo daily prayer cycle (Sǝbḥata Foṣǝlt and related offices) operates within this Noahide-priestly pattern — the patriarch's intercession secures the protection of his descendants.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 10:3 (Demons + Mastema + Babel), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the Lord our God bade us to bind all.' God's first response to Noah's prayer is TOTAL binding — every demon is to be confined. **Tewahedo theological anchor**: the divine intention is full restraint of evil; the partial loosening (10:8-9 — Mastema's petition granting 1/10) is a CONCESSION to fallen creaturely freedom, not an original-divine plan. Tewahedo theodicy reads this as the canonical structure of God-permits-bounded-evil-for-greater-good — evil is never original or necessary.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 10:7 (Demons + Mastema + Babel), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And He said: "Let the tenth part of them remain before him, and let nine parts descend into the place of condemnation."' God grants Mastema's petition partially — 1/10 of the demons remain free to harass humanity, 9/10 are bound. **Tewahedo numerical-bounded-evil anchor**: this 10%-bound, 90%-restrained ratio is preserved in Tewahedo demonological teaching as the divine bounding of cosmic evil — evil is NEVER unbounded, even when permitted; the tithe-pattern (1/10) signals that the demonic share is the inverse of the human tithe-offering.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 10:9 (Demons + Mastema + Babel), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And we explained to Noah all the medicines of their diseases, together with their seductions, how he might heal them with herbs of the earth.' The angels TEACH Noah a complete medical book — herbal remedies paired with demonological diagnoses. **Tewahedo medical-tradition anchor**: the Tewahedo traditional medical tradition (mädḫanit / herbal remedy plus the dǝbtära's prayer-and-ritual practice) reads Jubilees 10:11 as canonical warrant — physical herbs + spiritual diagnosis is the divinely-revealed mode of healing, originally taught to Noah by the angels.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 10:11 (Demons + Mastema + Babel), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Noah wrote down all things in a book as we instructed him concerning every kind of medicine. Thus the evil spirits were precluded from (hurting) the sons of Noah.' Noah WRITES the medical book — a written transmission of healing knowledge that is identified by Tewahedo tradition with the Mäṣḥafä Mädḫanit (Book of Medicine). **Tewahedo scribal-tradition anchor**: the writing-down of revealed knowledge by patriarchs (Enoch the scribe at Jub 4:23; Noah the medical scribe at 10:13; the heavenly tablets passim) establishes the priestly-scribal vocation as a divinely-instituted office, undergirding Tewahedo monastic scribal practice.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 10:13 (Demons + Mastema + Babel), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the thirty-third jubilee, in the first year in the second week, Peleg took to himself a wife, whose name was Lōmnā the daughter of Sina'ar, and she bare him a son in the fourth year of this week, and he called his name Reu; for he said: Behold the children of men have become evil through the wicked purpose of building for themselves a city and a tower in the land of Shinar.' The Tower-of-Babel narrative is introduced as a CORPORATE evil — the building of a CITY (not merely a tower) signals organised human autonomy against divine ordinance. **Tewahedo political-theology anchor**: the Tewahedo reading of the Tower as a city-state-building project grounds the canonical critique of imperial autonomy — the legitimate political form is the Noahide-allotted nation, not the post-Babel hegemonic city.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 10:18 (Demons + Mastema + Babel), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the Lord sent a mighty wind against the tower and overthrew it upon the earth, and behold it was between Asshur and Babylon in the land of Shinar, and they called its name "Overthrow."' The Tower is overthrown by WIND (rūaḥ / mänfäs) — the same divine wind/Spirit that hovered over Genesis 1:2 now reverses Babel. **Tewahedo Pneumatological anchor**: Acts 2 (Pentecost) reverses Babel's confusion through the SAME Spirit — the Tewahedo reading of the Spirit's action at Pentecost as the antitype of Jubilees 10:26 is sharper than in Western Christianity, drawing on the explicit Jubilees pneumatology that Western tradition lacks.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 10:26 (Demons + Mastema + Babel), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And they made for themselves molten images, and they worshipped each the idol the molten image which they had made for themselves, and they began to make graven images and unclean simulacra' — Jubilees traces the cascade of post-Babel apostasy through Serug's generation, presenting idolatry not as a single fall but as a slow societal drift. Tewahedo catechesis (Andəmta on Genesis 11) inherits this gradualist diagnosis: sin is taught, learned, and inherited within communities, so the antidote — Abram's break, then Sinai, then Christ's gathered ecclesia — likewise advances by community-formation, not isolated individual conversion.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 11:4 (Abraham cycle (11:4)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Serug grew up and dwelt in Ur of the Chaldees, near to the father of his wife's mother, and he worshipped idols' — Jubilees marks the precise generation in which the rot becomes nominal: Abram's great-grandfather Serug actively serves the idols of his in-laws. The Tewahedo Andəmta exegesis on Abram's election reads this verse as proof that elective grace stands against inherited line: God draws Abram from a pedigree of idolators, not from an unbroken righteous succession — a key anti-Pelagian and anti-genealogical-merit anchor in Tewahedo soteriology.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 11:8 (Abraham cycle (11:8)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the third week of that jubilee the unclean ravens came and devoured the seed which had been sown in the earth in order to destroy the earth' — Jubilees portrays the ravens as Mastema's instruments sent to ruin the agricultural blessing. Tewahedo readers see in the boy-Abram who drives away the ravens (11:19-21) the prototype of the priest who guards the offered seed; the Tewahedo blessing of the fields and the kahn (priestly) intercession against locust and crop-loss draw their canonical warrant from this passage. Abram is presented as priest-king before Mosaic ordination — anchoring the Tewahedo doctrine of universal pre-Mosaic priesthood from which the kǝhnät descends.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 11:18 (Abraham cycle (11:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'My father, what help or profit have we from those idols which thou dost worship and before which thou dost bow thyself? For there is no spirit in them, for they are dumb forms, and a misleading of the heart' — Abram's argument to Terah is preserved in Jubilees as a model of filial-yet-uncompromising witness. The Tewahedo monastic instruction tradition (Mäwasǝʾǝt) cites this verse as the pattern for confronting elders in error: respectful address ('my father') joined to plain doctrinal refutation. The Andəmta commentary frames it as the first canonical instance of a son catechizing his father — a permitted reversal where truth requires.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 12:4 (Abraham cycle (12:4)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'My son, hold thy peace, lest they slay thee' — Terah confesses privately to Abram that he too knows the gods are nothing but fears the community will kill them for saying so. Jubilees here exposes the social mechanism by which apostasy is enforced: not conviction but terror. Tewahedo persecution-memory (the Gragn Ahmed wars of the 1530s; martyrdoms under Italian fascism in 1936-37) reads this verse as the canonical warrant for distinguishing private faith from public witness, while still upholding the latter as the higher form — Abram refuses to be silenced (12:8-14).
entries.attribution: Jubilees 12:7 (Abraham cycle (12:7)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the night Abram arose and burned the house of the idols, and he burned all that was in the house, and no man knew it. And they arose in the night and sought to save their gods from the midst of the fire. And Haran hasted to save them, but the fire flamed over him, and he was burned in the fire, and he died in Ur of the Chaldees before Terah his father' — Jubilees attributes Haran's death (Gen 11:28) to a failed rescue of idols from Abram's iconoclasm. Tewahedo readings of the Gragn destruction of churches (1530s) and of contemporary church-burning in northern Ethiopia find canonical anchor here: those who serve images perish with them; the iconographic-but-not-idolatrous Tewahedo veneration is sharply distinguished from the literal-idol category Abram destroyed.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 12:12 (Abraham cycle (12:12)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'My God, my God, God Most High, Thou alone art my God, and Thee and Thy dominion have I chosen. And Thou hast created all things, and all things that are are the work of Thy hands. Deliver me from the hands of evil spirits who have dominion over the thoughts of men's hearts, and let them not lead me astray from Thee, my God' — Abram's first recorded prayer. The Tewahedo Andǝmta cites this as the canonical pattern for personal-devotional prayer: profession of monotheism + acknowledgement of creation + petition against demonic thought-influence. The structure parallels the Tewahedo daily Kidan zä-nägh (morning covenant) prayer: confession first, request second, with demonic-influence specifically named as the threat from which deliverance is sought.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 12:19 (Abraham cycle (12:19)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the Lord God said to me: open his mouth and his ears, that he may hear and speak with his mouth, with the language which has been revealed; for it had ceased from the mouths of all the children of men from the day of the overthrow of Babel' — the angel of presence is commanded to restore the pre-Babel Hebrew tongue to Abram. Jubilees frames Hebrew not as one human language among many but as the original Adamic tongue lost at Babel and divinely restored at the election of the covenant line. Tewahedo philology — which preserves Ge'ez as the liturgical-scriptural tongue of the Tewahedo-canonical 1 Enoch and Jubilees — reads this verse as canonical warrant for the dignity of sacred liturgical languages: Hebrew for Israel, Ge'ez for the Tewahedo, both as direct gifts of the angel of presence rather than mere developments.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 12:25 (Abraham cycle (12:25)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'Get thee up from this land, and from thy kindred and from the house of thy father unto a land which I will show thee, and I shall make thee a great and numerous nation' — Jubilees here records the call of Abram (paralleling Gen 12:1) as the climax of his prayer at 12:19 and his Hebrew-tongue restoration at 12:25. Abram's call thus comes AFTER his unaided monotheistic conversion (12:4) and his prayer for deliverance from demonic influence — the divine call ratifies and directs an already-converted soul rather than electing arbitrarily. Tewahedo monasticism reads this sequence as the canonical pattern for the call to monastic life: prior personal conversion + plain doctrine + petition + divine vocational confirmation, never the reverse.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 12:28 (Abraham cycle (12:28)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he built there an altar, and he offered thereon a burnt-offering to the Lord who had appeared unto him, and he called upon the name of the Lord' — at Bethel, prior to all Mosaic legislation, Abram constitutes the first patriarchal altar. The Tewahedo Liturgy of Abraham (Anaphora of the Patriarchs, used in periodic monastic-festal commemoration) draws its canonical warrant from this verse: legitimate altar precedes Mosaic priestly ordination by centuries, anchoring the Tewahedo conviction that the Christian altar is patriarchal-prototypical, not merely a Mosaic-replacement.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 13:8 (Abraham cycle (13:8)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Abram returned to the place where he had at the first made the altar, and he called there on the name of the Lord, and said: Thou art my God, the Eternal God' — after the Egypt-sojourn (13:11-15), Abram returns to the Bethel altar. Jubilees inscribes return-to-altar as the canonical post-failure rhythm. Tewahedo confession-practice (näsḫa) draws on this pattern: the penitent returns precisely to the same altar previously profaned, not to a substitute. The Andǝmta names this 'Abram's return' (mätsä Abram) as the type of restoration after Diaspora exile.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 13:16 (Abraham cycle (13:16)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the fourteenth year of this jubilee, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tergal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Sellasar, made war against Bera king of Sodom and against Birsha king of Gomorrah... And Abram numbered three hundred and eighteen of his trained men born in his house, and he pursued after them as far as Dan, and routed them by night' — the Genesis-14 Melchizedek narrative is preserved with the tithe-paid detail (13:25-27 in Charles). Jubilees uniquely emphasizes that the tithe was paid out of the rescued Lot's-property spoils and confirmed in heavenly tablets — making it the canonical first-tithe before Mosaic tithing law. Tewahedo monastic ǝʾǝsär (tithe) collection appeals to this passage as the priestly-pre-Mosaic warrant for tithing on agrarian + military goods alike.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 13:25 (Abraham cycle (13:25)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'After these things, in the fourth year of this week, on the new moon of the third month, the word of the Lord came to Abram in a dream, saying: Fear not, Abram, I am thy defender, and thy reward will be exceeding great' — Jubilees uniquely dates the covenant-of-pieces vision to the new moon of the third month, the date that becomes Pentecost (Jub 6:17). The Tewahedo Pentecost (Pärräqlēṭos, fiftieth day) thus has a TRIPLE canonical anchor: Noah's covenant (Jub 6:17), Abram's covenant (Jub 14:1), and Sinai (Ex 19) — three covenant-moments on the same calendar date. The covenant-renewal liturgy of the Tewahedo Pentecost commemorates all three jointly.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 14:1 (Abraham cycle (14:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'Take Me an heifer of three years, and a goat of three years, and a sheep of three years, and a turtle-dove and a pigeon' — the covenant-cutting sacrifice is enumerated. Jubilees emphasizes the threefold age (three years) of each large animal as cosmic-completeness symbol (parallel to the threefold sevens of jubilee reckoning). Tewahedo liturgical-numerology preserves this triadic symbolism: the threefold offering at the altar (bread + wine + incense), the threefold psalmody at the daily office (matins + sext + vespers), and the threefold theological framing of every Anaphora (creation + redemption + sanctification) all draw canonical warrant from the threefold animal-offering of Abram.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 14:13 (Abraham cycle (14:13)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And on that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying: To thy seed will I give this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates' — Jubilees preserves the land-promise within the covenant of pieces. The Tewahedo reading distinguishes the land promise to ethnic Israel (literal fulfilment from Joshua through the divided monarchy) from the universalized land promise to Abram's spiritual seed (the Tewahedo Church inherits the promise as the elected community of those who keep the covenant by faith — cf. Gal 3:7-9, an apostolic reading the Tewahedo retains against any 'Christ-against-Israel' supersessionist framework). The canonical doubled land-witness in Jubilees + Genesis is the warrant for the broad inheritance.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 14:18 (Abraham cycle (14:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Abram rejoiced and told all these things to Sarai his wife; and he believed that he should have a seed, but she did not bear' — Jubilees notes Abram's verbal sharing of the covenant with Sarai, an inclusion of the matriarch absent from the Genesis parallel. Tewahedo Marian theology reads this inclusion as the canonical precedent for full-disclosure of revelation to women: the matriarch is the legitimate hearer of covenant. The Tewahedo elaboration of the Wǝddase Maryam (Praise of Mary) draws on Sarai's reception-of-covenant-by-her-husband's-report as the type of Mary's fiat — the woman who receives the covenant news and consents.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 14:21 (Abraham cycle (14:21)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day, that soul shall be cut off from his people, for he has broken My covenant' — Jubilees doubles the Genesis-17 mandate, specifying the eighth-day timing with covenantal severity. Tewahedo Christian circumcision (gəzrät) preserved on the eighth day — uniquely among major Christian communions — draws canonical warrant directly from this verse. The Tewahedo holds that circumcision is not abrogated by baptism (the standard Western and Eastern Orthodox view) but transformed: the Christian receives BOTH circumcision (as patriarchal sign of belonging) and baptism (as new-covenant rebirth), without conflating them.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 15:14 (Abraham cycle (15:14)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'For the law of this ordinance is for all generations forever, that there is no circumcising of the days, and no omitting of one day out of the eight days' — Jubilees frames the eighth-day timing as permanently fixed, with no liturgical flexibility. The Tewahedo continues the eighth-day practice with this exact non-negotiability: a Christian male child whose parents delay circumcision past the eighth day must seek priestly counsel; the rite is not abolished by Christ but kept as a sign that the Tewahedo are children of Abraham in the patriarchal-fleshly as well as the new-covenant-spiritual sense. This is one of the Tewahedo's distinctive theological-anthropological positions vis-à-vis the rest of Christendom.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 15:25 (Abraham cycle (15:25)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'For the nature of all the angels of the presence and all the angels of sanctification has been so from the day of their creation, and before the angels of the presence and the angels of sanctification He hath sanctified Israel, that they should be with Him and with His holy angels' — Jubilees makes the astonishing claim that the highest angels are themselves circumcised (15:27). Tewahedo angelology preserves this: the seraphim and cherubim are imaged in iconographic tradition with the patriarchal sign, anchoring the Tewahedo conviction that circumcision is heavenly-cosmic in scope, not merely Mosaic-national. The mid-2nd-c. Jubilees here resolves the apparent paradox of an ostensibly bodily sign being also a heavenly mark: the highest angels were created bearing it.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 15:27 (Abraham cycle (15:27)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And there will be great wrath from the Lord against the children of Israel, because they have forsaken His covenant and have turned away from His word' — Jubilees prophesies Israel's future apostasy on the very day God establishes the circumcision covenant. The pattern (covenant-cut + foreseen-apostasy + remnant-preservation) is the canonical shape Tewahedo historiography reads in its own history: each great covenant moment (Frumentius's 4th-c. evangelization, Yared's 6th-c. liturgical codification, Yäkuno Amlak's 13th-c. dynasty-restoration, Twahǝdo-Kalcedonia 451-1959 stand) is followed by partial apostasy and remnant preservation. The remnant pattern is canonical, not accidental.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 15:33 (Abraham cycle (15:33)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And we announced to Sarah all that the angel had told us, and they both rejoiced with exceeding great joy' — the angel of presence reports the Isaac-birth annunciation to Sarah. Jubilees frames this as a formal annunciation-to-the-matriarch parallel to Mary's annunciation. The Tewahedo Marian-typology tradition (Wǝddase Maryam, Mälk'ǝa Maryam) draws on Sarah's annunciation as the canonical OT type: same angelic agent (the angel of presence corresponds to Gabriel in later identification), same response (joy), same miraculous-conception substance. The Tewahedo distinctive Marian liturgical depth has its OT-typological roots here.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 16:3 (Abraham cycle (16:3)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the middle of the sixth month the Lord visited Sarah and did unto her as He had spoken, and she conceived. And she bare a son in the third month, and in the middle of the month, on the day that the Lord had spoken to Abraham, on the festival of the first-fruits of the harvest, Isaac was born' — Jubilees dates Isaac's birth precisely to Shavuot (the Feast of First-Fruits / Weeks). The Tewahedo Pentecost preserves the Old-and-New-Covenant double commemoration: Isaac's birth (the promised seed) and the Spirit's descent (Acts 2, the promised Paraclete) on the same calendar date. Tewahedo Pentecost vigil chants explicitly invoke both.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 16:13 (Abraham cycle (16:13)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he built there an altar to the Lord who had delivered him, and who was making him rejoice in the land of his sojourning, and he celebrated a festival of joy in this month seven days' — Abraham celebrates the FIRST Feast of Tabernacles, seven days, at the Beersheba altar, the year of Isaac's birth (Jub 16:20-25). Tewahedo Sukkot (Mäskäl-related joy-week) draws canonical warrant: the seven-day festival was instituted by Abraham PRE-Mosaically, not at Lev 23. This parallels Jub 6:17's pre-Mosaic Feast of Weeks: Tewahedo liturgical pattern is that the great festivals are patriarchal restorations, not Mosaic novelties — Christ's coming brings them to fulfilment, but they pre-exist.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 16:20 (Abraham cycle (16:20)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And it is written on the heavenly tablets concerning Israel that they shall celebrate the feast of tabernacles seven days with joy, in the seventh month, acceptable before the Lord — a statute forever throughout their generations every year' — Jubilees confirms the heavenly-tablet inscription of the seven-day Tabernacles festival. Tewahedo liturgical historiography distinguishes festivals 'on the heavenly tablets' (pre-existent in the divine eternity, revealed through canonical Scripture) from merely-ecclesiastical commemorations: Tabernacles, Weeks, Atonement, Sabbath are in the former class. The seven-day duration is preserved in Tewahedo Mäskäl-week observance.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 16:29 (Abraham cycle (16:29)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Sarah said to Abraham: cast out this bondwoman and her son, for the son of this bondwoman will not be heir with my son, with Isaac' — Jubilees follows the Genesis 21 sequence: Sarah's demand, Abraham's grief, the divine ratification (17:6, 'in Isaac shall thy seed be called'). Tewahedo readings sharpen this scene against any Marcionite anti-Jewish reading: Ishmael is NOT cursed (17:20, God promises to bless him with twelve princes) but he is NOT the line of covenant-bearing seed. The Tewahedo distinction between general-providential blessing (extended to all Abraham's descendants) and elect-covenant blessing (channeled through Isaac then Jacob) draws canonical warrant here.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 17:11 (Akedah preamble (17:11)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And it came to pass in the seventh week, in the first year thereof, in the first month in this jubilee, on the twelfth of this month, there were voices in heaven regarding Abraham, that he was faithful in all that He told him, and that he loved the Lord, and that in every affliction he was faithful' — Jubilees places the Mastema accusation against Abraham at the precise date of the future Passover (the first month, twelfth day — eve of Nisan 14). Tewahedo Pascha (Fasika) liturgy reads this as the canonical placement: the Akedah is offered AS PASSOVER, not merely typologically connected. Mastema's accusation against the faithful one is overthrown on the same date that the Lamb defeats the firstborn-slaying angel of Ex 12 — typological inversion preserved in Tewahedo Holy-Week chant.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 17:15 (Akedah preamble (17:15)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in every test which He had tested him he was found faithful, and his soul was not impatient, and he was not slow to act, for he was faithful and a lover of the Lord' — Jubilees ascribes to Abraham a settled disposition of patient faithful love (a hapax phrase in Charles, 'a lover of the Lord' / Ge'ez 'mafqäre ǝgziʾabəḥer'). Tewahedo monastic ideal preserves this Jubilees phrase as the goal of contemplative life: not merely obedient service but loving disposition that makes the soul un-impatient under repeated testing. Maḫǝbär Qǝddus (holy-fellowship monastic order) draws its charism from this verse: 'lovers-of-the-Lord' is the Tewahedo monastic self-designation.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 17:18 (Akedah preamble (17:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I stood before him, and before the prince Mastema, and the Lord said: Bid him not to lay his hand on the lad, nor to do anything to him, for I have shown that he fears the Lord' — Jubilees uniquely makes the angel of presence (not the Lord directly) the one who stays Abraham's hand, with the angel positioned BETWEEN Abraham and Mastema. The Tewahedo Akedah ikon tradition depicts this positioning literally: the angel between Abraham and an accusing figure, with the divine voice from above. The angel-of-presence Christological identification (a long Tewahedo patristic tradition reads the angel-of-presence as the pre-incarnate Word) makes the Akedah scene Christological even in its OT form.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 18:11 (Akedah (18:11)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Abraham called that place The Lord hath seen, so that it is said in the mount the Lord hath been seen — that is Mount Zion' — Jubilees explicitly identifies the Akedah mountain (Moriah) with Mount Zion (parallel to 2 Chr 3:1's Temple-mount identification). The Tewahedo eucharistic tradition draws this canonical identification into liturgical theology: every altar is mystically the Akedah mount AND the Temple mount AND Calvary AND the heavenly Zion. The fourfold identification (Moriah-Zion-Calvary-Heavenly-Zion) is preserved in Tewahedo Anaphora prayers and is the canonical anchor for the doctrine that 'the altar is in heaven and on earth at once.'
entries.attribution: Jubilees 18:13 (Akedah (18:13)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he observed this festival every year, seven days with joy, and he called it the festival of the Lord, according to the seven days during which he went and returned in peace. And accordingly has it been ordained and written on the heavenly tablets regarding Israel and its seed that they should observe this festival seven days with the joy of festival' — Abraham institutes a seven-day Akedah-commemoration festival, written on the heavenly tablets. Tewahedo liturgical historiography recognizes this as an Akedah-anniversary observance distinct from Pascha proper but liturgically connected. The seven-day duration and the joy-character (despite the sober content) prefigures the Tewahedo Holy-Week-into-Easter pattern: sober commemoration culminating in resurrection joy, all within one continuous festal week.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 18:18 (Akedah (18:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of Machpelah which is over against Mamre, that is, Hebron, in the land of Canaan' — Jubilees confirms the Machpelah burial (Gen 23). Tewahedo Marian-typology reads Sarah's burial in the Promised Land — not in Ur or Haran — as the canonical anchor for the doctrine that the matriarch's body must rest in the Land of inheritance. Mariological extension: Mary's bodily Assumption (Filsäta) is the eschatological consummation of Sarah's literal Land-burial — Mary, the antitype of Sarah, is taken up into the heavenly Land that is the consummation of the earthly one. Tewahedo iconography of Filsäta sometimes pairs Mary's Assumption with Sarah's burial cave as type-and-antitype.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 19:3 (Sarah's death + Rebekah (19:3)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the fourth year thereof Isaac took to himself a wife, and her name was Rebecca the daughter of Bethuel, the son of Milcah, the sister of Laban and father of Rebecca, the son of Nahor, the brother of Abraham, the sister of Isaac his wife' — Jubilees follows the elaborate kinship geometry of Gen 24 to emphasize that Rebekah is a covenant-line spouse, not a Canaanite. Tewahedo marriage canon (zǝmd zǝr) draws on this verse for the kinship-careful pattern of Christian marriage: blood-kinship within bounds is positively desired (against random outside marriage that risks doctrinal-and-cultural drift), while incest is forbidden. The Tewahedo practical pastoral norm — endogamy preferred within Orthodox community boundaries — has its canonical warrant in the patriarchal practice preserved by Jubilees.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 19:13 (Sarah's death + Rebekah (19:13)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Abraham blessed Jacob and said: he shall walk in My ways, and his children shall walk in My ways, and his seed shall be a blessing in the midst of the earth. And let not the spirits of Mastema rule over thee and over thy seed to turn thee from the Lord, who is thy God from henceforth and for ever' — Abraham's blessing of Jacob (his grandson) before Isaac's own blessing, with explicit Mastema-repulsion clause. The Tewahedo grandparental blessing tradition preserves this pattern: the grandfather's blessing of the grandson includes a Mastema-repulsion clause analogous to Jub 19:28. The Tewahedo baptismal-and-childhood liturgy retains a comparable formula in the priestly blessing of children.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 19:28 (Sarah's death + Rebekah (19:28)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he commanded them that they should observe the way of the Lord, that they should work righteousness, and love each his neighbour, and act on this manner amongst all men, that they should each so walk with regard to them as to do judgment and righteousness on the earth, that they should circumcise their sons according to the covenant which He had made with them, and not deviate to the right hand or the left of all the paths which the Lord had commanded us' — Abraham's testament to all his sons (legitimate and concubine-born) commands love-of-neighbour as the ethical core. Tewahedo catechesis names Jub 20:2 as the canonical 'second great commandment' antecedent (Lev 19:18 is the parallel; Mt 22:39 fulfils): love-of-neighbour is not a New-Covenant innovation but the patriarchal testament-content.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 20:2 (Abraham's testament (20:2)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And, my children, observe the commandment of Abraham your father, and be not separated from the worship of the Lord. And, my children, beware of all whoredom and uncleanness, and of all pollution of sin' — Abraham's testament forbids whoredom, idolatrous association, and ritual impurity as a triad. The Tewahedo monastic-and-lay catechesis preserves this triad as the negative-ethical core of inheritance: each child of the covenant must avoid sexual impurity, idolatrous syncretism, and ritual pollution. The Tewahedo täzkär (memorial) for the departed includes a renewal of this Abrahamic charge — the deceased is commended to the next generation as a witness to the three negative bounds.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 20:7 (Abraham's testament (20:7)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And as regards the blood of all flesh that ascendeth on the altar, place ye salt thereon; and as for the blood, eat it not, for it is the soul; and let no blood be left in the flesh which thou eatest' — Abraham's priestly instructions to Isaac repeat the no-blood-consumption command (Jub 6:7, 7:34 antecedents). Tewahedo dietary law preserves the no-blood rule with priestly emphasis: the canonical-Tewahedo prohibition against eating blood (drawn from Gen 9:4 + Lev 17 + Acts 15 + this Jubilees triple-witness) marks the Tewahedo apart from most Western Christian practice. The salt-on-blood prescription is preserved in Tewahedo altar practice.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 21:7 (Abraham's priestly instructions (21:7)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And there is no greater sin in His sight than this — to eat the blood of any flesh; and they that eat shall be rooted out of the land' — Abraham frames blood-consumption as a sin of uniquely-rooting-out severity. Tewahedo penitential canon (mäṣḥafä qəddase confession-list) catalogues unintentional blood-consumption (improperly bled meat) as a sin requiring specific priestly absolution. The Tewahedo's distinctive abstention from non-kosher-style butchery without specific priestly blessing of the slaughter draws canonical warrant from Jub 21:18 — the prohibition is presented as a category-of-its-own, separate from the general dietary code.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 21:18 (Abraham's priestly instructions (21:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And do thou, my son, observe His commandments and His ordinances and His judgments, and walk not after the abominations, and after the graven images, and after the molten images' — Abraham's closing charge to Isaac: covenant-faithfulness expressed positively (keep the commandments) and negatively (no idolatry in any form). The Tewahedo iconographic tradition has been careful to distinguish itself from this prohibition: Tewahedo ikons are NOT graven images (they are painted boards, not sculpted statues; venerated as windows-to-the-real, not worshipped as substitutes for it). The patriarchal warrant for the Tewahedo iconography-yes-statues-no boundary is implicit in this verse's careful threefold listing of forbidden artifact types: abominations (idolatrous practices), graven images (sculpture), molten images (cast metal) — none of which describe the Tewahedo painted ikon.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 21:22 (Abraham's priestly instructions (21:22)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And it came to pass in the first week in the forty-fourth jubilee, in the second year, that is, the year in which Abraham died, that Isaac and Ishmael came from the Well of the Oath to celebrate the feast of weeks — that is, the feast of the first-fruits of the harvest — to Abraham, their father, and Abraham rejoiced because his two sons had come' — Jubilees preserves Abraham's celebration of the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot / Pentecost) in his final year, with BOTH Isaac and Ishmael in fellowship at the patriarchal altar. The Tewahedo Pentecost liturgy preserves a 'family-reunion-at-the-altar' theme: estranged-but-not-cursed branches of Abraham's seed gathered at the table. The Tewahedo's distinctive pastoral practice of welcoming Ishmaelite (Muslim) Ethiopian Christians-from-Muslim-families to communion-table preparation has its canonical Jubilees anchor here.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 22:1 (Abraham's final blessing (22:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he called Jacob and said: my son Jacob, may the God of all bless thee and strengthen thee to do righteousness, and His will before Him, and may He choose thee and thy seed that ye may become a people for His inheritance according to His will alway. And do thou, my son Jacob, remember my words, and observe the commandments of Abraham, thy father' — Abraham's final blessing of Jacob (his preferred grandson over Isaac's other line through Esau) directly anticipates the Jacob-not-Esau election preserved by Jubilees. The Tewahedo Jacobite-Israelite identification (the Tewahedo Church reads itself as the legitimate Israelite-Jacobite continuation, with the Solomonic dynasty as the canonical-political extension of the Davidic line through Menelik I as Solomon's son in the Kǝbrä Nägäśt tradition) finds its earliest canonical warrant in Abraham's direct-to-Jacob blessing here. The grandfather's blessing of Jacob over his father Isaac's potential to favor Esau is itself read as canonical priority-of-grace over inherited-order.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 22:11 (Abraham's final blessing (22:11)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Jacob was cooking pottage, and Esau came from the field hungry; and he said to Jacob his brother: give me of this red pottage. And Jacob said to him: sell me thy birthright, and I will give thee bread, and also some of this pottage' — Jubilees preserves the Gen 25 transaction with the explicit verbal contract. Tewahedo Andǝmta exegesis frames this as the canonical case-study in the Tewahedo doctrine of consequential-choice (mərč'a-bä-yäwär̄əd, 'choosing-that-cuts-downward'): Esau's transaction is binding precisely because it was freely entered. The Tewahedo emphasizes against any 'irresistible-grace' framework that some choices truly close future possibilities — the birthright is not recoverable later (Heb 12:17, picked up by Tewahedo Pauline preaching), even though tears are sincere.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 24:3 (Esau and Isaac in Gerar (24:3)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Esau ate and was filled, and despised the birthright; for this reason was Esau called Edom, on account of the red pottage which Jacob gave him for his birthright' — Jubilees gives the etymology of 'Edom' (red) and explicitly attaches it to the birthright-despising rather than to the red color generally. Tewahedo theological-anthropology reads 'Edom' as the canonical name of the soul-orientation that prefers immediate gratification to long-term covenantal goods; the Tewahedo monastic Doctrine of the Stomach (literal asceticism opposed to over-eating) draws on this verse as the canonical OT warrant for fasting-against-the-stomach-as-mind-clouder.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 24:7 (Esau and Isaac in Gerar (24:7)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the famine was over the land, and Isaac departed to go down into Egypt in the second year of this week, and went to the king of the Philistines to Gerar, unto Abimelech. And the Lord appeared unto him and said unto him: go not down into Egypt; dwell in the land that I shall tell thee of' — God prevents Isaac from leaving the Promised Land even during famine. Tewahedo readings of this episode contrast it with the later Egyptian sojourn (which Jacob does undertake in Jub 45) — the difference is divine command: where God commands return to the Land, exile-flight is forbidden; where God permits exile, sojourn is acceptable. The Tewahedo diaspora theology (those who remain in Ethiopia during persecution vs. those who emigrate) finds its canonical discernment-pattern here: divine guidance, not circumstance, governs the legitimacy of staying-or-going.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 24:11 (Esau and Isaac in Gerar (24:11)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he built an altar there, and he called on the name of the Lord, and he pitched his tent there, and his servants digged a well' — Isaac's altar at Beersheba, the pre-Mosaic continuation of Abram's Bethel altar (Jub 13:8). Jubilees emphasizes that the patriarchal-altar tradition is unbroken from Abram through Isaac through Jacob (Jub 32:1) — the legitimate altar passes father-to-son before the Mosaic-priestly investiture. The Tewahedo Anaphora-of-the-Patriarchs (used in periodic monastic-festal commemoration) draws its canonical warrant from this three-generation patriarchal-altar chain: legitimate altar is hereditary AND pre-Mosaic, anchoring the Tewahedo conviction that the Christian altar is patriarchally-prototypical.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 24:22 (Esau and Isaac in Gerar (24:22)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the second year of this week in this jubilee, Rebecca called Jacob her son, and spake unto him, saying: my son, do not take thee a wife of the daughters of Canaan, as Esau, thy brother, who took him two wives of the daughters of Canaan' — Rebekah's command parallels but precedes Isaac's command of Jub 25:5 + Gen 28:1. Jubilees thus gives the matriarch the FIRST anti-intermarriage command. The Tewahedo emphasis on the spiritual authority of the mother in family-religious-formation finds canonical warrant here: doctrinal-marriage discernment passes through the matriarch FIRST. The Tewahedo Marian liturgy (Wǝddase Maryam) draws on this maternal-spiritual-authority pattern for the elevation of Mary's intercessory role.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 25:1 (Rebekah's blessing of Jacob (25:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Rebecca lifted up her hands toward heaven and stretched out the fingers of her hands, and she blessed the Most High God, who had created the heaven and the earth, and she gave Him thanks and praise. And she said: blessed be the Lord God, and may His holy name be blessed for ever and ever, who hath given me Jacob as a pure son and a holy seed' — Rebekah's prayer is a formal blessing of God WITH RAISED HANDS toward heaven. The Tewahedo liturgical posture of orans (hands raised, palms forward, in standing prayer) is the canonical Christian inheritance of this Rebekah-prayer posture; the Tewahedo daily office preserves the raised-hands stance for the doxological climaxes of the morning office, anchored in this matriarchal canonical witness.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 25:11 (Rebekah's blessing of Jacob (25:11)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And at that hour, when the spirit of righteousness descended into her mouth, she placed her two hands on the head of Jacob, and said' — Rebekah's blessing is explicitly Spirit-inspired ('the spirit of righteousness descended into her mouth'). Jubilees thus presents a pre-Pentecostal canonical episode of prophetic-Spirit-inspired speech, parallel to later prophetic-speech episodes. The Tewahedo doctrine of inspired-utterance (näfsä qǝddus) finds canonical OT-typological anchor here: the same Spirit that inspires prophets and apostles spoke through Rebekah at Jacob's blessing. The Tewahedo grandmother / mother prayer-of-blessing tradition (the matriarchal blessing carries authority beyond mere well-wishing) draws warrant from this verse.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 25:14 (Rebekah's blessing of Jacob (25:14)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'May the Lord of the world love thee as the heart of thy mother and her affection rejoice in thee; bless thee. And may He give thee a blessing of righteousness, and grant thee help, and give to thee a blessing of length of days. Mayest thou see Mahalalel in thy lifetime, the resurrection unto eternal life' — Rebekah's blessing climaxes with an explicit resurrection-unto-eternal-life clause, a remarkable mid-2nd-c. BCE Jewish text witnessing the resurrection hope. The Tewahedo canonical resurrection-doctrine (Tǝnśaʾe) draws on this Jubilees passage as a Tewahedo-distinctive OT-typological anchor: the resurrection hope is canonically embedded in patriarchal-matriarchal blessing, not just in late-Daniel apocalypse or the prophets.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 25:23 (Rebekah's blessing of Jacob (25:23)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Rebecca took goodly raiment of her elder son Esau, which was with her in the house, and she clothed Jacob her younger son with them, and put the skins of the kids upon his hands and on the exposed parts of his neck' — Jubilees follows the Gen 27 deception narrative without softening it. Tewahedo Andǝmta exegesis on this passage takes a distinctive position: the deception is NOT condoned but is canonically PERMITTED by divine providence to bring about the predetermined blessing — Isaac's intent to bless Esau was itself contrary to the earlier 'the elder shall serve the younger' (Gen 25:23 = Jub 19:31). The Tewahedo theological reading: God's providence works through human action including human moral ambiguity without destroying free will or sanctioning the deceit per se. (The Tewahedo distinction between divine-permission and divine-command is sharper than the Western Augustinian framing.)
entries.attribution: Jubilees 26:13 (Jacob receives Isaac's blessing (26:13)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Isaac said unto his son: how hast thou found it so quickly, my son? And Jacob said: because thy God caused me to find. And Isaac said unto Jacob: come near, that I may feel thee, my son, if thou art my son Esau or not. And Jacob went near to his father Isaac, and he felt him and said: the voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau' — Jubilees preserves the iconic 'voice of Jacob, hands of Esau' line. Tewahedo monastic Maḫǝbär Qǝddus tradition reads this verse spiritually: the voice (intentionality, prayer-speech) reveals true spiritual identity even when the hands (outward action) are disguised — the canonical antecedent to the desert-fathers' discipline of attending to one's interior voice rather than external appearance as the locus of spiritual self-knowledge.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 26:18 (Jacob receives Isaac's blessing (26:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'God give thee of the dew of heaven, and of the dew of the earth, and plenty of corn and wine: let peoples serve thee, and nations bow down to thee. Be lord over thy brethren, and let thy mother's sons bow down to thee; cursed be every one that curseth thee, and blessed be every one that blesseth thee' — Isaac's blessing of Jacob (mistakenly received). Jubilees preserves the comprehensive blessing without modification. Tewahedo reading: the Solomonic-dynasty Tewahedo-Jacobite continuation (Kǝbrä Nägäśt tradition: the Tewahedo Church receives the canonical Jacobite blessing through the Solomonic dynasty's Davidic descent and the Tewahedo's covenantal-spiritual descent through baptism) finds its canonical anchor here. The 'cursed be every one that curseth thee' clause is the warrant for the Tewahedo's distinctive imprecatory-protective prayer tradition against anti-Tewahedo aggressors.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 26:24 (Jacob receives Isaac's blessing (26:24)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the words of Esau, her elder son, were told to Rebecca in a dream, and Rebecca sent and called Jacob her younger son, and said unto him: behold, Esau thy brother will take vengeance on thee so as to kill thee' — Jubilees uniquely makes Rebekah's foreknowledge of Esau's murderous plot a divinely-given dream, not mere intuition. The Tewahedo dream-discernment tradition (the matriarchal-prophetic dream that saves the patriarch is a recognized canonical category) draws warrant: legitimate dreams from God can be relied on for major decisions when corroborated by the dreamer's righteous standing and the moral content of the dream. Rebekah's dream meets both tests.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 27:1 (Jacob's flight and Bethel vision (27:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he dreamt that night, and behold, a ladder was set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven, and behold, the angels of the Lord ascended and descended on it: and behold, the Lord stood upon it. And He spake to Jacob, and said: I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac; the land whereon thou art sleeping, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed after thee' — Jubilees preserves the Bethel ladder vision of Gen 28:12-13. Tewahedo Marian-typology reads Jacob's ladder as the canonical OT image of Mary as the ladder-between-heaven-and-earth; the Wǝddase Maryam (Praise of Mary) explicitly invokes 'Mary the ladder of Jacob' in the Monday-evening cycle. The angels-ascending-and-descending detail is the canonical proof-text for the Tewahedo doctrine that angels are not static but actively traffic between heaven and earth on behalf of the elect (Heb 1:14 picks this up apostolically).
entries.attribution: Jubilees 27:19 (Jacob's flight and Bethel vision (27:19)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Jacob vowed a vow, saying: if the Lord will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat, and raiment to put on, so that I return in peace to my father's house, then shall the Lord be my God, and this stone which I have set up as a pillar for a memorial in this place, shall be the house of God: and of all that thou givest me, I shall give the tenth to thee, my God' — Jacob's vow combines covenant-faithfulness, sanctuary-establishment, AND tithing. Jubilees uniquely treats the pillar (mäṣbäḳ) as legitimately establishable by the patriarch BEFORE any Mosaic-altar legislation; the Tewahedo täbot tradition (each Tewahedo church has its consecrated täbot — the tablet representing the ark) finds canonical anchor here: the sanctifiable-stone is a patriarchal-prerogative restored in the Tewahedo täbot. The tithe-of-everything-given is the canonical anchor for the Tewahedo ǝʾǝsär comprehensiveness (not just produce but all gifts received).
entries.attribution: Jubilees 27:27 (Jacob's flight and Bethel vision (27:27)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Jacob went on his journey to the land of the east, to Laban the brother of Rebecca, and he was with him, and served him for Rachel his daughter one week' — Jubilees specifies one week as the initial service period, with the 'seven years' of Gen 29:20 elsewhere preserved as fourteen years for both wives (Jub 28:9-10). The Tewahedo monastic-novitiate pattern (the novice serves a senior monk for a probationary period before formal acceptance) finds canonical-typological anchor in Jacob's service-for-marriage: bodily-and-laborious commitment proves intention before covenant-relationship is consummated. The Tewahedo discernment-pattern (long service before commitment) is canonically rooted here.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 28:1 (Jacob in Haran (28:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Laban said unto Jacob: it is not so done in our country, to give the younger before the elder: do this seven days' celebration, and we will give thee her also for the service which thou shalt serve me other seven years' — Laban substitutes Leah for Rachel. Jubilees preserves Laban's deception. Tewahedo Andǝmta exegesis notes the canonical irony: Jacob who deceived his older-brother Esau is now deceived by his uncle Laban who insists on elder-first priority. The Tewahedo Christian moral-formation tradition draws on this episode: divine providence often arranges that the deceiver-from-position-of-weakness becomes the deceived-from-position-of-need — not as retributive punishment but as character-forming pedagogy. Jacob's later integrity is forged through Laban's deception.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 28:6 (Jacob in Haran (28:6)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the Lord opened the womb of Leah, and she conceived and bore unto Jacob a son, and he called his name Reuben' — Leah conceives first as the unloved-wife consolation. Jubilees follows Gen 29:32 in attributing the womb-opening to the Lord's compassion on the un-favored. Tewahedo Marian-and-matriarchal piety draws on this canonical pattern: God preferentially attends to the un-favored matriarchs in the patriarchal narratives (Leah, Hagar, the various un-favored wives). The Tewahedo pastoral attention to widowed-or-childless women — extending special intercessory prayer for them — finds canonical anchor in this divine-preference pattern.
