entries.attribution: Jubilees 28:11 (Jacob in Haran (28:11)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Jacob sent messengers to Esau his brother to the land of Seir, to the country of Edom; and Jacob acknowledged what Esau had done to him, for he loved him very much from the day his father sent him from his presence, until he was settled in Egypt' — Jubilees uniquely preserves Esau's eventual love for Jacob alongside the Gen 33:4 reconciliation narrative. Tewahedo theological reading: even the rejected-line brother retains genuine fraternal affection in Jubilees' framing — the eschatological reconciliation between covenant-bearing and providential-non-bearing branches is canonically anticipated here. The Tewahedo's distinctive pastoral approach to non-Orthodox Christians (Catholic Ethiopians, Protestant Ethiopians, etc.) draws on this canonical fraternal-love-preserved pattern.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 29:13 (Jacob's return and Esau reconciliation (29:13)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Jacob built a house for himself in Salem, in the mountain of Heshbon, and he dwelt there a long time, and he sent unto his father presents and unto his mother twice a year, again and again' — Jubilees adds the detail of Jacob's twice-yearly gift-sending to his parents during his sojourn east of Jordan. Tewahedo Andǝmta exegesis on the fifth commandment (honor thy father and thy mother) cites this verse as the canonical case-study for honoring-from-distance: when geographical separation prevents in-person care, the regular twice-yearly remembrance (gifts, communication) preserves the substance of the command. The Tewahedo diaspora pastoral counsel for emigrant children draws practical-canonical guidance from this verse.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 29:19 (Jacob's return and Esau reconciliation (29:19)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the land, saw her, and he seized her and lay with her, and he defiled her, and she was a little girl, a child of twelve years' — Jubilees specifies Dinah's age as twelve, framing the crime not just as defilement but as child-rape. The Tewahedo canonical anti-child-abuse stance (which goes beyond the standard Western moral framing into Tewahedo-distinctive ecclesiastical-penalty severity) finds canonical anchor here: the doubled-aggravation of force-AND-childhood is the canonical example of a worst-case category. The Tewahedo penitential canon distinguishes adult-and-mutual-consent failings from defilement-of-a-child as categorically separate, drawing on Jub 30:2's age-specification.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 30:2 (Dinah and Shechem (30:2)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the sons of Jacob spake deceitfully unto Shechem and Hamor his father, and dealt craftily with them and beguiled them. And Simeon and Levi came unexpectedly to Shechem and executed judgment on all the men of Shechem, and slew all the men whom they found in it, and left not a single one remaining in it: they slew all in torments because they had dishonoured their sister Dinah' — Jubilees frames the Simeon-and-Levi attack as 'executed judgment' rather than mere revenge. Tewahedo just-war theology reads the Levi-Simeon action as proto-judicial: the defilement created a covenantal-emergency that demanded a judicial response, not a private revenge. The Tewahedo's distinctive (compared to most Western Christianity) acceptance of measured-violence in defense of the covenant-community-against-sexual-aggression has its canonical anchor in this Jubilees framing.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 30:4 (Dinah and Shechem (30:4)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And to Levi we gave the office of the priesthood and to the Levites: to do the service before the Lord as we do continually, and that Levi and his sons may be blessed for ever; for he was zealous to execute righteousness and judgment and vengeance on all those who arose against Israel' — Jubilees uniquely makes Levi's zeal at Shechem the EARNED warrant for the Levitical priesthood (not just the later golden-calf zeal of Ex 32). The Tewahedo priestly-tradition (the kǝhnät as receivers-of-priesthood-by-zeal-for-purity, not just by descent) finds the strongest canonical anchor here: the priesthood is BOTH hereditary AND earned-by-righteous-action — the original priestly investiture was won, not merely inherited.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 30:18 (Dinah and Shechem / Levi's zeal (30:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and they are written down on the heavenly tablets as friends and as righteous ones' — the Simeon-and-Levi action is reckoned as righteousness, parallel to Phinehas's later zeal-as-righteousness reckoning at Num 25:13. Tewahedo doctrine of righteousness-by-faith-AND-by-zealous-action (against any 'faith alone abstracted from action' framing) draws canonical anchor here. The 'written down on the heavenly tablets' formula recurs throughout Jubilees and Tewahedo readers attach to it a doctrine of eternal-heavenly-record: certain canonical actions are not just remembered but inscribed for eschatological vindication. The Tewahedo täwlǝd-bä-mäṣǝḥaf (book-of-life inscription) doctrine has canonical roots here.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 30:23 (Dinah and Shechem / Levi's zeal (30:23)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And on the new moon of the first month, the Lord said unto Jacob: arise, and go up to Bethel, and dwell there, and make there an altar to the God who appeared to thee, who fled from the face of Esau thy brother' — Jubilees dates Jacob's return to Bethel to the new moon of the first month (eve of Passover). The Tewahedo theme of return-to-the-place-of-vision (the disciple returns to the locus of initial calling for re-consecration) finds canonical-temporal anchor: the new-moon-of-the-first-month date links Jacob's Bethel re-consecration to the Passover-Pascha cluster of dates — return is liturgically tied to Christ's Paschal mystery for the Tewahedo reader.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 31:1 (Isaac's visit to Bethel (31:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he turned to Levi first, and began to bless him first, and said unto him: may the Lord of all, the Lord of all the ages, bless thee and thy sons throughout all the ages. And may the Lord give to thee and to thy seed greatness and great glory, and cause thee and thy seed, from amongst all flesh, to approach Him to serve in His sanctuary as the angels of the presence and as the holy ones' — Isaac blesses Levi BEFORE Judah, contrary to chronological birth-order. Jubilees emphasizes that the priestly blessing comes BEFORE the royal blessing — the priestly-ministerial vocation is canonically PRIOR to the royal-political vocation. Tewahedo ecclesiology preserves this primacy: the kǝhnät (priesthood) takes precedence over the nəguś (king) in canonical-spiritual order, even when the king is the political-protector of the church. The Tewahedo's distinctive emphasis on the priestly-prophetic-warning of unjust kings finds canonical anchor here.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 31:14 (Isaac's visit to Bethel (31:14)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he turned to Judah and said: may God give thee strength and power to tread down those that hate thee; be thou a prince, thou and thy sons, over the sons of Jacob; may thy name and the name of thy sons go forth and traverse every land and region. Then shall the Gentiles fear before thy face, and all the nations shall quake. In thee shall be the help of Jacob, and in thee shall be found the salvation of Israel' — Isaac's blessing of Judah explicitly foretells salvation-coming-from-Judah, anticipating Gen 49:10 (Shiloh prophecy) and Davidic messianism. Tewahedo Christology reads this as a doubled OT-canonical proof of Christ's Davidic-Judah ancestry: not only the late Gen 49:10 prophecy but also the early Isaac-blessing prophecy at Jub 31:18. The Kǝbrä Nägäśt tradition draws the Tewahedo-Solomonic-dynasty's Davidic-Judah claim through this verse.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 31:18 (Isaac's visit to Bethel (31:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And his father Isaac blessed Jacob, and the two sons of Jacob, Levi and Judah, and his sons. And he gave them all his blessings and gave them his books and the books of his fathers Abraham and his grandfather, and he committed them to Jacob to keep them up and to renew them for his sons until this day' — Jubilees uniquely speaks of 'the books of his fathers Abraham' transmitted Isaac → Jacob → Levi-Judah. The patriarchal manuscript-tradition (a pre-Mosaic written canonical literature) is Jubilees-distinctive and the Tewahedo Andǝmta tradition has long taken seriously the implication: the Mosaic Torah is a redaction of older patriarchal writings, not a fresh Sinai-only revelation. The Tewahedo's distinctive manuscript-preserving monastic charism (the gədl 'biography' tradition; the mäṣḥaf säwasǝw 'grammar of language' tradition) sees itself as continuator of the canonical-patriarchal book-keeping practice.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 31:23 (Isaac's visit to Bethel (31:23)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Jacob abode there that night, and he sent away from him all his flocks and all his possessions to his father Isaac and to his mother Rebecca. And Jacob tithed all the clean animals, and made a burnt-offering, and he gave the tithe to Levi his son, and the second tithe he ate himself before the Lord' — Jubilees uniquely preserves Jacob's institution of the tithe-of-tithes pattern (one tithe to the priest, one tithe consumed by the offerer before the Lord) as a pre-Mosaic patriarchal ordinance. The Tewahedo monastic ǝʾǝsär practice (one tithe to the church / priesthood, a second consumed in festive remembrance) draws canonical anchor here: the Levitical tithe and the ma'aser-šeni (festive tithe consumed by the offerer) are BOTH patriarchal, not just Deut-15-Mosaic. The Tewahedo's distinctive double-tithe practice is canonically pre-Mosaic in this framing.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 32:9 (Bethel altar and Levi's priesthood (32:9)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he saw in a vision of the night, and behold, an angel descended from heaven with seven tablets in his hands, and he gave them to Jacob, and he read them, and knew all that was written therein, what would befall him and his sons throughout all the ages' — Jubilees uniquely presents Jacob's reception of seven heavenly tablets containing the entire prophetic future of his descendants. Tewahedo Marian-canonical understanding of revelation (the Mary-as-receiver-of-the-Word echoes the patriarchal pattern of inscribed-revelation-given) draws on this canonical pre-existence-of-the-Word-in-tablets motif. The Tewahedo doctrine of the canonical Scripture as 'eternal in the heavens' (the Mäṣḥafä-zä-säma'i, the heavenly book) finds Jubilees as a key OT canonical anchor.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 32:21 (Bethel altar and Levi's priesthood (32:21)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Deborah Rebecca's nurse died, and they buried her beneath Bethel under the oak, and he called the name of that place "The oak of weeping"' — Deborah-the-nurse's burial is briefly preserved (parallel Gen 35:8). Jubilees uniquely names the oak Allon-bacuth (oak of weeping). The Tewahedo cult-of-departed-faithful-elders (täzkär commemoration on the 40th day, 80th day, anniversary of death) draws on the patriarchal pattern of marking the burial-tree with a remembrance-name. The Tewahedo monastic practice of planting trees at the gravesites of beloved spiritual mothers (including nurses, deaconesses, female monastics) has its canonical anchor in Deborah's Bethel oak: the burial-tree as living memorial.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 32:25 (Bethel altar and Levi's priesthood (32:25)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he was a great burden to her in her travail, and his soul came near to depart from her, and she had hardly delivered him when she died. And she called his name "son of my sorrow," but Jacob his father called his name Benjamin' — Rachel dies in childbirth bearing Benjamin (Gen 35:18 parallel). Jubilees preserves the doubled naming (Ben-oni / Benjamin). Tewahedo readings see in the doubled naming the canonical type of suffering-transmuted-into-joy: the mother's last word names the cost of motherhood; the father's name names the elevation of the cost into covenantal gladness. The Tewahedo Marian theology of suffering-with-Christ-as-redemptive-fellowship (cf. Lk 2:35 sword-piercing Mary's soul) draws on this canonical matriarchal pattern: the cost of bearing is real AND is renamed by covenantal interpretation.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 32:33 (Bethel altar and Levi's priesthood (32:33)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Reuben saw Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid, the concubine of his father, bathing in water in a secret place, and he loved her. And he hid himself at night, and he entered the house of Bilhah at night, and he found her sleeping alone on a bed in her house. And he lay with her, and she awoke and saw, and behold Reuben was lying with her in the bed' — Jubilees preserves the Gen 35:22 incident in painful detail. The Tewahedo penitential canon's strongest category — incest, especially with a parent's spouse or partner — finds canonical anchor here. The Tewahedo's distinctive practice of detailed-confession-by-category (the Confessor walks the penitent through specific Scripture-named sins for self-examination) draws Jub 33:2 into the canonical sin-list for the spiritual-paternal-bed category.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 33:2 (Reuben's incest (33:2)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he came to his father Jacob, and he confessed to him that he had defiled the bed of his father; and Jacob mourned exceedingly because of him, and he smote him not, because Reuben himself had confessed to him; and he had pity on him' — Jubilees uniquely preserves Reuben's voluntary confession-to-the-father and Jacob's clemency-because-of-confession. The Tewahedo confession-and-absolution pattern (näsḫa) draws on this verse for the canonical principle that voluntary disclosure to the spiritual father materially mitigates the punitive disciplinary response, even where the sin's gravity is unchanged. The 'smote him not because Reuben had confessed' clause is the Tewahedo canonical warrant for the confessor's clemency in response to genuinely-voluntary admission.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 33:9 (Reuben's incest (33:9)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Reuben was not pardoned in heaven, because he was older than Joseph, and because he should not have done this thing — for he could have known that his father had her, but he loved her not as his sister' — Jubilees distinguishes terrestrial pardon (Jacob's clemency) from heavenly judicial-reckoning. Tewahedo theological precision: divine pardon and disciplinary-canonical pardon are NOT identical; the priest can absolve from canonical penalty (Heb. nash'a; Tewahedo näsḫa) without thereby exhausting the heavenly judicial dimension, which remains the Lord's. The Tewahedo's distinct doctrine on the limits of priestly absolution (against the maximalist Catholic plenary-indulgence model) draws canonical anchor here.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 33:10 (Reuben's incest (33:10)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And they sat down to eat bread, and they sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of gold; and they brought him down into Egypt, and they sold him to Potiphar the eunuch the chief cook of Pharaoh' — Jubilees follows the Gen 37 sale of Joseph with a notable detail (twenty pieces of gold; sold to the Ishmaelites). Tewahedo Holy-Week typology preserves the canonical Joseph-as-Christ correspondence: sold for twenty pieces of gold (cf. Mt 26:15 thirty pieces of silver for Christ — the parallel-but-distinct sums anchor the doubled betrayal motif). Tewahedo liturgical commemoration of the Joseph-betrayal date on Wednesday of Holy Week draws on this canonical typological pattern.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 34:11 (Joseph sold and annual fast (34:11)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'For this reason it is ordained for the children of Israel that they should afflict themselves on the tenth of the seventh month — on the day that the news which made him weep for Joseph came to Jacob his father — that they should make atonement for themselves thereon with a young goat on the tenth of the seventh month, once a year, for their sins; for they had grieved the affection of their father regarding Joseph his son' — Jubilees uniquely connects the Day of Atonement (10th of 7th month, Lev 16) to the day on which Jacob received the news of Joseph's loss. The Tewahedo Day of Atonement (Astereyo) is canonically anchored TRIPLY in Jubilees: the Watchers judgment (Jub 5:17-18), the Noahide atonement pattern (Jub 6 indirectly), AND now Jacob's Joseph-grief (Jub 34:18). The Tewahedo's distinctive emphasis on grief-of-affection (not just sin-against-commandment) as the canonical heart of Atonement Day finds anchor here.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 34:18 (Joseph sold and annual fast (34:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Esau is to thee from time eternal a foe, but I trust that thou wilt confess thy ways to him and that he will yet repent of his evil purpose, and that mercy will reach him' — Rebekah's deathbed words to Jacob preserve a remarkable canonical hope for Esau's eventual repentance. Tewahedo eschatological hope (the universalism-leaning emphasis that the Tewahedo holds in tension with apokatastasis-rejection — the Tewahedo neither dogmatically affirms nor dogmatically denies universal-final-repentance) finds canonical matriarchal anchor here: even the most-rejected covenant-line brother is canonically hoped-for. The Tewahedo's distinctive pastoral generosity toward non-Tewahedo Christians and even toward those of other faiths in salvation-trust questions draws on Rebekah's witness.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 35:6 (Death of Rebekah (35:6)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And she died, the same day, and her two sons buried her, Esau and Jacob, in the double cave near Sarah her mother-in-law' — Esau and Jacob buried Rebekah TOGETHER in the Machpelah cave, in fraternal cooperation at her funeral despite their lifelong rivalry. Jubilees emphasizes this unique reconciliation-at-the-mother's-grave moment. The Tewahedo pastoral tradition of family-reunion-at-funerals (estranged-family-members reconciling at the matriarch's or patriarch's funeral) draws canonical warrant here: even where the relationship cannot be repaired in life, the death of the parent provides a divinely-arranged occasion for partial reconciliation. The Tewahedo's family-funeral liturgy preserves a moment of joint-prayer-by-estranged-children, anchored typologically in this verse.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 35:18 (Death of Rebekah (35:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the sixth year of this week, in the forty-fourth jubilee, Isaac called his two sons, Esau and Jacob, and they came to him, and he said unto them: my sons, I am going the way of my fathers, to the eternal house where my fathers are' — Isaac's dying-charge frames death as 'the way of my fathers, to the eternal house.' Jubilees presents an explicit intermediate-state-as-fellowship-with-the-departed-righteous doctrine, antecedent to Lk 16:22 (Abraham's bosom) and the Tewahedo prayer 'in the bosom of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob.' The Tewahedo funeral-liturgy phrase 'in the eternal house with the fathers' is the direct verbal-inheritance of Jub 36:1 — the patriarchal-formulary preserved across millennia.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 36:1 (Isaac's testament (36:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And I command you, my sons, that ye love one another, the one his brother as a man loves his own soul, and let each strive in that which he can do for his brother, and do righteousness on the earth between you; and ye shall love one another as your own selves' — Isaac's testament commands love-of-brother-as-one's-own-self, the canonical doubled-witness with Jub 20:2 (Abraham's testament) and Lev 19:18. The Tewahedo's distinctive heavy emphasis on family-and-monastic-community fraternal love (not as innovation but as canonical-patriarchal commandment) draws warrant from the patriarchal-testament triad: Abraham (Jub 20:2), Isaac (Jub 36:7), and the eventual Mosaic codification (Lev 19:18). The Tewahedo monastic Maḫǝbär Qǝddus 'beloved-brothers' charism is the canonical-patriarchal inheritance applied to spiritual-kinship community.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 36:7 (Isaac's testament (36:7)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the third year of the sixth week of this jubilee, the sons of Esau the elder brother of Jacob, gathered themselves together, and Esau heard, and his soul was vexed, and they came against Jacob to make war' — Jubilees uniquely preserves a major narrative of armed conflict between Esau's clan and Jacob's family, absent from the canonical Genesis. Tewahedo political-theology reads this as the canonical anchor for defensive-war doctrine: the covenant-community may take up arms against treacherous-relative aggressors precisely because the violation comes from inside the extended-family rather than from a distant foe. The Tewahedo wars of national defense (against the 16th-c. Gragn invasions, the 19th-c. Mahdists, the 20th-c. Italian fascist occupation) draw canonical warrant from this passage.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 37:1 (Esau-Jacob war (37:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Jacob said unto Esau: hast thou not made the oath with me, even my father, and these our nine fathers? Why didst thou come now to dishonour us by reason of thy sons coming up against us with a multitude?' — Esau is confronted with his violation of the Jub 35:9 oath (which he swore to Rebekah on her deathbed and to Isaac at Jub 36:18). The Tewahedo doctrine of oath-binding (the qǝddase oath has eternal-vertical weight) finds canonical anchor here: oaths sworn to a dying parent are inviolable; the treacherous-relative is rendered legitimately-engageable by his own oath-breaking, not by Jacob's choice. Tewahedo monastic vow-tradition treats vow-breaking as the canonical-equivalent of Esau's treachery.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 37:25 (Esau-Jacob war (37:25)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Judah's sons drew their bows, and shot at Adoram and slew him; and Levi took Reuben aside, and they sent against the men who were on the right and the left, and they slew them' — Jubilees credits Judah and Levi specifically with the battlefield victory over Esau's forces. The Tewahedo Solomonic-dynasty (descending from Judah through David) preserves a memory of the Judah-as-battlefield-leader patriarchal-canonical pattern: the Tewahedo king (nəguś) takes the field with the priest (kǝhnät) accompanying — the Judah-Levi battlefield partnership is the canonical-patriarchal antecedent of the Tewahedo king-and-priest joint-leadership pattern at moments of national crisis.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 38:2 (Esau-Jacob war (38:2)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the Lord gave Joseph favour in the sight of Potiphar, and Potiphar set him over all that he had, and the Lord prospered all that he did' — Jubilees preserves the Gen 39:2-3 prosperity-under-Joseph narrative. Tewahedo Joseph-as-Christ Holy-Week typology reads this verse as the canonical pattern: the rejected-righteous-brother prospers in the household of his Gentile master, prefiguring Christ's victorious-rejection-vindication. The Tewahedo Holy-Week Wednesday commemoration (Joseph's day) draws on this verse for the Christ-prefiguring-prosperity-in-affliction motif.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 39:2 (Joseph in Egypt (39:2)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And after these things, in the third year of this week, the wife of his master lifted up her eyes and looked at Joseph, and she loved him' — Jubilees follows the Gen 39 sequence with the Potiphar's-wife temptation. Tewahedo monastic-chastity formation reads this verse as the canonical pattern: external temptation comes first as the look-of-the-eyes (the visual seizure precedes the verbal proposition). The Tewahedo desert-fathers' discipline of custody-of-the-eyes (mäḫläla aʿyəntä) finds canonical anchor in the Joseph-narrative's careful presentation of the temptation sequence: eyes → words → propositions → physical confrontation, each stage offering a distinct opportunity for refusal.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 39:6 (Joseph in Egypt (39:6)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Joseph remembered the Lord and the words which Jacob, his father, used to read from amongst the words of Abraham, that no man should commit fornication with a woman who hath a husband, that for him the punishment of death hath been ordained in the heavens before the Most High Lord' — Joseph's refusal is grounded in the patriarchal-canonical pre-Mosaic adultery law from Abraham (cited as the words 'Jacob used to read'). Tewahedo doctrine of cumulative-canonical formation: Joseph the young man can refuse adultery because he has been catechized by his father from his grandfather's words — the canonical-pedagogical chain Abraham → Jacob → Joseph is the canonical anchor for the Tewahedo family-catechism tradition. The Tewahedo father's responsibility to read patriarchal-canonical books to his children before puberty is canonically rooted here.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 39:10 (Joseph in Egypt (39:10)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the king commanded that they should arouse Joseph out of the prison: and they arose him out of the prison, and shaved him, and clothed him with new raiment, and presented him before the king' — Jubilees preserves the Gen 41:14 raising-from-prison narrative. Tewahedo Holy-Week Friday-into-Saturday-into-Sunday liturgical pattern reads this as the canonical sequence: Joseph is raised from the pit-prison (cf. tomb), shaved (cf. body-preparation), clothed with new raiment (cf. resurrection-glorification), presented before the king (cf. ascension). The four-fold raised-shaved-clothed-presented sequence is preserved typologically in Tewahedo Easter-day liturgy: the priest enacts each stage in the Resurrection commemoration.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 40:5 (Joseph rises (40:5)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the king said unto Joseph: I have dreamed two dreams, and there is no man who can interpret them. And now I have heard concerning thee, that when thou hearest dreams thou dost interpret them' — Pharaoh acknowledges Joseph's wisdom-from-the-Lord. Jubilees presents Joseph as the canonical-OT example of Spirit-wisdom-given-to-the-rejected-righteous: the prison-vindicated dreamer becomes the interpreter for the king who cannot understand his own dreams. The Tewahedo monastic discernment-tradition (märǝḥǝbǝr — 'spiritual fatherhood' charism) draws on this canonical OT pattern: the genuinely-Spirit-led-interpreter sees what the worldly-king cannot, and the worldly-king must acknowledge his dependence on Spirit-given counsel.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 40:7 (Joseph rises (40:7)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he gave him to wife Asenath, the daughter of Potiphar, the priest of Heliopolis, the chief cook' — Jubilees preserves Joseph's marriage to Asenath, the daughter of Potiphar the priest of Heliopolis (later Egyptian apocryphal-Jewish literature substantially develops Asenath's conversion). The Tewahedo tradition of canonical-conversion of Gentile-spouse: Joseph's wife is a Gentile-pagan-priest's daughter, yet she becomes the mother of Ephraim and Manasseh (Israel's continuation). The Tewahedo's distinctive pastoral practice of welcoming and catechizing the Gentile-or-non-Orthodox spouse of an Orthodox member into full sacramental fellowship has its OT canonical anchor in Asenath's reception.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 40:10 (Joseph rises (40:10)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the fifth year Tamar was reckoned unto Onan, his second son, that he should take her, and Onan said: I will not give my seed to my brother, the seed of Tamar — and the Lord slew him before my face for the wickedness which he did, and slew Onan also for the same' — Jubilees preserves Onan's sin of refusing to raise up seed for Tamar (Gen 38:9). Tewahedo doctrine on the obligation of the brother-in-law to raise up seed for the dead brother (the yǝbäm or levirate-relative obligation) finds canonical anchor here: the obligation is so weighty that its refusal is named alongside the worst-category covenant violations. The Tewahedo modern canonical-pastoral practice of supporting widows from within the extended family draws warrant from this passage.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 41:8 (Judah and Tamar (41:8)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Tamar conceived, and she bore twin sons; and she called the name of the one Perez, and the name of the other Zerah' — Jubilees follows the Gen 38 narrative of Perez and Zerah. The Tewahedo Christological-genealogy tradition: Perez is the ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18-22 = Mt 1:3) and ultimately of Christ. Tamar — the Canaanite-presumed-prostitute-daughter-in-law — preserves the Davidic-Messianic line through her courageous-faithful action where Judah faltered. The Tewahedo Marian-typology tradition reads Tamar (with Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba, and Mary) as the four-women-in-the-Messianic-genealogy, each receiving canonical-pastoral honor as faithful-female-link-in-the-Messianic-line.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 41:23 (Judah and Tamar (41:23)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And we showed to Judah that he should not seek her any more, because of the judgment of the Holy of holies; and Tamar was acquitted, and she became more righteous than he. And he had relations with her no more' — Judah's confession 'she is more righteous than I' (Gen 38:26) is preserved with explicit divine ratification: Tamar is canonically vindicated, Judah is canonically rebuked. Tewahedo penitential canon reads this as the canonical pattern for the confession-of-the-stronger-sinner-against-the-weaker-victim: Judah's straightforward acknowledgment 'she is more righteous than I' is the model formula for confession when the wronged party turns out to be canonically-just. The Tewahedo confessor's näsḫa-of-acknowledgment formula draws verbal anchor here.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 41:25 (Judah and Tamar (41:25)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the first year of the third week of the forty-fifth jubilee a famine began to come into the land, and the rain refused to be given to the earth, for none whatever fell' — Jubilees preserves the Gen 42:1 famine context. The Tewahedo agrarian-monastic tradition reads famine-narratives canonically: corporate suffering is the divine instrument for canonical-reunification (Jacob's family is reunified through famine-driven travel). The Tewahedo täzkar-ǝgziʾabəḥer (commemoration of God) tradition during years of agricultural distress draws on the Joseph-famine pattern: collective suffering as the matrix of providential mercy preparing reconciliation.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 42:1 (Joseph reveals himself (42:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he commanded that he should keep one of them in prison, but the others he sent away with corn, and he said: bring Benjamin to me' — Joseph's demand for Benjamin's presence as the condition for the brothers' return preserves the Gen 42 narrative. Tewahedo canonical-reading: the demand-for-Benjamin is functionally the demand-for-Jacob's-fully-trusting-the-arrangement, since Benjamin is Jacob's last-remaining-child-of-Rachel and is dearer than even Joseph was. The Tewahedo pastoral pattern of asking the penitent to entrust the most precious thing as the canonical-test of repentance draws on this canonical OT pattern.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 42:16 (Joseph reveals himself (42:16)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the third year of that week Jacob sent his sons to Egypt to buy them food, and Benjamin went with them' — Jacob finally consents to Benjamin's going to Egypt. Tewahedo discernment-tradition reads this verse as the canonical pattern of the father's permission-after-resistance: the patriarchal-father initially refuses, the canonical circumstances tighten, the refusal yields to entrustment — the entrustment is canonical-discipline-yielding-providential-good. The Tewahedo gədl (saintly-biography) genre traces this pattern in Tewahedo saints' lives: initial resistance to a divine call yields to consent through canonical-discipline, and the consent then becomes vehicle of providential good.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 43:1 (Silver-cup test (43:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he commanded the steward of his house: hide my silver cup in the sack of my brother Benjamin; and let his money for the corn be also therein' — Joseph's silver-cup ruse-test of his brothers' loyalty to Benjamin. Tewahedo penitential canon reads this canonically: Joseph's ruse is not a sin (deception-with-good-end is permitted to the wronged-righteous-party) but a canonical-permission. The Tewahedo confessor's-ruse tradition (the confessor may pose hypothetical scenarios or staged tests to discern the penitent's true disposition before granting full absolution) draws canonical warrant from this Joseph-canonical-test pattern.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 43:18 (Silver-cup test (43:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the first year of the third week in the forty-fifth jubilee, in the second month, Jacob went down to Egypt, his sons with him, and they came to the well of the oath in the seventh of this second month, and he tarried there seven days' — Jacob deliberately tarries seven days at Beersheba (well of the oath) before proceeding to Egypt. Jubilees uniquely preserves the seven-day delay as a canonical-liturgical pause. Tewahedo monastic-departure tradition: before any major journey or transition, a seven-day prayerful pause at a place of patriarchal-altar memory (Beersheba was Abraham's altar of the well of the oath, Gen 21:33; Jub 24:25). The Tewahedo seven-day-week is canonically a unit of canonical-discernment-pause before action — pattern rooted in Jacob's pause.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 44:1 (Jacob to Egypt (44:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the Lord appeared to him in a vision in the night, and said unto him: Jacob, Jacob. And he said: behold, here am I. And He said: I am the God of thy fathers, the God of Abraham, and Isaac; fear not to go down into Egypt, for I will make thee there into a great people. I will go down with thee, and I will bring thee up, and in this land shalt thou be buried, and Joseph shall put his hand upon thy eyes' — God explicitly promises to accompany Jacob to Egypt and to bring him back. Tewahedo Immanuel-typology reads this as the canonical-OT proof of God's accompanying-presence with his people-in-exile: 'I will go down with thee.' The Tewahedo distinctive ecclesiology of God-with-the-Diaspora — extending to the Tewahedo's own historical experience of dispersion under persecution — draws on this verse. The 'Joseph shall put his hand upon thy eyes' detail anchors the Tewahedo deathbed-ritual of the eldest-son closing the parent's eyes at the moment of death.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 44:5 (Jacob to Egypt (44:5)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And these are the names of the sons of Jacob who went into Egypt with their father: Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob; and these are the names of the sons of Reuben: Hanoch, and Pallu, and Hezron, and Carmi — five' — Jubilees preserves the comprehensive Israelite-clan genealogy that descends to Egypt (Gen 46:8-27). The Tewahedo Senodos-genealogical tradition (each Tewahedo bishop traces a genealogy backward to one of the seventy Israelites who descended to Egypt) finds canonical anchor here. The Tewahedo monastic-genealogical chronicle tradition (each major monastery preserves its founder's genealogy backward through canonical-Israelite lineage) treats Jub 44:11-33 as a foundational text.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 44:11 (Jacob to Egypt (44:11)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Israel went into the country of Egypt, into the land of Goshen, and Joseph went to meet his father Jacob in the land of Goshen, and he fell on his father's neck and wept' — Jubilees preserves the Gen 46:29 emotional reunion. Tewahedo iconographic tradition treats the Joseph-meets-Jacob embrace as a canonical-typological-image of the Father-receiving-the-prodigal-son-with-tears (cf. Lk 15:20 'his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him'). The Tewahedo Holy-Week prodigal-Sunday observance draws on the Joseph-Jacob embrace as canonical OT prefiguration: the embrace, the falling on the neck, the tears, all preserved verbally in the Gospel.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 45:1 (Jacob settled in Egypt (45:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and Jacob and his sons dwelt in the land of Goshen, in the best part of the land of Egypt, and Joseph nourished them' — Jacob blesses Pharaoh (Gen 47:7, 10). The patriarch-blessing-the-Gentile-king pattern is canonical-Tewahedo political-theology: the Orthodox patriarch (in the Tewahedo case, the abun or patriarch of the Ethiopian Church) may legitimately bless the civil-political ruler — even when the ruler is non-Orthodox or non-Christian — because civil authority is divinely ordained (Rom 13:1). The Tewahedo coronation-prayer tradition (the abun's blessing of the newly-crowned nəguś) draws canonical-patriarchal warrant from Jacob's blessing of Pharaoh.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 45:13 (Jacob settled in Egypt (45:13)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Jacob blessed his son Joseph, and the sons of Joseph, and ate the bread of Egypt with him during seventeen years; and he served Joseph as a father in everything according to his desire' — Jubilees uniquely emphasizes Jacob 'served Joseph as a father in everything': the patriarchal-father subordinates himself to his providentially-elevated son for the rest of his life. Tewahedo monastic-humility tradition: the spiritual father is not above receiving spiritual fatherhood from his own child where the child's office requires it — Jacob is Joseph's biological father but accepts Joseph's authority as Egypt's governor. The Tewahedo distinctive practice of the elder-bishop bowing to a younger-but-higher-ranking bishop in canonical-liturgical-procession draws warrant from Jacob's example.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 45:16 (Jacob settled in Egypt (45:16)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And Joseph died being a hundred and ten years old; seventeen years he lived in the land of Canaan, and ten years he was a servant, and three years in prison, and eighty years he was under the king, ruling all the land of Egypt' — Jubilees gives the precise breakdown of Joseph's 110 years: 17 + 10 + 3 + 80 (canonical biographical precision). Tewahedo monastic-biographical tradition (gədl genre) follows this precision-of-stages-pattern: each gədl of a Tewahedo saint enumerates the precise canonical-stages of the saint's life (childhood + monastic-discipleship + spiritual-warfare + active ministry + death). The Tewahedo gədl literary form's canonical anchor is the Jubilees-Joseph-biographical precision.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 46:5 (Joseph dies; slavery begins (46:5)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And he that knew not Joseph reigned in the land of Egypt, and went forth from Memphis, and entered into Goshen, and spoke unto the Israelites in his own language. And he multiplied them and the king persecuted them' — Jubilees preserves the Ex 1:8 'new king arose who knew not Joseph' moment as the canonical onset of Egyptian persecution. Tewahedo persecution-memory: every generation of Tewahedo Christians has known the 'king who knew not Joseph' figure — the persecutor who has lost the memory of an earlier covenant-of-mutual-benefit. The canonical category 'king who knew not Joseph' is preserved in Tewahedo theological lexicon as the type of the cyclical-amnesiac-persecutor.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 46:13 (Joseph dies; slavery begins (46:13)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the king of Egypt went forth against the Canaanites with chariots and a multitude of horsemen and with much people, and he smote them and slew them all, and pursued them as far as the borders of Canaan' — Jubilees uniquely preserves a battlefield account of the persecuting Pharaoh's wider military campaigns. The pattern (the persecutor of the covenant-people is also a wider regional aggressor) is canonically established. Tewahedo political-theology distinguishes legitimate-defensive-war from imperial-aggressive-war: the pharaoh of the persecution is also the pharaoh of regional-imperial-aggression. The two are not coincidentally co-occurring but causally linked: the covenant-amnesiac is also the regional-imperial-aggressor. The Tewahedo's resistance to Mussolini's 1936 invasion was framed in exactly this canonical category — the imperial-aggressor of 1936 was also the persecutor-of-Tewahedo-Christianity in occupied territory.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 46:14 (Joseph dies; slavery begins (46:14)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the seventh week, in the seventh year, in the forty-seventh jubilee, thy father went forth from the land of Canaan, and thou wast born in the fourth week, in the sixth year thereof, in the forty-eighth jubilee; this was the time of tribulation on the children of Israel' — Jubilees precisely dates Moses' birth to a canonical-tribulation-period (parallel to the canonical-precision of Christ's birth being dated to a tribulation-period under Herod). Tewahedo Mosaic-Christological typology reads this as the doubled OT-NT pattern: the deliverer is born in the canonical-tribulation-context; the Herod-figure (whether Pharaoh of Ex 1 or Herod of Mt 2) seeks the deliverer's life from his infancy. The Tewahedo Holy Innocents commemoration draws on this canonical-doubled deliverer-imperilled-from-birth pattern.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 47:1 (Moses' birth (47:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And thy mother hid thee three months, and they told regarding her. And she made an ark for thee, and covered it with pitch and asphalt, and placed it in the flags on the bank of the river, and she placed thee in it three days, and thy sister Miriam guarded thee from a distance' — Jubilees preserves the Ex 2:1-4 Moses-in-the-ark narrative with the explicit three-day-detail. The Tewahedo Moses-as-Christ-type tradition reads the three-day-ark-in-the-water as the canonical OT prefiguration of Christ's three-day burial. The 'placed three days' detail (which is not in Exodus) anchors the typological reading: Moses-in-the-ark for three days = Christ-in-the-tomb for three days. Tewahedo Easter-vigil liturgy preserves the Moses-ark / Christ-tomb correspondence in the readings.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 47:5 (Moses' birth (47:5)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the daughter of Pharaoh came to bathe in the river, and she heard thy voice crying, and she told her maidens to bring thee forth, and they brought thee unto her. And she took thee out of the ark, and she had compassion on thee. And thy sister said unto her: shall I go and call to thee one of the Hebrew women, who shall nurse and suckle this babe for thee? And she said unto her: go. And she went and called thy mother, and she gave her wages, and she nursed thee' — Moses is rescued by the daughter of Pharaoh, suckled by his own mother. Tewahedo readings preserve a canonical-irony: the daughter of the persecutor is the deliverer's first-Gentile-protector. The Tewahedo distinctive pastoral practice of warmly welcoming and catechizing the children of those who persecuted the Tewahedo (the children of fascist-occupation-collaborators after 1941, for example) draws canonical anchor from Pharaoh's-daughter's-compassion canonical category.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 47:9 (Moses' birth (47:9)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And in the sixth year of the third week of the forty-ninth jubilee thou didst depart and dwell in the land of Midian five weeks and one year. And thou didst return into Egypt in the second week in the second year in the fiftieth jubilee. And thou thyself knowest what He spake unto thee on Mount Sinai, and what prince Mastema desired to do with thee when thou wast returning into Egypt on the way when thou didst meet him at the lodging-place' — Jubilees uniquely identifies the night-encounter at the lodging (Ex 4:24, 'the Lord met him and sought to kill him') as Mastema's attack rather than the Lord's. This is a profound theological clarification: the Mastema-attack reading protects the divine goodness while preserving the canonical narrative. Tewahedo theodicy preserves the Jubilees clarification: episodes ascribed to the Lord in the older canonical text are read as divinely-permitted Mastema-attacks where the moral content of the action would be otherwise inscrutable.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 48:1 (Exodus (48:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And did not he wish with all his power to slay thee, and deliver the Egyptians from thy hand, when he saw thee was being sent to execute judgment and vengeance on the Egyptians?' — Jubilees explicitly names Mastema's motivation: he sought to kill Moses to protect his Egyptian-demonological-fiefdom from the coming judgment. Tewahedo demonological theology preserves this: the demons of false-worship-and-political-oppression are not neutral but actively defend their territorial claim against the deliverer. The canonical pattern (Mastema attempts to kill Moses → Mastema attempts to kill the deliverer at every subsequent moment of canonical-history → Mastema attempts to kill Christ from infancy, cf. Herod) is the Tewahedo demonological-historical reading.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 48:2 (Exodus (48:2)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And we permitted them to do all evil deeds, but we did not permit them to be healed by the hands of the Egyptians; and the Lord smote them with malignant ulcers' — Jubilees uniquely preserves the angelic-orchestration of the plagues: the angels of presence permit specific demonic-tormentations against Egypt and explicitly prevent Egyptian healing. Tewahedo angelology reads this as the canonical pattern for the angelic-providential-orchestration of historical-judgment: angels neither cause nor merely-observe judgment but actively manage its scope and persistence. The Tewahedo distinctive Friday-and-Wednesday prayers (the weekly fast-days commemorating Christ's betrayal and crucifixion) include intercessory petitions invoking angelic-orchestration against contemporary historical evils.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 48:13 (Exodus (48:13)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the Israelites were prepared and ready to be saved, and on the fifteenth day of the third month, even on Passover, they sang a song of praise, having been delivered from the hands of the Egyptians, and from the unclean sea' — Jubilees preserves the Red-Sea crossing-as-Passover-canonical-anchor: deliverance is liturgically datable to Passover. The Tewahedo Fasika (Passover-Easter) liturgical tradition preserves the canonical-doubled-celebration: the Old-Covenant Red-Sea crossing AND the New-Covenant resurrection occur on the same canonical-liturgical date. The 'song of praise' detail (Ex 15) is sung in Tewahedo Easter-vigil liturgy preserving the canonical-OT-NT-doubled celebration.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 48:18 (Exodus (48:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'For on this night — the beginning of the festival and the beginning of the joy — ye were eating the Passover in Egypt, when all the powers of Mastema had been let loose to slay all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh to the firstborn of the captive maid-servant in the mill, and to the cattle. And this is the sign which the Lord gave them: into every house on the lintels of which they saw the blood of a lamb of the firstlings, the destroyer should not enter to slay, but should pass over' — Jubilees uniquely makes Mastema's powers (not 'the destroyer' of Ex 12 anonymously) the agent of the firstborn-slaying. The Passover-blood-on-the-lintels canonically restrains the Mastema-attack. Tewahedo Fasika theology preserves this: the blood-of-the-lamb (eucharistic anti-type) is the canonical defense against the demonic-firstborn-slaying threat. Every Tewahedo communicant is, by canonical-typology, 'within the bloodstained doorway' that Mastema cannot enter.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 49:2 (Passover (49:2)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And all Israel was eating the flesh of the Passover lamb, and drinking the wine, and was praising and blessing the Lord God of their fathers, and was ready to go forth from under the yoke of Egypt, and from the evil bondage' — Jubilees explicitly preserves the lamb-AND-wine pairing at the original Passover. Tewahedo Fasika eucharistic-theology reads this as the canonical doubled-anchor: bread/lamb + wine, the eucharistic-canonical structure, is patriarchal-Mosaic, not later-apostolic. The 'flesh of the Passover lamb + wine' is the canonical-OT eucharistic-prototype. Tewahedo Fasika liturgy preserves the canonical lamb-flesh-and-wine doublet: the Tewahedo Anaphora of the Apostles draws on this pre-Christic eucharistic-prototype as the Mäṣḥafä-Kufāle canonical-OT eucharistic anchor.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 49:6 (Passover (49:6)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And let the children of Israel come and observe the Passover on the day of its fixed time, on the fourteenth day of the first month, between the evenings, from the third part of the day to the third part of the night; for two portions of the day are given to the light, and a third part to the evening' — Jubilees fixes the precise time of Passover observance (third-of-the-day to third-of-the-night). Tewahedo Fasika preserves the precise canonical-temporal observance with the same threefold-day structuring. The 'two portions of the day given to the light, a third part to the evening' canonical-cosmology informs the Tewahedo liturgical-day reckoning: light-portions and evening-portion are canonically structured into the Tewahedo daily-office (matins + sext + vespers, three offices precisely matching the canonical-thirds).
entries.attribution: Jubilees 49:10 (Passover (49:10)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And let the children of Israel observe it, and celebrate it from year to year throughout all their generations, once in the year, on the fourteenth day of the first month, between the evenings, in the second week. And no man may eat it in the morning, nor in any time of the day, save in the time of the night until the rising of the sun. And the man that observeth it on the fourteenth day in the evening, he shall acquit himself of his guilt' — Passover observance acquits-of-guilt: the canonical Passover is canonically-atoning. Tewahedo Fasika theology preserves this: the proper observance of the canonical-Passover IS itself the canonical-atonement-for-the-year's-sin. The Tewahedo's distinctive emphasis on liturgical-act-AS-atonement (against any 'mere commemoration' reading of the eucharist) draws warrant from Jub 49:15: the observance itself acquits, not just the recollection-of-the-historical-event.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 49:15 (Passover (49:15)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And after this law I made known unto thee the days of the Sabbaths in the desert of Sin which is between Elim and Sinai. And I told thee of the Sabbaths of the land on Mount Sinai, and I told thee of the jubilee years in the sabbaths of years' — Jubilees frames the book's entire content as the divinely-revealed system of Sabbaths-AND-jubilees given to Moses on Sinai. The book IS Mäṣḥafä-Kufāle ('Book of Divisions') — the canonical book-OF-divisions of time. Tewahedo liturgical-cosmology preserves Jubilees' Sabbath-and-jubilee structure as the canonical framework for the Tewahedo täzkar (commemoration) calendar: every Tewahedo täzkar is calculated using the Jubilees-Mosaic Sabbatical-of-Sabbaticals system, anchored in this verse.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 50:1 (Sabbath and Jubilee finale (50:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'And the jubilees will pass by, until Israel is cleansed from all guilt of fornication, and uncleanness, and pollution, and sin, and error, and dwelleth with confidence in all the land, and there will be no more a Satan or any evil one, and the land will be clean from that time for evermore' — Jubilees presents an explicit eschatological-cleansing of the land, with Satan removed, and the land permanently clean. The Tewahedo eschatological-hope draws canonical anchor here: the final consummation is not merely individual-spiritual-resurrection but cosmic-territorial-cleansing-and-the-permanent-removal-of-demonic-presence. The Tewahedo distinctive emphasis on the consecration-of-the-land (the Tewahedo's sacred-geography tradition that sees specific Ethiopian holy mountains and lakes as canonically-sanctified-territory) finds canonical anchor in Jubilees' jubilee-of-jubilees-eschatology.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 50:4 (Sabbath and Jubilee finale (50:4)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'But the Sabbath day of the Lord thy God ye shall not do any work thereon, but that which ye have prepared for yourselves on the sixth day, so as to eat, and drink, and rest, and keep Sabbath from all work on that day, and to bless the Lord your God, who has given you a day of festival, and a holy day; and a day of the holy kingdom for all Israel is this day among their days for ever' — Jubilees inscribes the Sabbath as 'a day of the holy kingdom for all Israel' — a day liturgically tasting the Kingdom of God in advance. Tewahedo Saturday-Sabbath theology (uniquely among major Christian communions in preserving Saturday-Sabbath alongside Sunday-Lord's-Day) reads the Sabbath as canonical foretaste-of-the-Kingdom. The Tewahedo monastic Saturday-vigil tradition (more elaborate than Sunday in some monastic communities) draws warrant from Jub 50:9's 'holy kingdom day' framing.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 50:9 (Sabbath and Jubilee finale (50:9)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: 'Whoever does any work thereon, or goes a journey, or tills (his) farm whether in his house or any other place, and whoever lights a fire, or rides on any beast, or travels by ship on the sea, and whoever strikes or kills anything, or slaughters a beast or a bird, or whoever catches an animal or a bird or a fish, or whoever fasts or makes war on the Sabbaths: the man who does any of these things on the Sabbath shall die' — Jubilees gives the strictest possible Sabbath-prohibition list, with the canonical 'shall die' formula. The Tewahedo Saturday-Sabbath observance preserves this strictness in canonical-pastoral form: Saturday is a day of complete rest, abstention from agricultural-and-commercial work, and elevated-spiritual-focus. The Tewahedo's distinctive observation of BOTH Saturday (canonical-OT Sabbath) and Sunday (Christ's-resurrection-Lord's-Day) gives the Tewahedo the canonical-fullness of weekly-time-sanctification, anchored in Jub 50.
entries.attribution: Jubilees 50:12 (Sabbath and Jubilee finale (50:12)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.

entries.summary: Ephrem reads Israel's prodigious multiplication in Egypt as the patriarchal blessing of Gen 1:28 surviving inside a hostile crown: the seed cannot be extinguished, because the messianic line is the seed-bearer of the world. Tewahedo commentary follows this reading when teaching that the Hebrew people are preserved through Egyptian captivity precisely so that the Saviour may issue from them.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus I.1 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Pharaoh's edict that every male Hebrew infant be cast into the river is, for Ephrem, the first scriptural sign of Mastema-mirror tyranny: the murderous power decrees the very fate it will suffer. The plague of the firstborn and the Red Sea reverse Pharaoh's decree on his own house. Tewahedo reads this as the canonical pattern by which oppressor measures are returned upon oppressors.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus I.4 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: When the mother of Moses sees that her child is 'goodly' (asteios), Ephrem reads this not as physical beauty alone but as divinely-bestowed countenance, a foreshadowing of the 'fairest of the sons of men' (Ps 45:2). The radiance her eyes detect is the same radiance that will shine from Moses' face at Sinai and from the face of Christ at the Transfiguration.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus II.2 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: The three-month hiding of the infant Moses, ended by his being laid in an ark of bulrushes pitched with bitumen, is for Ephrem the first Pascal typology of the Old Testament: the ark is the tomb, the three months are the days of burial in cipher, and the deliverer is preserved through the very waters that should have destroyed him. Tewahedo carries this reading as part of its Pascal lectionary catechesis: Moses-in-the-ark anticipates Christ-in-the-tomb.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Sermo de Domino Nostro 3-4 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: Pharaoh's daughter, drawing the Hebrew infant out of the river and giving him a name, is for Ephrem the first prefiguration of the Gentile Church receiving the Word from among the Hebrews. The Egyptian princess does what her father refuses to do; the daughter of the oppressor saves the deliverer of the oppressed. Tewahedo cites this as a canonical anchor for Gentile-incorporation into the people of God.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus II.5 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Moses meeting Zipporah at the well in Midian, after defending her father's flock from hostile shepherds, is read by Ephrem as the second well-betrothal after Jacob and Rachel: a prophet meeting his bride at a well of living water. The pattern recurs at Sychar, where the true Bridegroom meets the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well (Jn 4). Tewahedo treats Ex 2:21 as a canonical link in the well-betrothal chain culminating in the Bridegroom-Christ.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus II.10 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: The bush that burns yet is not consumed is, for Ephrem, the first canonical type of the Theotokos: the holy fire of divinity dwelling within the bush of Mary's flesh without consuming it. Tewahedo iconography seats the burning bush among its earliest Marian types, and the bush is a regular figure in Marian hymnody: 'the bush that bore the fire and was not burned.'
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Nativity I.18; cp. Hymns on the Crucifixion I.2-3 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: 'Loose thy shoe from off thy foot, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground' — Ephrem hears in this not only Moses' singular calling but the rule for entering the sanctuary, that what carries the dust of the world is removed before standing where God has descended. Tewahedo carries this as the canonical warrant for entering the Beta Maryam barefoot, a practice preserved in every Tewahedo church to this day.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus III.2 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: 'I AM THAT I AM' is, for Ephrem, the divine Name revealed in advance of the Incarnation as the very ground on which the Word may later say 'Before Abraham was, I am' (Jn 8:58). The Name is not given to Moses as a label but as a confession: God reveals himself as the eternal subsisting One whose being underwrites every act of deliverance. Tewahedo reads Ex 3:14 and Jn 8:58 as a single canonical disclosure.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Sermo de Domino Nostro 4-5 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: Moses' hand made leprous in the bosom and then restored is, for Ephrem, the sign of the Incarnation given before the fact: humanity has become diseased in its hidden parts, and the Lord places it within his own bosom to bring it forth healed. The same hand that becomes leprous becomes healing for the leprous — a foreshadowing of the Word's assumption of the very flesh he will cleanse.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus IV.3 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Water turned to blood at Moses' word is the sign of judgment; water turned to wine at Cana is the sign of joy. Ephrem reads the two miracles as a single canonical inclusio: the first prophet inverts the river to bring judgment on Egypt; the true Lord inverts the water-pots to bring gladness to the wedding. The Word who turned the Nile to blood for accusation turns the jars of purification into the wine of the new covenant.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus IV.5 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: The hostile encounter at the lodging-place, where the Lord seems to seek Moses' life, Ephrem reads as a covenant-rupture answered by covenant-restoration: it is the failure to circumcise Moses' son that opens the breach, and Zipporah's prompt circumcision that closes it. The Tewahedo reading harmonizes the canonical witness with Jub 48:1-2, which names Mastema as the immediate agent; the divine permission and the demonic accusation work together to vindicate the covenant.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus IV.20 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: 'I will take you to me for a people, and I will be to you a God' — Ephrem hears in this verse the completion of the Abrahamic-Isaac-Jacob promise: the patriarchal seed becomes a peoplehood under a single covenanted Name. Tewahedo cites Ex 6:7 as the canonical formula on which both Sinai and the New-Covenant 'I will be their God and they shall be my people' (Jer 31:33; Rev 21:3) depend.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus VI.3 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Aaron's rod swallowing the rods-turned-serpents of the magicians is, for Ephrem, an early figure of the Crucified Christ swallowing the dragon: the wood that becomes a serpent becomes a devouring serpent, and the devouring is itself the salvation. The Cross — wood that becomes the throne of the Serpent-conqueror — accomplishes in reality what the rod accomplished in type.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion IV.10-12 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: The lamb is to be set aside on the tenth day of the month — and on this very tenth day, Ephrem reads, the true Lamb entered Jerusalem to be set aside for the slaughter. The four days between the setting-aside and the killing correspond to the Holy-Week interval between Palm Sunday and Crucifixion. Tewahedo Pascal catechesis preserves this counting in its Holy-Week observances.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion II.5-7 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: The lamb is roasted whole, eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. Ephrem reads each prescription as eucharistic precedent: the unbroken lamb is the unbroken body of Christ; the unleavened bread is the bread that carries no leaven of malice; the bitter herbs are the bitter cup of the Passion. Tewahedo Anaphora retains this canonical OT prototype as one of its earliest Pascal anchors.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion II.8 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: Blood struck upon the two side-posts and the upper lintel of the door traces, for Ephrem, the very figure of the Cross over each Israelite household: a mark in the shape of the salvation that the blood signifies. The destroyer who passes over the marked door does so because the mark is the Cross before the Cross. Tewahedo cites this as a canonical eucharistic-demonic-defense anchor: the Pascal blood marks the household; the eucharist marks the soul.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion III.1-3 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'Neither shall ye break a bone thereof' — Ephrem treats this prescription as one of the most precise prophetic anchors in the Old Testament, fulfilled verbatim at Jn 19:36 when the soldiers do not break Christ's legs. The Lamb of God remains the unbroken lamb of Exodus. Tewahedo reads Ex 12:46 and Jn 19:36 as a single canonical disclosure of the same lamb.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion III.10 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: The pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, leading Israel through the wilderness, is for Ephrem the canonical figure of Christ's two natures: the cloud that veils the fire is the humanity that veils the divinity, yet the veiling does not extinguish the radiance. Tewahedo reads the pillar as the first systematic OT diptych of the Incarnation.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XIII.7 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Moses stretches out the rod over the sea, and Ephrem hears in the gesture the shape of the Cross extended over the waters of baptism. The rod that splits the sea is the same wood that, in the new dispensation, splits the waters of death so that the baptized may walk through on dry ground. Tewahedo reads the Red Sea and the baptismal font as a single canonical passageway.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion V.4-6 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: Israel passes through the sea on dry ground with the waters as a wall on either hand. Paul reads this as 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea' (1 Cor 10:2); Ephrem follows Paul and reads Ex 14:22 as the founding scriptural figure of Christian baptism. Tewahedo carries this as the principal OT type of its baptismal liturgy: the people pass through the waters and emerge a people.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XIV.6 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Pharaoh's host drowned in the very waters through which Israel walks dry is, for Ephrem, the canonical anti-type of baptism: what saves the believer destroys the pursuer. The devil and the powers of the old age are drowned in the font as Pharaoh was drowned in the sea. Tewahedo reads the renunciation of Satan in its baptismal rite as the liturgical correlate of the Red-Sea drowning.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XIV.10 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: 'I will sing unto the Lord, for he hath triumphed gloriously' — the first canonical hymn of victory, sung on the shore of the sea by the redeemed. Ephrem treats Ex 15:1 as the prototype of all Pascal hymnody: every Easter song of the Church is a continuation of Moses' shore-song. Tewahedo mäzmur-tradition recognizes the Song of Moses among its earliest canonical warrants for hymnic praise after deliverance.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XV.1 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: The Lord shows Moses a tree, and the tree cast into the bitter waters of Marah makes them sweet. Ephrem reads the wood as the Cross before its time: what sweetens the waters of the world is the wood of the Cross cast into them. Tewahedo Holy-Week catechesis cites Ex 15:25 as one of its principal OT cross-typology anchors.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion VIII.4 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'I will rain bread from heaven for you' — the manna of the wilderness is for Ephrem the direct prophetic anchor of Jn 6: 'I am the bread which came down from heaven.' The wilderness bread sustains the body for a day; the Eucharist sustains the soul for eternity. Tewahedo Anaphora cites Ex 16:4 and Jn 6 together as the OT-NT diptych of the eucharistic gift.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XVI.2 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: When Israel sees the manna they say 'man hu' — 'what is it?' — and the question itself becomes the name. Ephrem hears in this the canonical instinct that the heavenly food cannot be named by its likeness to anything earthly; the name is a confession of mystery. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites this as the OT antecedent of its own anaphoral language of 'mystery,' 'gift,' and 'medicine of life.'
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XVI.6 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: The rock struck by Moses' rod pours out water for the thirsty people, and Ephrem joins Paul (1 Cor 10:4) in reading the rock as Christ. The striking is the Crucifixion; the water is the Spirit and the eucharistic stream (Jn 19:34 — blood and water from the pierced side). Tewahedo treats Ex 17:6 and Jn 19:34 as a single canonical disclosure of the smitten Christ releasing the rivers of living water.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion IX.2-4 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: When Moses lifted up his hands Israel prevailed against Amalek; when he let them down Amalek prevailed. Ephrem reads the cruciform posture as the secret of the victory: Moses' arms outstretched are the Cross fore-figured, and the war is won not by the sword in the valley but by the cross-shape on the hill. Tewahedo carries this as the canonical OT type of Christian intercessory prayer in the cross-posture.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XVII.5 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Sinai wrapped in fire and smoke is, for Ephrem, the OT diptych of Pentecost: there the fire descends on a mountain and the people may not come near; here the fire descends on heads and tongues so that the people themselves become the mountain. Tewahedo reads Ex 19:18 and Acts 2 as the before-and-after of the divine fire — the same fire that thundered now rests on the believer without consuming.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XIX.8 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: 'I am the Lord thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage' — Ephrem reads the Pascal preface as the ground of every command that follows. The commandments are not arbitrary statutes but the rule-of-life of a delivered people; only the delivered are addressed by the Decalogue. Tewahedo catechesis preserves this priority of deliverance before commandment.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XX.1 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: 'Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy' — Ephrem reads Sabbath-rest as the canonical sign that creation is given a goal beyond labour: the Sabbath foreshadows the eighth-day rest of the Resurrection. Tewahedo alone among the major communions preserves both observances together — Saturday-Sabbath retained from Sinai and Sunday-Lord's-Day added from the Resurrection — and reads Ex 20:8 as the canonical anchor of the double observance.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XX.4 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Moses takes the blood and sprinkles it on the people, saying 'Behold the blood of the covenant, which the Lord hath made with you concerning all these words.' Ephrem hears in this the very formula that Christ will adopt verbatim at the Last Supper: 'This is the blood of the covenant.' Tewahedo Anaphora reads Ex 24:8 and Mt 26:28 as a single covenantal sentence completed by the Cross.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion VI.3-5 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: 'Let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them' — Ephrem reads this verse as the canonical warrant for every consecrated dwelling-place of God: the tabernacle prefigures the Incarnation ('the Word was made flesh and tabernacled among us,' Jn 1:14), and the Incarnation prefigures the Church. Tewahedo cites Ex 25:8 as the principal canonical anchor of its tabot tradition — the Ark-as-sanctuary at the center of every Tewahedo church.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XXV.2 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Two cherubim of gold beaten out of one piece, their wings stretched over the mercy seat, are for Ephrem the canonical sign that the divine throne rests over a place of propitiation, not over a tribunal alone. The mercy seat between the wings is the OT type of the Cross where mercy meets the Law. Tewahedo iconography preserves the cherub-flanked tabot in every sanctuary.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XXV.9 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: The plate of pure gold on the high priest's forehead, engraved 'Holiness to the Lord' — Ephrem reads this as the priestly title borne by the high priest in figure and by Christ in fulfilment: the True Priest carries the holiness of the Lord on his very person, not as an ornament but as his essence. Tewahedo priestly vestments retain the canonical pattern of the Aaronic mitre as a deliberate iconographic echo.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XXVIII.12 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Moses' intercession after the golden calf, in which he pleads against the wrath of God on behalf of the people, is for Ephrem the canonical OT prefiguration of Christ's high-priestly intercession (Jn 17; Heb 7:25). The mediator does not stand with the accuser but with the accused, even when the accused are guilty. Tewahedo reads Ex 32:11 as the principal OT figure of mediatorial prayer.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XXXII.4 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Moses breaks the first tablets at the foot of the mountain when he sees the calf; the second tablets are given after intercession and re-ascent. Ephrem reads the two givings as the canonical figure of the two Testaments: the first Adamic covenant broken at the foot of the mountain, the second covenant given through the One who ascends and descends. Tewahedo carries this as the principal OT figure of the OT-NT twofold canonical witness.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XXXII.10 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: 'There shall no man see me and live' — and yet Moses sees the Lord's back as he passes by. Ephrem reads the verse as the canonical disclosure that full vision of God is reserved for the Incarnation: only when the Word is made flesh may humanity behold the divine face without being consumed. Tewahedo reads Ex 33:20 and 1 Jn 1:1 ('which we have seen with our eyes') as a single canonical arc from veiled vision to face-to-face Word.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Sermo de Domino Nostro 7-8 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.

entries.summary: Moses descends with face shining and must put on a veil that the people may bear his presence. Paul reads the veil as the figure of the obscurity that remains over the OT until Christ takes it away (2 Cor 3:13-16). Ephrem follows Paul and reads Ex 34:30 as the canonical anchor of the veiled-to-unveiled progression: in the OT the prophet's borrowed glory must be covered; in the NT the believer beholds the Lord's own glory unveiled.
