entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XXXIV.11 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: When the tabernacle is finished, the cloud covers it and the glory of the Lord fills it. Ephrem reads the closing verse of Exodus as the canonical anticipation of the Apocalyptic vision: 'the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them' (Rev 21:3). The whole book moves from the house of bondage to the house of glory. Tewahedo eschatological catechesis treats Ex 40:34 as the OT bookend of the canonical hope completed in Rev 21.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XL.16 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: Cyril reads the angel's 'Hail, thou that art highly favoured' as the scriptural witness that Mary is uniquely graced — not merely a vessel selected at random but a creature on whom the eternal counsel of God has already rested. The greeting is itself an anticipation of the Incarnation: the angel speaks to her as already enclosing the favour that is about to descend in her womb. Tewahedo Marian theology cites this verse as one of its earliest patristic anchors of the Theotokos confession.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily I (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: The Magnificat — 'My soul doth magnify the Lord' — is for Cyril the first prophetic hymn of the New Covenant, spoken by the very mouth that bears the Word. Mary magnifies not by adding anything to God but by uniquely participating in his self-giving: she 'magnifies' the Lord precisely as the bearer of his enfleshment. Cyril reads the song as the OT prophetic genre — the canticles of Hannah, Miriam, Deborah — now fulfilled and surpassed in the Mother of the incarnate Word.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily II (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: Zacharias's tongue is loosed at the moment he writes 'His name is John,' and Cyril hears in the restoration the canonical sign that speech is given by faith and withheld by unbelief. The priestly silence imposed in the Holy Place is broken when the prophet consents to the angelic message; the canticle Benedictus follows immediately. Tewahedo lectionary preserves Zacharias's release as the OT-priestly-to-NT-prophetic hinge of the Lukan infancy.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily III (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'No room in the inn' — Cyril hears the verse as the canonical sign that the Word enters the world rejected from the start, foreshadowing the Cross's final rejection. The manger is itself a eucharistic image: the food-trough of beasts becomes the resting-place of the Bread that comes down from heaven. Tewahedo Nativity hymnody draws directly on this Cyrillian reading of the manger as proto-altar.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily I on the Nativity (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: Simeon's 'Nunc dimittis' is for Cyril the canonical confession that the seeing of the infant Christ IS the seeing of salvation: the eyes that behold the babe have beheld the salvation God prepared 'before the face of all peoples.' Cyril notes that Simeon does not say 'I have seen one who will save' but 'mine eyes have seen thy salvation' — the infant is the salvation, not merely its instrument. Tewahedo Compline preserves Nunc Dimittis as one of its earliest canonical-hymn anchors.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily IV (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: The twelve-year-old in the Temple says 'I must be about my Father's business,' and Cyril hears in the words the first public utterance of the Son's consciousness of his own divine sonship. The very child who is subject to his earthly parents declares without violation of that subjection that the Father in heaven is his proper Father. Tewahedo Christology cites Lk 2:49 as one of its earliest canonical anchors of the two-natures-in-one-person confession that Cyril would later make definitive against Nestorius.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily V (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: John's 'He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire' is for Cyril the canonical disclosure that Christian baptism is fundamentally pneumatological — the water is the outer sign of an inner gift of the Spirit. The fire is not destruction but the purifying-and-illuminating fire of the Pentecostal descent. Tewahedo baptismal theology reads Lk 3:16 alongside Acts 2 as the canonical diptych of the Spirit's outpouring in the New Covenant.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily VI (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: Christ's reply to the devil — 'Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve' — is for Cyril the canonical Adamic reversal: where the first Adam consented to the serpent's offered elevation, the New Adam refuses every offered kingdom that does not come through the cross. The temptation is the wilderness-pendant of the Eden episode. Tewahedo Lenten lectionary places the Temptation narrative at the gateway of the Great Fast for precisely this Cyrillian reading.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily VII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: After reading from Isaiah, Christ declares 'This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.' Cyril reads the synagogue homily as the canonical announcement that the Anointed-One's program is the program of Is 61: good tidings to the poor, release to the captives, sight to the blind, acceptable year. Tewahedo public-reading lectionary still pairs Isaiah 61 with Luke 4 on Nazareth-synagogue feast days to preserve this Cyrillian fulfilment-arc.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: Peter's response to the miraculous catch — 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord' — is for Cyril the first canonical confession of Christ's divinity by the future chief apostle: only divine power could so command the deep, and only divine holiness compels such a confession of unworthiness. Cyril notes that Christ does not depart but rather summons Peter from sinfulness to apostleship. Tewahedo ordination liturgy preserves the Petrine 'depart from me' as the canonical posture of the one called to priesthood.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XIII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: When Christ tells the paralytic 'Man, thy sins are forgiven thee,' Cyril hears the canonical claim of divine prerogative — only God forgives sins, as the scribes themselves know. The subsequent healing of the body is offered as the visible sign of the invisible remission. Cyril emphasizes the order: sins forgiven first, then body restored, so that the priority of soul over body is canonically established. Tewahedo penitential theology cites Lk 5:20-24 as the principal Lukan anchor of sacramental absolution.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XIV (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'The Son of Man is Lord also of the sabbath' — Cyril reads the declaration as the canonical assertion of Christ's divinity by way of his lordship over the Mosaic institution. The same Word who instituted the Sabbath in creation and re-instituted it at Sinai stands as its Lord. Tewahedo Saturday-Sabbath theology cites Lk 6:5 as the canonical warrant that the Lord of the Sabbath is precisely the One who fulfills, not abrogates, its rest in himself.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XX (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: The Lukan Beatitudes — 'Blessed are ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God' — are for Cyril the canonical pendant to the Matthean form: where Matthew preserves the inner-disposition reading (poor in spirit), Luke preserves the outer-condition reading (literally poor). Cyril harmonizes the two as a single canonical blessing of those whose poverty — whether of possession or of spirit — opens them to the kingdom. Tewahedo monastic catechesis draws explicitly on the Lukan form.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XXIX (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: When Christ marvels at the centurion — 'I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel' — Cyril reads the praise as the canonical anticipation of the Gentile mission. The Gentile believes without having seen the temple; the Israelite, having the temple before his eyes, often does not. Cyril treats Lk 7:9 as the Lukan precursor of his beloved Pauline 'there is neither Jew nor Greek' (Gal 3:28). Tewahedo missiology cites the centurion as a canonical Gentile-faith anchor.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XXXVI (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much' — Cyril reads the saying not as forgiveness CAUSED by love but as forgiveness MANIFESTED by love. The woman's tears at the Pharisee's table are the visible token that her sins are already remitted; the love comes from the remission, the remission is not the wage of the love. Tewahedo penitential rite preserves this Cyrillian ordering: absolution precedes the works of penance, never the reverse.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XL (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'Where is your faith?' — Christ's rebuke to the terrified disciples in the storm is for Cyril the canonical anchor of the disciples' still-developing recognition of his divinity. The Word who rebukes the wind is the same Word who, in Job and the Psalms, treads upon the waves of the sea. The storm-stilling is a theophanic act, and the disciples' question 'who then is this?' answers itself. Tewahedo Christology cites Lk 8:25 as a canonical anchor of the disciples' graduated confession of the Word's divinity.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XLIII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: Peter's 'Thou art the Christ of God' is for Cyril the apostolic confession that defines the Church. The confession is not Peter's discovery — it is the Father's revelation through him — and yet it is Peter's voice that utters it on behalf of the Twelve. Cyril treats the Lukan form alongside the Matthean expansion (Mt 16:16-18) as a single canonical confession-and-commission diptych. Tewahedo Petrine theology cites Lk 9:20 as the canonical anchor of the apostolic confessional core.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XLIX (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: The voice from the cloud at the Transfiguration — 'This is my beloved Son: hear him' — is for Cyril the canonical Father-Son disclosure made visible to Peter, James, and John. The Transfiguration is the proleptic glimpse of the post-Resurrection glory: the same flesh that walks the wilderness shines with the uncreated light. Tewahedo Transfiguration feast (Buhe) preserves Cyril's reading of the divine voice as the canonical paternal attestation of the Son's inseparable divinity.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LI (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: Cyril reads the Good Samaritan parable as a Christological allegory from at least the third Christian century, and his exegesis carries the canonical pattern: the wounded man is Adam-fallen-among-thieves; the priest and Levite are Law and Prophets, unable to save; the Samaritan is the despised-and-rejected Christ; the inn is the Church; the two denarii are the Old and New Testaments; the promise to return is the Second Coming. Tewahedo monastic exegesis preserves this allegory wholesale.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: Mary at Christ's feet 'hath chosen that good part' — Cyril reads the saying as the canonical anchor of contemplative priority: the service to the body (Martha) is necessary but the service to the Word (Mary) is the 'one thing needful,' and Mary's portion will not be taken from her. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 10:42 as one of its earliest canonical anchors of the primacy of prayer and scripture-reading over outward works.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXIX (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: The Lukan Pater Noster — 'When ye pray, say, Our Father which art in heaven' — is for Cyril the canonical form by which the Word teaches the saints to address God in his own filial voice. The 'Our' is ecclesial: no one prays the prayer alone; even the hermit in the desert prays as a member of the body. Tewahedo daily-office incorporates the Pater Noster at every hour, drawing directly on Cyril's reading of it as the canonical-filial address form.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee' — the rich fool's death-warrant in the parable is for Cyril the canonical warning against the postponement-of-the-soul that worldly wealth enables. The man addresses HIS OWN SOUL ('soul, thou hast much goods') as if it belonged to him to dispose; God's reply discloses that the soul is on lease. Tewahedo monastic memento-mori catechesis draws directly on this Cyrillian reading.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXXIX (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'This woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan hath bound, lo, these eighteen years, ought not she to be loosed from this bond on the sabbath day?' — Cyril reads Christ's defence of the Sabbath healing as the canonical exposure of the Pharisaic perversion of the rest-commandment into a bondage. The Sabbath was made for the loosing of bonds, not for their maintenance. Tewahedo Sabbatical theology cites Lk 13:16 as the canonical anchor of the freedom-form of Sabbath rest.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XCVI (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'Whosoever doth not bear his cross, and come after me, cannot be my disciple' — Cyril reads the saying as the canonical anchor of voluntary martyrdom: the disciple's own cross-bearing is the imitation that conforms him to the Master. The discipleship cost-calculation that follows (tower-builder, king-going-to-war) is the prudential prelude. Tewahedo monastic profession includes the voluntary embrace of the spiritual cross in direct dependence on this Cyrillian reading.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CIV (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'When he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him' — Cyril treats the Father's running as the canonical signature of the Lukan parable: the divine compassion does not wait for the sinner to arrive but goes out to meet him while he is still far. The first robe, the ring, and the shoes are the baptismal restoration of dignity. Tewahedo penitential theology cites Lk 15:20-22 as the principal canonical anchor of God-runs-to-meet-the-returning-sinner imagery.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CVII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: Cyril reads the Rich-Man-and-Lazarus narrative as canonically settling several intermediate-state questions: that there is consciousness after death; that the just are gathered to a place of refreshment ('Abraham's bosom'); that the unjust suffer torment in conscious recognition; that the chasm fixed between the two is uncrossable; that Moses and the Prophets are sufficient witnesses to deter the living. Tewahedo eschatology draws on Lk 16:19-31 as the principal canonical Lukan anchor of the intermediate-state doctrine.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXI (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: Only the Samaritan among the ten cleansed lepers returns to give thanks at Christ's feet, and Cyril reads the verse as the canonical Lukan anchor of the eucharistic posture: the cleansed turn back to the cleanser in thanksgiving (eucharistia). The nine who do not return are not cured of the deeper leprosy of ingratitude. Tewahedo Anaphora preserves the Cyrillian reading: the proper response to divine cleansing is the return-to-the-altar with thanks.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXIII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: The publican standing afar off, smiting on his breast, saying 'God be merciful to me a sinner' — Cyril treats this prayer as the canonical Lukan form of the Jesus-prayer: short, exact, self-acknowledging, mercy-petitioning. The publican goes down to his house justified, not the Pharisee. Tewahedo monastic prayer tradition preserves the publican's prayer as the canonical seed of the continual prayer of the heart.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXX (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: The blind beggar at Jericho — 'Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me' — gives, for Cyril, the canonical short-form messianic address. The blind man sees by faith what the seeing crowd does not see: the Davidic sonship of the passing Christ. Tewahedo invocation of the Jesus-prayer preserves the blind-beggar address as one of its earliest canonical forms.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXVI (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'This day is salvation come to this house' — Cyril reads the Zacchaeus pericope as the canonical Lukan diptych to Lk 15: in Lk 15 the lost son returns to the father; in Lk 19 the lost son is sought-and-found by the Father. The Son of Man came TO SEEK AND TO SAVE — the seeking is the divine initiative. Tewahedo missiology cites Lk 19:10 alongside Lk 15:20 as the canonical seeking-and-running diptych.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXVII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: Christ's weeping over Jerusalem is for Cyril the canonical disclosure of the Lord's mercy precisely toward the city about to reject him. The tears do not soften the prophetic announcement of the city's destruction; they intensify it as the announcement of a real and grievous loss. Cyril rejects every reading that would treat the tears as mere stagecraft. Tewahedo Holy-Week lectionary preserves Lk 19:41-44 as the Palm-Sunday-eve reading of the Lord's lament.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'Render therefore unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's, and unto God the things which be God's' — Cyril treats the saying as the canonical two-spheres principle: civic duty is real but subordinate, and never displaces the duty to God. The denarius carries Caesar's image; the soul carries God's. The implicit argument is that the soul is rendered to God by being conformed to his image. Tewahedo political theology cites Lk 20:25 as the canonical two-kingdoms anchor.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'This poor widow hath cast in more than they all' — Cyril reads the widow's mite as the canonical anchor of the all-or-nothing form of Christian almsgiving: the gift is measured not by the amount given but by the proportion of one's substance, and the widow who gives her last two coins gives literally everything. Tewahedo monastic voluntary poverty draws on Lk 21:3-4 as one of its earliest canonical anchors of total renunciation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me' — Cyril treats the Lukan institution narrative as the canonical anchor of his entire eucharistic theology: that the bread broken IS the body of Christ, that the body of Christ given for the believers is the same body born of the Virgin, that the Eucharist is the ongoing communication of the life-giving flesh of the Word. Tewahedo Anaphora cites Lk 22:19 as one of its principal canonical warrants of the real presence.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLI (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'His sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground' — Cyril treats the Gethsemane sweat as the canonical anchor of the Lord's true humanity: the agony is real, the prayer is real, the consenting will is real. Against any Apollinarian reduction of the human will, Cyril insists that the Word in his humanity wills our salvation through real prayer to the Father. Tewahedo Holy-Thursday lectionary preserves Lk 22:44 as the canonical anchor of the Lord's prayerful humanity.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLVI (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do' — Cyril treats the first word from the Cross as the canonical fulfilment of Is 53:12 ('he made intercession for the transgressors'). The intercessory office of the High Priest is exercised from the altar of the Cross itself. The 'they know not' is a real plea for ignorance-extenuation: those who execute Christ are bidden to the same forgiveness offered to all. Tewahedo Good-Friday liturgy preserves Lk 23:34 at the head of the seven words.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CL (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'Today shalt thou be with me in paradise' — Cyril reads the promise to the good thief as the canonical anchor of three doctrines: (1) Christ retains the prerogative of paradise even at the moment of his apparent defeat; (2) confession-from-the-cross suffices for salvation; (3) the saints enter paradise immediately at death and do not wait. The 'today' rules out every reading that defers the saints' beatific reception to the Last Day alone. Tewahedo intermediate-state doctrine cites Lk 23:43 as a principal canonical anchor.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLI (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit' — Cyril treats the Lukan death-cry, drawn from Ps 31:5, as the canonical anchor of every Christian's death-bed prayer: the soul is commended to the Father who created it, by the same words the eternal Son used. The Word does not lose his divinity at the cry of dereliction; the soul-Father committal is the calm answer to the Markan-Matthean cry. Tewahedo funeral office cites Lk 23:46 as the canonical commendation-prayer.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'He took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him' — Cyril reads the Emmaus recognition as the canonical Lukan disclosure that the Risen Christ is known IN the breaking of the bread. The same gesture that instituted the Eucharist on Holy Thursday opens the disciples' eyes on Easter evening. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Lk 24:30-31 as the canonical anchor that every Eucharist is an Emmaus-recognition.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLV (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: 'He was parted from them, and carried up into heaven' — Cyril treats the Lukan Ascension as the canonical inauguration of the Word-made-flesh's session at the Father's right hand: the same humanity assumed from the Virgin is enthroned in glory. The Ascension is not the departure of the Word from his flesh but the elevation of the flesh into the divine glory. Tewahedo Ascension feast (Ǝrgät) cites Lk 24:51 alongside Acts 1:9-11 as the canonical diptych of the heavenly enthronement.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLVI (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the setting-apart of the Levites for tabernacle service, Ephrem reads the census-and-separation pattern of Num 1:50 as the canonical model for ordered ministry: the people are numbered for their tribes, but one tribe is numbered for the Lord himself. The Levites' exemption from the military census is not privilege but conscription into a more dangerous service — the daily handling of the holy things. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Num 1:50 as the Old-Testament warrant for the consecration of the däbtära and the priest-monks; the consecrated are numbered for the sanctuary first, for the nation only afterward.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 1:50. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13 (Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.

entries.summary: On the Nazirite vow, Ephrem reads Num 6:2 as the canonical Old-Testament antecedent of the monastic profession: a person separates himself unto the Lord by a deliberate vow, abstaining from wine, leaving hair uncut as the visible token of consecration. The Nazirite is voluntary, time-bound, and lay — anyone may take the vow. Tewahedo monastic tradition cites Num 6 as the typological warrant for the bahǝtawi (solitary ascetic) and for the temporary monastic vows undertaken during fasts and pilgrimages; the uncut hair and untrimmed beard of the bahǝtawi visibly preserve the Nazirite sign.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 6:1-21. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.summary: Ephrem reads the threefold Aaronic blessing (Num 6:24-26 — 'The Lord bless thee... make his face shine upon thee... lift up his countenance upon thee') as the canonical priestly anchor that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit may be invoked under three benedictions before the Tabernacle reveals the Trinity. The triadic shape, the divine-face theology, and the placement of the Name upon Israel are read by Ephrem as the seed-form of every later Christian benediction. The Tewahedo Mass (Qǝddase) preserves Num 6:24-26 as the canonical dismissal-blessing; the priest extends the blessing over the people in the exact threefold form, sealing the eucharistic act.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 6:22-27. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.summary: On the command to keep the Passover at its appointed season in the second year (Num 9:2), Ephrem reads the verse as establishing the canonical annual rhythm of Pascha: Passover is not a one-time deliverance but a perpetual yearly observance constitutive of covenant identity. The wilderness Passover anticipates every later celebration: in the desert, in the land, in exile, and finally in the eucharistic Pascha of the Church. Tewahedo Fasika observance cites Num 9:2 alongside Exo 12 as the canonical doubled-anchor for the non-negotiable yearly celebration; to skip Pascha is to step outside the covenant rhythm.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 9:1-14. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.summary: On the cloud covering the tabernacle by day and the appearance-of-fire by night (Num 9:15), Ephrem reads the doubled pillar — cloud and fire — as the canonical visible-sign of continuous divine indwelling: the Lord neither withdraws by day nor leaves the camp dark by night. The same cloud that veiled Sinai's fire now veils and reveals the tabernacle's glory. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Num 9:15 as the canonical anchor of the perpetual veil-and-glory pattern preserved in the curtained sanctuary: the tabot is veiled in cloud, illumined by lampstand fire, both signs of the abiding Lord.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 9:15-23. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.summary: On the silver trumpets sounded for war and for festivals (Num 10:9-10), Ephrem reads the doubled liturgical-and-military use of the trumpet as the canonical pattern: the same sign that summons the people to battle summons them to rejoicing — both belong to the Lord, both invoke remembrance before him. Tewahedo liturgical practice preserves the silver-trumpet tradition in the qabaro and silver-trumpet of the great feasts (Mäsqäl, Timqät); the same trumpet that announces the procession of the tabot announces the day of remembrance. Num 10:9 is the canonical anchor for the trumpet-as-prayer in Ethiopian worship.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 10:1-10. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.summary: On the Lord's taking of the Spirit that was upon Moses and putting the same Spirit upon the seventy elders (Num 11:17, 25), Ephrem reads the verse as the canonical Old-Testament antecedent of Pentecost: the one Spirit is shared without diminution, the leader's portion does not decrease when others receive. The seventy elders prefigure both the seventy disciples of Lk 10:1 and the assembled hundred-and-twenty of Acts 1-2. Tewahedo pneumatology cites Num 11:17 + Joel 2:28 as the canonical doubled-Old-Testament-witness to the Pentecost gift of the Spirit on all flesh.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 11:14-30. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.summary: On 'Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth' (Num 12:3), Ephrem reads the meekness-of-Moses note as the canonical Old-Testament prefigurement of the Beatitude 'blessed are the meek' (Mt 5:5) and of Christ's own 'I am meek and lowly of heart' (Mt 11:29). Moses' meekness is not weakness but the refusal to defend himself against his own sister and brother; the Lord defends him because he will not. Tewahedo monastic spirituality cites Num 12:3 as the canonical Old-Testament anchor for the cardinal monastic virtue of mätayāqǝbǝr (humility) — the desert father is meek in the pattern of Moses.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 12:1-15. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.summary: On 'My servant Moses... is faithful in all mine house' (Num 12:7), Ephrem reads the Lord's defense of Moses as the canonical typological seed of Hebrews 3:5-6: Moses is faithful as a servant in the house, Christ as a son over the house. The household-of-God image is rooted here; the apostolic writer's distinction between servant and son is exegetically inevitable from Num 12:7's vocabulary. Tewahedo christology cites Num 12:7 + Heb 3 as the canonical doubled-witness that Moses prefigures but does not equal the Son who built the house — the typological gap is preserved.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 12:6-8. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Heb 3:5-6.

entries.summary: On the spies' report of 'the sons of Anak, who come of the Nephilim' in Canaan (Num 13:33), Ephrem reads the survival of Nephilim-stock beyond the Flood as the canonical anchor of the continuing struggle against Watchers-progeny: not all giants perished in the deluge, and the conquest of Canaan is itself a continuation of the Flood-judgment. Tewahedo angelology, drawing on 1 Enoch 7-9 (Mäṣḥafä Hēnok), preserves this reading; the Anakim are the residual giants whose presence in Canaan justifies the herem-conquest as cosmic purgation, not merely political dispossession.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 13:25-33. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. 1 Enoch 7-9, trans. R.H. Charles (Oxford: Clarendon, 1912 — PD).

entries.summary: On Moses' citation of the divine self-disclosure 'The Lord is longsuffering, and of great mercy, forgiving iniquity and transgression... by no means clearing the guilty' (Num 14:18), Ephrem reads the formula as the canonical liturgical prayer-of-pardon adopted into the Septuagint Psalter (Ps 86:15, 103:8, 145:8) and extended into every later Christian confession-rite. The verse holds together the two halves of the Name: mercy and justice, neither cancelling the other. Tewahedo penance liturgy (näsḫa-of-näsḫa) cites Num 14:18 as the canonical Old-Testament anchor for the priestly absolution formula; the same formula governs the Lenten qǝne and the Holy Thursday foot-washing.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 14:13-25. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.summary: On the swallowing of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram by the earth (Num 16:32), Ephrem reads the judgment-against-priestly-rebellion as the canonical anchor of the gravity-of-priesthood: those who usurp the priestly office without divine appointment fall through the very earth that should bear them. Korah's rebellion is doubled in Jude 11 ('perished in the gainsaying of Core') and read as type of every later schismatic seizure of office. Tewahedo canon-law cites Num 16:32 + Jude 11 as the canonical doubled-warrant for the gravity of unauthorised priesthood; only the lawfully-ordained may approach the tabot.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 16:1-35. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Jude 11.

entries.summary: On Aaron's rod that 'budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds' (Num 17:8), Ephrem reads the blossoming-of-the-dead-staff as the canonical Marian-rod typology: a dry rod brings forth life out of season because the Lord wills it, prefiguring the Virgin who bears the Word without seed. The Tewahedo Wǝddase Maryam preserves this reading explicitly — Mary is the 'rod of Aaron' (in Geʿez: bä-ṭwāf zä-Aron) whose blossoming is the seedless Conception of the Word. Num 17:8 is therefore the canonical Old-Testament Marian-iconographic anchor in Ethiopian devotion, alongside the burning bush (Ex 3:2) and the ladder of Jacob (Gen 28:12 + Jub 27:19).
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 17:1-13. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Tewahedo Marian liturgical witness: Wǝddase Maryam (Praises of Mary).

entries.summary: On the red heifer 'wherein is no blemish, and upon which never came yoke' (Num 19:2), Ephrem reads the unyoked, unblemished, wholly-burnt red heifer as the canonical Old-Testament type of Christ's atoning sacrifice — taken up explicitly by Hebrews 9:13-14 as the lesser-to-greater argument: if the ashes of a heifer sanctified the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ purge the conscience. The red colour anticipates the blood, the unyoked freedom anticipates Christ's voluntary submission, the outside-the-camp burning anticipates Calvary outside Jerusalem (Heb 13:11-12). Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Num 19 + Heb 9 as canonical doubled-witness to Christ's once-for-all purifying sacrifice.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 19:1-22. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Heb 9:13-14, 13:11-12.

entries.summary: On Moses' striking of the rock twice at Meribah (Num 20:11), Ephrem reads the doubled-strike as the proximate cause of Moses' exclusion from the land: the Lord had commanded that he speak to the rock, not strike it. The exegetical key, taken up by Paul (1 Cor 10:4 — 'that Rock was Christ'), is that Christ is struck once for the people's salvation; to strike him twice violates the typology of the once-for-all sacrifice (Heb 9:28, 10:10). Tewahedo christology cites Num 20:11 + 1 Cor 10:4 + Heb 9-10 as the canonical triple-witness that the Rock-Christ is smitten once and yields life-giving water forever.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 20:1-13. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. 1 Cor 10:4; Heb 9:28.

entries.summary: On the bronze serpent lifted on the standard for the healing of the bitten (Num 21:8-9), Ephrem reads the lifted-up-serpent as the canonical Old-Testament prefigurement of the Crucifixion — taken up verbatim by Christ himself in Jn 3:14: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up.' The bronze that looks like serpent but contains no venom prefigures Christ-in-the-likeness-of-sinful-flesh-but-without-sin (Rom 8:3). Looking-and-living is the canonical pattern of faith. Tewahedo Mäsqäl theology cites Num 21:8 alongside Jn 3:14 as the canonical doubled-anchor of the Cross-as-healing-standard for the bitten world.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 21:4-9. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Jn 3:14 (verbatim Christological appropriation).

entries.summary: On the Lord's opening of the mouth of Balaam's ass to rebuke the prophet (Num 22:28), Ephrem reads the wonder as the canonical anchor of the doctrine that the Lord may speak truth from the most unworthy vessels: a Gentile diviner is humbled by his own beast, and the prophecy that follows (Num 24:17) issues from the same mouth that needed an ass's instruction. The verse becomes the typological seed of 2 Peter 2:16's denunciation of Balaam — and of the broader patristic principle that the prophetic gift can pass through mouths whose private life condemns them. Tewahedo pastoral theology cites Num 22:28 as the canonical Old-Testament anchor: receive the word for its truth, not for the messenger's worthiness.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 22:21-35. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. 2 Pet 2:16.

entries.summary: On Balaam's fourth oracle — 'I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel' (Num 24:17) — Ephrem reads the doubled-image (Star + Sceptre) as the canonical Old-Testament prophecy of the Messiah's advent: the Star is the sign that appears to the Gentile Magi (Mt 2:2 — 'we have seen his star in the east'), the Sceptre is the Davidic kingship received by the Son of David. The Gentile diviner Balaam prophesies through gritted teeth the salvation of the world. Tewahedo nativity-iconography cites Num 24:17 as the canonical Old-Testament doubled-anchor of the Star-of-Bethlehem and the Davidic-Solomonic Sceptre — both inherited by the Tewahedo Solomonic dynasty's self-understanding.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 24:15-19. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Mt 2:2.

entries.summary: On Phinehas's spear-thrust and the Lord's grant of 'my covenant of peace' (Num 25:11-13), Ephrem reads the zealot-priest's act as the canonical anchor of priestly-zeal: not bloodlust, but a refusal to tolerate the pollution of the camp by Baal of Peor. The covenant-of-peace given for an act of violence is the paradox: peace with God is procured by hating what God hates. Tewahedo priestly tradition cites Num 25:11 as the canonical Old-Testament warrant for the priestly-zeal expected of the qes (parish priest) and the märigeta (cantor) — those who cannot tolerate liturgical pollution receive the covenant of peace. The doubling with Jub 30:18 (Levi's priesthood earned-by-zeal at Shechem) makes Num 25:11 + Jub 30:18 the canonical Tewahedo doubled-warrant for priesthood-by-zeal.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 25:1-15. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Jub 30:18 (R.H. Charles trans., 1902 — PD).

entries.summary: On the Lord's selection of Joshua as Moses' successor — 'Take thee Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the spirit, and lay thine hand upon him' (Num 27:18) — Ephrem reads the laying-on-of-hands as the canonical Old-Testament antecedent of apostolic succession: the spirit-bearing successor is consecrated by the laying-on of the predecessor's hands, ratified by the assembly. The transmission is bodily and visible, not merely charismatic. Tewahedo episcopal-consecration cites Num 27:18 + 1 Tim 4:14 as the canonical doubled-witness for the unbroken chain of laying-on-of-hands that grounds the Patriarchate of Ethiopia in apostolic-Mosaic continuity.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 27:12-23. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. 1 Tim 4:14, 2 Tim 1:6.

entries.summary: On 'the Lord thy God is a consuming fire, even a jealous God' (Deu 4:24), Ephrem reads the doubled-image (consuming fire + jealous God) as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Hebrews 12:29 ('for our God is a consuming fire' — verbatim citation). The fire-image is not destructive wrath but the purifying jealousy that refuses rival affections. Tewahedo theology cites Deu 4:24 + Heb 12:29 as the canonical doubled-witness that the encounter-with-God is always simultaneously consoling and consuming; the Eucharist itself receives the same description in the Tewahedo Anaphora of Athanasius: 'this is the burning coal which Isaiah saw'.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 4:23-31. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Heb 12:29 (verbatim citation).

entries.summary: On the prologue to the Decalogue's restatement — 'I am the Lord thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage' (Deu 5:6) — Ephrem reads the placement of the redemption-formula BEFORE the commandments as the canonical anchor of the order-of-salvation: grace precedes obligation, the Exodus precedes Sinai. The Decalogue is given to a people already redeemed, not to a people earning redemption. Tewahedo catechetical theology cites Deu 5:6 as the canonical Old-Testament anchor for the order baptism-precedes-commandments: the catechumen is delivered from Egypt (baptism) BEFORE receiving the Tewahedo moral-life formation.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 5:1-21. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.summary: On the Shema — 'Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God is one Lord' (Deu 6:4) — Ephrem reads the confession as the canonical Old-Testament Trinitarian seed-form: the threefold name (Lord / our God / Lord) coupled with the affirmation of one (eḥad) holds together the unity and plurality that the New Testament will unfold. The Hebrew eḥad (compound unity, not yaḥid solitary singleness) opens the conceptual space for the later Nicene-Constantinopolitan confession of three persons of one substance. Tewahedo Trinitarian theology cites Deu 6:4 + the dominical 'baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost' (Mt 28:19) as the canonical Old-Testament-to-New-Testament continuity: the same one Lord is the Holy Trinity.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 6:4-9. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Mt 28:19.

entries.summary: On 'And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might' (Deu 6:5), Ephrem reads the threefold-totality of love as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of the Great Commandment that Christ cites as 'the first and great commandment' (Mt 22:37-38). Heart, soul, might: nothing of the human person is exempt from the demand. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Deu 6:5 + Mt 22:37 as the canonical doubled-witness that monastic poverty (yielding might), monastic chastity (yielding heart), and monastic obedience (yielding soul) are the threefold practical realization of the one Shema-commandment.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 6:4-9. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Mt 22:37-38.

entries.summary: On 'Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and serve him' (Deu 6:13), Ephrem reads the doubled-verb (fear + serve) as the canonical Old-Testament anchor invoked by Christ at the third Temptation: 'Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve' (Mt 4:10). The Septuagint's substitution of 'worship' (proskunēseis) for 'fear' (phobēthēsē) preserves the doubled-verb structure that Christ retains. Tewahedo christology cites Deu 6:13 + Mt 4:10 as the canonical doubled-witness that Christ in his humanity submits to the Father-alone-worshipped, providing the typological model for every Tewahedo refusal of demonic or imperial worship.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 6:10-19. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Mt 4:10 (Christological appropriation at the Temptation).

entries.summary: On 'man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the Lord doth man live' (Deu 8:3), Ephrem reads the manna-pedagogy as the canonical anchor cited by Christ at the first Temptation (Mt 4:4 / Lk 4:4 — verbatim citation). The manna teaches that humanity's deepest hunger is for the Word, not for bread; the Eucharist resolves both hungers in one. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Deu 8:3 + Jn 6:51 ('I am the living bread which came down from heaven') + Mt 4:4 as the canonical triple-witness: Christ is the Word-who-is-Bread, fulfilling the Deuteronomic pedagogy in the Eucharistic anaphora.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 8:1-10. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Mt 4:4, Jn 6:51.

entries.summary: On 'Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked' (Deu 10:16), Ephrem reads the heart-circumcision command as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Paul's 'circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter' (Rom 2:29). The Deuteronomic call to interior circumcision is not a substitute for the bodily rite but its ground: the outward sign is empty without the inward reality. Tewahedo theology — uniquely among Christian communions still practising bodily circumcision per Jub 15:14-25 — cites Deu 10:16 as the canonical Old-Testament witness that BOTH circumcisions are required: the bodily sign that distinguishes the people and the heart-circumcision that perfects it.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 10:12-22. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Rom 2:29; Jub 15:14-25 (R.H. Charles, 1902 — PD).

entries.summary: On 'the place which the Lord your God shall choose out of all your tribes to put his name there' (Deu 12:5), Ephrem reads the centralization-of-worship command as the canonical Old-Testament typological anchor that flows through Shiloh → Jerusalem → Zion → the Eucharistic altar of every local church. The Lord chooses ONE place for his Name in the Old Covenant; in the New Covenant, every Eucharistic altar is THE chosen place because the Body broken there IS the New-Covenant tabot. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Deu 12:5 as the canonical anchor for the doctrine that the Eucharist gathers Jerusalem's centralization into every parish — the tabot-bearing altar IS the chosen place.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 12:1-14. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.summary: On the Deuteronomic recapitulation of Passover — 'Observe the month of Abib, and keep the passover unto the Lord thy God' (Deu 16:1) — Ephrem reads the THIRD Mosaic Passover legislation (after Exo 12 and Num 9) as the canonical triple-witness that Pascha is the non-negotiable hinge of the covenant year. The repetition is not redundant but emphatic: the Lord wills that Israel never forget the month of deliverance. Tewahedo Fasika theology cites Exo 12 + Num 9:2 + Deu 16:1 as the canonical triple-Mosaic anchor that the yearly Pascha is constitutive of covenant identity — eucharistically fulfilled in the Tewahedo Holy-Week Anaphora.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 16:1-8. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.summary: On the king's Torah — 'when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall write him a copy of this law in a book' (Deu 17:18-19) — Ephrem reads the king-as-Torah-scribe command as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of the doctrine that the king is FIRST a guardian of the law, only secondarily a ruler of the people. The king does not stand above the Torah; he copies it with his own hand and reads it all the days of his life. Tewahedo Solomonic-dynasty self-understanding, codified in the Kǝbrä Nägäśt (Glory of the Kings), cites Deu 17:18 as the canonical Old-Testament warrant for the Ethiopian-emperor-as-Torah-guardian — the emperor at coronation receives both crown and Tabot, and is sworn to defend both.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 17:14-20. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Tewahedo dynastic witness: Kǝbrä Nägäśt.

entries.summary: On 'The Lord thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken' (Deu 18:15), Ephrem reads the prophet-like-Moses promise as the canonical Old-Testament messianic anchor cited verbatim by Peter in Acts 3:22 ('A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me') and by Stephen in Acts 7:37 — the apostolic preaching's primary Old-Testament prophecy-of-Christ proof-text alongside Ps 110:1. The 'like-Moses' qualification is fulfilled in Christ at the Transfiguration where Moses and Elijah appear with him on the mountain. Tewahedo christology cites Deu 18:15 + Acts 3:22 + the Buhe Transfiguration as the canonical triple-witness of the Mosaic-prophet identity of Christ.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 18:9-22. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Acts 3:22 (verbatim apostolic citation), Acts 7:37.

entries.summary: On 'he that is hanged is accursed of God' (Deu 21:23), Ephrem reads the curse-on-the-hanged-corpse statute as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Paul's atonement-formula in Galatians 3:13: 'Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree' — verbatim citation. The Deuteronomic curse is not abolished but absorbed: Christ takes the curse upon himself precisely by hanging on the tree. Tewahedo atonement theology cites Deu 21:23 + Gal 3:13 as the canonical doubled-anchor of the substitutionary cross — the Cross is canonical-curse-bearing, the Christ is canonical-curse-bearer, the redemption is canonical-completion.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 21:22-23. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Gal 3:13 (verbatim Pauline citation).

entries.summary: On 'Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn' (Deu 25:4), Ephrem reads the agricultural-mercy statute as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Paul's argument for ministerial support: cited at 1 Cor 9:9 and 1 Tim 5:18 with the gloss 'Doth God take care for oxen? or saith he it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes, no doubt, this is written.' The verse becomes the apostolic warrant for the priest's right to be sustained by the eucharistic offerings of the people. Tewahedo canonical-economy cites Deu 25:4 + 1 Cor 9:9 as the canonical doubled-witness for the lay-support of the priest and the monastery — the worker is worthy of his hire.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 25:1-19. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. 1 Cor 9:9, 1 Tim 5:18.

entries.summary: On 'Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them' (Deu 27:26), Ephrem reads the final Ebal-curse as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Paul's argument in Galatians 3:10 ('as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them' — verbatim citation). The total-law requirement makes salvation-by-works impossible: no one keeps all things. The verse becomes the typological seed of the apostolic gospel of grace. Tewahedo soteriology cites Deu 27:26 + Gal 3:10 as the canonical doubled-witness that the law diagnoses the curse the Cross removes.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 27:11-26. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Gal 3:10 (verbatim Pauline citation).

entries.summary: On 'the Lord thy God will circumcise thine heart, and the heart of thy seed, to love the Lord thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, that thou mayest live' (Deu 30:6), Ephrem reads the heart-circumcision-by-divine-action as the canonical Old-Testament promise of grace fulfilled in the new covenant: what Deu 10:16 commands ('circumcise your heart'), Deu 30:6 promises the Lord himself will accomplish. The same gospel-of-grace structure (command becomes promise) flows through Jer 31:33 and Ez 36:26 into Acts 2's Pentecost. Tewahedo theosis-theology cites Deu 30:6 as the canonical Old-Testament anchor: the Spirit-given heart-circumcision IS theosis — God's own action transforming the human heart to love him with the love that he commands.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 30:1-10. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Jer 31:33, Ez 36:26, Acts 2.

entries.summary: On 'the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it' (Deu 30:14), Ephrem reads the near-Word promise as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Paul's exposition of the gospel-of-faith in Romans 10:8 ('The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach' — verbatim citation). The Deuteronomic word-near-to-you is appropriated by Paul as the gospel: salvation is not ascending to heaven (incarnation already happened) or descending to the abyss (resurrection already happened) but confessing with the mouth and believing with the heart. Tewahedo catechesis cites Deu 30:14 + Rom 10:8-10 as the canonical doubled-witness that the gospel is mouth-and-heart confession.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 30:11-20. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Rom 10:8-10 (verbatim Pauline citation).

entries.summary: On the Song of Moses' line 'when the Most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the sons of God' (Deu 32:8, LXX / Dead Sea Scrolls reading 'sons of God' / b'nei Elohim — preserved in the Masoretic-correction tradition), Ephrem reads the verse as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of the doctrine of angelic-territorial-governance: the Most High assigned each nation to the oversight of an angelic prince, retaining Israel as his own portion (Deu 32:9). Tewahedo angelology preserves this doctrine prominently — the Synaxarium accounts of Saint Michael as guardian-prince of Ethiopia, the Tewahedo Mäshafä Hēnok (1 Enoch) traditions of the seventy shepherds (1 En 89-90), and the Mäṣḥafä Kufāle (Jubilees) accounts of the angel-of-the-presence assigned to Israel (Jub 1:27, 2:1, 15:31-32) all flow from Deu 32:8's canonical seed. Tewahedo cites Deu 32:8 + Jub 15:31-32 + 1 En 89:59 as the canonical triple-witness of angelic-territorial-governance.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 32:7-9. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD (LXX/DSS reading retained against Masoretic correction). Cf. Jub 15:31-32, 1 En 89:59 (R.H. Charles, 1902/1912 — PD).

entries.summary: On the Song of Moses' climactic self-disclosure — 'See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me: I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal' (Deu 32:39) — Ephrem reads the kill-and-make-alive paired-action as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of resurrection-monotheism: the SAME God who brings death brings life, the SAME God who wounds heals. There is no Manichaean dualism (one god of life, another of death). The verse anticipates 1 Sam 2:6 ('The Lord killeth, and maketh alive') and is fulfilled in the dominical 'I am the resurrection, and the life' (Jn 11:25). Tewahedo Easter (Fasika) theology cites Deu 32:39 + Jn 11:25 as the canonical doubled-witness of the resurrection-monotheist God.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 32:39-43. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. 1 Sam 2:6, Jn 11:25.

entries.summary: On Moses' blessing of Levi — 'Who said unto his father and to his mother, I have not seen him; neither did he acknowledge his brethren, nor knew his own children: for they have observed thy word, and kept thy covenant' (Deu 33:9) — Ephrem reads the praise of Levi's denial-of-kin-for-sake-of-God as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of the dominical 'He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me' (Mt 10:37) and the Levitical-monastic ideal of leaving-family-for-God. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Deu 33:9 + Mt 10:37 as the canonical doubled-witness for the bahǝtawi's renunciation of family ties — the desert father is a Levite in the pattern of Deu 33:9, whose covenant-keeping is honoured precisely because it preferred God to kin.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 33:8-11. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Mt 10:37.

entries.summary: On Moses' burial 'in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day' (Deu 34:6), Ephrem reads the divinely-hidden grave as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Jude 9's account of the archangel Michael's dispute with the devil over Moses' body — preserved in the Assumption of Moses tradition received by the Ethiopian canon. The hidden grave prepares Moses for his Transfiguration appearance with Elijah (Mt 17:3, Lk 9:30-31), suggesting a translation-pattern parallel to Enoch (Gen 5:24) and Elijah (2 Ki 2:11). Tewahedo Astə'arǝgya-Mussē (Translation of Moses) commemorates this hidden-grave tradition; Deu 34:6 + Jude 9 + the Buhe Transfiguration form the canonical triple-witness of Moses' translated-glorified state.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Deuteronomy, on 34:1-12. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Jude 9, Mt 17:3; Tewahedo liturgical witness: Astə'arǝgya-Mussē.

entries.summary: On 'Zacharias, of the course of Abia... his wife was of the daughters of Aaron' (Lk 1:5), Cyril reads the doubled priestly pedigree (Zacharias by course + Elizabeth by lineage) as the canonical anchor of the New-Testament-emerging-from-the-Old-Testament-priesthood: the forerunner of the Lord is born to a fully-Aaronic family, the last priestly-house representative whose voice will yield to the One greater than himself. Tewahedo liturgical theology cites Lk 1:5 as the canonical anchor for the Aaronic origin of the Christian priesthood: the same priestly succession that Zacharias represented continues through Christ's apostles into the Tewahedo episcopate.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily I (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Gabriel's 'Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard' (Lk 1:13), Cyril reads the angelic 'fear not' as the canonical pattern of every later divine annunciation: the angel speaks reassurance before announcement, because divine presence is overwhelming even when its content is good news. The same 'fear not' will be spoken to Mary (Lk 1:30), to the shepherds (Lk 2:10), and by the risen Christ to the women (Mt 28:10). Tewahedo angelology cites Lk 1:13 as the canonical anchor of the angelic-greeting-formula preserved in the Mäshafä Sǝʾatat (Book of Hours).
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily II (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Gabriel's 'The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God' (Lk 1:35), Cyril reads the doubled-pneumatology (Spirit-comes-upon + Highest-overshadows) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the Incarnation: not Adoption (the Spirit acts at conception, not at baptism), not Apollinarianism (the holy thing born IS the Son of God in his humanity), not Nestorianism (one subject is named, not two). The Tewahedo Theotokos doctrine cites Lk 1:35 as the canonical Lukan doubled-anchor with Mt 1:20 — the Spirit's-overshadowing makes Mary the bearer of God-in-flesh, not merely the bearer of a man.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily II-III (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Mary's 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word' (Lk 1:38), Cyril reads the fiat-mihi as the canonical anchor of the doctrine that the Incarnation requires human consent — a free-and-deliberate Yes from the side of Mary, not coerced. The Virgin's obedient response reverses Eve's refusal (Tertullian's typology, received by Cyril): Eve disbelieved and brought death, Mary believed and brought life. Tewahedo Marian piety cites Lk 1:38 as the canonical anchor of the doctrine that Mary is the New Eve whose deliberate Yes restores the human race to filial obedience — preserved in the Wǝddase Maryam refrain 'Behold, the handmaid of the Lord.'
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily III (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Elizabeth's Spirit-inspired exclamation 'Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb' (Lk 1:42), Cyril reads the doubled-beatitude (Mary blessed + the Fruit blessed) as the canonical Old-Testament-prophetic-Spirit-utterance preserved in the Lukan canticle structure: Elizabeth is the FIRST New-Testament prophetess, anticipating the broader Pentecost outpouring (Acts 2:18). Tewahedo Marian liturgy cites Lk 1:42 as the canonical anchor of the Ave-Maria pattern preserved in the Wǝddase Maryam and the Salam (Greeting) prayers; the Greeting (sälam) of Mary is the first New-Testament Marian title.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily IV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Zacharias's Benedictus phrase 'and hath raised up an horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David' (Lk 1:69), Cyril reads the horn-of-salvation image as the canonical Davidic-messianic anchor: the horn signifies the strength of royal power, the house of David situates the Messiah in the legitimate covenantal lineage. The Benedictus is the second canonical canticle of Luke (after the Magnificat); Zacharias as priest prophesies the Messiah's Davidic descent under the influence of the Spirit. Tewahedo morning-office cites the Benedictus (with the Magnificat and Nunc Dimittis) as the canonical Lukan triad of Spirit-inspired infancy-canticles preserved in the Mäwasǝʾt (Antiphonary).
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily V (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the angels' 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men' (Lk 2:14), Cyril reads the angelic-hymn as the canonical Lukan anchor of the eucharistic Gloria: heaven and earth united in the act of praising God for the Incarnation. The doubled-line structure (heavenly glory + earthly peace) preserves the cosmic scope of the redemption: the Word's becoming-flesh reconciles the two realms. Tewahedo Mass cites Lk 2:14 as the canonical liturgical anchor for the 'Gloria in excelsis' (Sǝbḥat lä-ʿǝgziʾabḥer) preserved at the opening of every Anaphora; the Christmas Day proper extends the same canticle.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily VIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's circumcision 'when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child' (Lk 2:21), Cyril reads the eighth-day circumcision as the canonical Lukan anchor that Christ deliberately submits to the Mosaic law (Gal 4:4 — 'made under the law'), preserving the Abrahamic covenant-sign in his own flesh. The naming 'Jesus' at the moment of circumcision links the covenant-sign to the salvation-name. Tewahedo theology — UNIQUELY among major Christian communions still practising bodily circumcision per Jub 15:14-25 — cites Lk 2:21 as the canonical NT anchor for the doctrine that Christ's circumcision honors the covenant-sign Christians continue to observe alongside the heart-circumcision (Deu 30:6).
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Gal 4:4; Jub 15:14-25 (R.H. Charles trans., 1902 — PD).

entries.summary: On Simeon's prophecy to Mary 'yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also' (Lk 2:35), Cyril reads the sword-image as the canonical Lukan anchor of the Marian compassion-at-the-Cross — preserved more fully in Jn 19:25 ('there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother'). The sword is not Mary's physical death but the maternal-soul-piercing of watching her Son crucified. Tewahedo Marian piety cites Lk 2:35 as the canonical Old-Testament-prophetic anchor that Mary's joys are inseparable from her sorrows; the seven-swords iconography preserved in the Tewahedo Wǝddase Maryam draws together the doxology of the Virgin with her maternal-passion compassion.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On 'the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him' (Lk 2:40), Cyril reads the growth-formula as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's true humanity: the Word who is eternally complete deliberately assumes the developmental rhythm of human infancy, growing in body and (in his human nature) in the experiential outworking of his hypostatically-united wisdom. Cyril's reading is anti-Apollinarian: Christ has a true human soul that grows. The Tewahedo Miaphysite Christology preserves this doctrine — Christ's growth is real growth in his humanity, not theatrical pretense.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On 'Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man' (Lk 2:52), Cyril reads the fourfold growth-formula (wisdom + stature + favour-with-God + favour-with-man) as the canonical Lukan anti-Apollinarian anchor: the Word does not pretend to grow but truly progresses in the integrated dimensions of his assumed humanity. Cyril's exegesis preserves both the eternal completeness of the Word and the genuine developmental finitude of the assumed nature without confusion. Tewahedo Miaphysite Christology cites Lk 2:52 as the canonical doubled-witness with Lk 2:40 against any Christology that denies Christ's true human soul-growth.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On John's 'preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins' (Lk 3:3), Cyril reads the formula as the canonical Lukan anchor that distinguishes John's baptism (signum of repentance) from Christian baptism (sacramentum of regeneration). John's baptism prepares; Christian baptism effects. The Greek aphesin hamartiōn (remission of sins) is the same phrase the Lord uses at the Last Supper (Mt 26:28); John's preaching points forward to the blood-of-the-new-covenant by which the remission becomes effective. Tewahedo baptismal theology cites Lk 3:3 + Mt 26:28 as the canonical doubled-witness that JBaptist's call-to-repentance is the necessary preparation for the effective sacrament of baptismal regeneration.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XVI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On 'the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him' (Lk 3:22), Cyril reads Luke's distinctive 'bodily shape' (sōmatikō eidei) as the canonical anchor of the doctrine that the Spirit's descent at the Jordan is not symbolic appearance but a real visible epiphany: the Father, Son, and Spirit are simultaneously and visibly manifested to the Baptist (cf. Jn 1:33-34). Tewahedo Timqät (Theophany) liturgy cites Lk 3:22 as the canonical anchor of the doctrine that the Jordan baptism is THE Trinitarian-epiphany feast — Christ in the water, the Spirit upon, the Father's voice. The Tewahedo annual Timqät procession with the tabot to the water re-enacts the canonical Lukan formula.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Jn 1:33-34. Tewahedo liturgical witness: Timqät (Theophany).

entries.summary: On 'Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age' (Lk 3:23), Cyril reads the precise age-marker at the start of Christ's public ministry as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christ's public ministry begins at the priestly-eligibility age of Levitical service (Num 4:3 — Levites enter active service at thirty). The chronological precision is theological: the true high-priest begins his ministry at the canonical age. Tewahedo episcopal-canon-law preserves a related minimum-age tradition for episcopal consecration, cited as the apostolic-Mosaic warrant for thirty-year-old priestly mature service.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Num 4:3.

entries.summary: On the climax of the Lukan genealogy '...which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God' (Lk 3:38), Cyril reads the back-to-Adam-and-God terminus as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ-as-Second-Adam (1 Cor 15:45) — the Word assumes the humanity of Adam universally, not merely the lineage of Abraham (as in Mt 1's genealogy). Luke's genealogy is theological: Christ is heir of all humanity, the Restorer of the entire Adamic race. Tewahedo soteriology cites Lk 3:38 + 1 Cor 15:45 as the canonical doubled-witness that Christ's redemption is universal-Adamic in scope, not limited to ethnic Israel.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. 1 Cor 15:45.

entries.summary: On 'Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost returned from Jordan, and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness' (Lk 4:1), Cyril reads the doubled-pneumatology (full-of-Spirit + led-by-Spirit) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the Spirit-anointing at the Jordan flows immediately into the public ministry's testing: there is no gap between empowerment and trial. Cyril preserves the parallel pattern in apostolic-Christian life: Spirit-baptism (sacramental Confirmation) precedes-but-does-not-prevent the wilderness of testing. Tewahedo monastic-formation cites Lk 4:1 as the canonical anchor that the Spirit who fills also leads-into-wilderness; the bahǝtawi tradition is the appropriation of this Lukan pattern.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XXII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's Nazareth-synagogue reading of Isaiah 61 — 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor' (Lk 4:18) — Cyril reads the Christ's-self-identification-with-the-Isaian-Servant as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ as the Anointed-One (Messiah = Christos): the same Spirit who descended visibly at the Jordan is the Spirit who has been upon Christ from his conception (Lk 1:35), now publicly proclaimed at the inauguration of his ministry. Tewahedo christology cites Lk 4:18 + Is 61:1 as the canonical doubled-witness that the Messianic anointing is pneumatological in essence — the Christ is the Spirit-anointed one whom the prophets foretold.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Is 61:1.

entries.summary: On the Capernaum demoniac's involuntary confession 'I know thee who thou art; the Holy One of God' (Lk 4:34), Cyril reads the demon-recognition as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the demons see through the veil of the flesh to the divinity of the Word (cf. James 2:19 — 'the devils also believe, and tremble'). The demons' knowledge is true but joyless, contrasted with the human disciples' progressive faith. Tewahedo exorcism-rite (preserved in the Mäshafä Wǝddase Maryam supplications) cites Lk 4:34 as the canonical anchor of the doctrine that the Holy Name itself drives out demons; the priest invokes Christ-the-Holy-One in the formulas of the rite.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XXXI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. James 2:19.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'I must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also: for therefore am I sent' (Lk 4:43), Cyril reads the dei (it-is-necessary) + apestalmai (I-am-sent) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's missional self-understanding: the Word's earthly ministry is mission-bound from above, not crowd-driven from below. The verb apostellō becomes the New-Testament technical-term for divine-sending; Christ's apostolic-mission is the model for the apostolic-mission of the disciples (Jn 20:21 — 'as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you'). Tewahedo missionary theology cites Lk 4:43 + Jn 20:21 as the canonical doubled-witness that the Tewahedo evangelistic mission to the Beta-Israel and surrounding nations participates in Christ's own apostolic-sending.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XXXIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Jn 20:21.

entries.summary: On Christ's commission to Simon 'Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men' (Lk 5:10), Cyril reads the fishers-of-men image as the canonical Lukan anchor of the apostolic-vocation: Peter who failed at fishing all night succeeds at men-fishing under Christ's word, foreshadowing the apostolic catch of three-thousand on the Day of Pentecost (Acts 2:41). The verb zōgrōn (capture-alive) is positive: the apostolic mission rescues, does not destroy. Tewahedo apostolic theology cites Lk 5:10 + Acts 2:41 as the canonical doubled-witness that the apostolic mission is the bringing-into-life of those caught by the gospel; the Tewahedo episcopate continues the apostolic catch.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XXXV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Acts 2:41.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'putting forth his hand, [he] touched him, saying, I will: be thou clean' (Lk 5:13), Cyril reads the touch-of-the-leper as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the Incarnation reverses the contagion-pattern of impurity: the leper does NOT defile Christ, Christ cleanses the leper. Christ's bodily-touch is sacramental — the Word-made-flesh transfers life and cleanness by physical contact. Tewahedo healing-rite theology cites Lk 5:13 as the canonical anchor for the bodily-touch component of the laying-on-of-hands healing rite and for the priestly anointing-with-oil (cf. James 5:14); the priest's hand carries Christ's cleansing.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XXXVI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. James 5:14.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power upon earth to forgive sins' (Lk 5:24), Cyril reads the title 'Son of Man' coupled with divine-prerogative-to-forgive as the canonical Lukan anchor of the Christological argument that runs through the Synoptics: only God forgives sins (so the scribes correctly observe at Mk 2:7), the Son of Man forgives sins, therefore the Son of Man is divine. The miracle of healing the paralytic is the sign confirming the antecedent claim. Tewahedo absolution-theology cites Lk 5:24 as the canonical anchor for the priestly absolution formula — the priest forgives in persona Christi, exercising the authority Christ gave the apostles (Jn 20:23).
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XXXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mk 2:7, Jn 20:23.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance' (Lk 5:32), Cyril reads the mission-statement as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the Incarnation is medicinal-soteriological in character: Christ-the-Physician comes for the sick. The pairing with Lk 19:10 ('the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost') frames the entire Lukan trajectory as a search-and-rescue mission. Tewahedo penance-theology cites Lk 5:32 as the canonical anchor of the doctrine that the priest's call-to-confession follows the dominical pattern: not exclusion of sinners but invitation to repentance.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XXXIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Lk 19:10.

entries.summary: On Christ's choice of the Twelve 'whom also he named apostles' (Lk 6:13), Cyril reads the act-of-naming-twelve as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of apostolic foundation: the twelve are not crowd-volunteers but Christ-selected after a night of prayer (Lk 6:12). The number twelve corresponds typologically to the twelve patriarchs/tribes; the new Israel is constituted with apostolic foundation. Tewahedo episcopal theology cites Lk 6:13 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the apostolic origin of the episcopate — the bishop's authority traces by laying-on-of-hands through unbroken succession to the apostolic Twelve.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XLI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you' (Lk 6:27), Cyril reads the love-your-enemies command as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christian ethics transcends Old-Testament-reciprocity: the love-of-enemies is impossible without participation in the Father's own love (Mt 5:45 — 'he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good'). The command is not natural-virtue but supernatural-grace. Tewahedo monastic ethics cites Lk 6:27 + Mt 5:44-45 as the canonical doubled-witness for the bahǝtawi's practice of love-of-enemies — the desert prayer 'forgive my enemies as Thou hast forgiven me' is the appropriation of this command.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XLIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mt 5:44-45.

entries.summary: On the Lukan Golden Rule 'And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise' (Lk 6:31), Cyril reads the positive-formulation (do-as-you-would) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christian ethics is active-positive, not merely abstinence-from-evil. Where Hillel's negative Golden Rule said 'what is hateful to you, do not do to others,' the dominical positive Golden Rule commands proactive good.
