Tewahedo catechesis cites Lk 6:31 as the canonical Lukan anchor for the active-positive structure of Christian charity preserved in the seven works of mercy taught in the Mäshafä Sǝʾatat (Book of Hours) catechetical material.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XLIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful' (Lk 6:36), Cyril reads the Lukan be-merciful command as the distinctive Lukan parallel to Matthew's 'Be ye therefore perfect, as your Father which is in heaven is perfect' (Mt 5:48) — Luke's choice of 'merciful' (oiktirmones) rather than 'perfect' (teleios) highlights the Father's mercy as the defining attribute that Christian ethics imitates. Tewahedo soteriology cites Lk 6:36 + Mt 5:48 as the canonical doubled-witness for the theosis-pattern: Christian perfection IS divine mercy received and extended.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XLV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mt 5:48.

entries.summary: On the raising of the Nain widow's son — 'and there came a fear on all: and they glorified God, saying, That a great prophet is risen up among us' (Lk 7:12, 16) — Cyril reads the first resurrection-miracle in Luke as the canonical Lukan anchor of Christ's master-over-death authority, prefiguring the Lazarus raising (Jn 11) and ultimately Christ's own resurrection. The Nain widow's son is the third raising-from-the-dead in scripture (after Elijah at Zarephath and Elisha at Shunem); Christ's act surpasses the prophets — he raises without prayer, by his own word. Tewahedo funeral office cites Lk 7:12 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christ's compassion at the bier of the widow's son is the model for priestly compassion at every funeral.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XLVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's answer to JBaptist's disciples 'the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, to the poor the gospel is preached' (Lk 7:22), Cyril reads the sixfold sign-list as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christ's identity is demonstrated by the Isaian Messianic signs (Is 35:5-6 + Is 61:1) — the same prophet whom John quoted at his preaching now points back to him. The signs are cumulative-eschatological: the Messianic age has arrived. Tewahedo christology cites Lk 7:22 + Is 35 + Is 61 as the canonical triple-witness of the prophetic-fulfillment evidence of Christ's identity.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XLVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Is 35:5-6, Is 61:1.

entries.summary: On the title 'The Son of man is come eating and drinking; and ye say, Behold a gluttonous man, and a winebibber' (Lk 7:34), Cyril reads the eating-and-drinking-Christology as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the Word's true humanity includes ordinary table-fellowship: Christ does not impose monastic asceticism on his ministry (unlike John). The dominical pattern (Luke especially) is the table-as-pulpit. Tewahedo monastic theology preserves the doubled-witness: the monastic ascetic follows John's pattern, but the parish priest follows Christ's table-fellowship pattern; both are canonical.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XLIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's direct absolution-formula 'And he said unto her, Thy sins are forgiven' (Lk 7:48), Cyril reads the second-person performative declaration (apheōntai sou hai hamartiai) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the priestly absolution-formula: Christ-in-Person speaks forgiveness directly, paralleled by the Johannine commission to the apostles (Jn 20:23 — 'Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them'). Tewahedo penance-theology cites Lk 7:48 + Jn 20:23 as the canonical doubled-witness for the priestly absolution: the priest declares 'thy sins are forgiven' in persona Christi, exercising the apostolic commission.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Jn 20:23.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace' (Lk 7:50), Cyril reads the doubled-dismissal (faith-has-saved + go-in-peace) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of justifying faith: the sinful woman's faith is the operative cause of her salvation, the peace is the eschatological dismissal-formula. The phrase recurs at Lk 8:48 (Jairus's daughter / hemorrhaging woman) and Lk 17:19 (Samaritan leper) and Lk 18:42 (blind beggar) — four 'thy-faith-hath-saved-thee' formulas in Luke, an emphatic Lukan refrain. Tewahedo dismissal-formula in the Eucharistic anaphora preserves a parallel structure: 'Go in the peace of the Lord.'
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's interpretation of the Sower parable 'Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God' (Lk 8:11), Cyril reads the seed = word-of-God identification as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the dynamic Word: the Word that creates (Gen 1) is the same Word that saves (the Gospel) and the same Word that perseveres (the canonical Scripture). The Word is seed because it carries its own life within itself. Tewahedo Bible-doctrine cites Lk 8:11 as the canonical Lukan anchor for the doctrine of Scripture-as-living-seed; the Tewahedo manuscript tradition's reverence for the canonical word as bearing-its-own-life is rooted here.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the description of the freed Gerasene demoniac '[they] found the man, out of whom the devils were departed, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind' (Lk 8:35), Cyril reads the threefold-restoration (sitting-at-feet + clothed + right-mind) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christian sanity as the restoration of catechetical posture: the freed soul takes its rightful disciple-position at the feet of the Lord, with the moral garments of virtue and the rational integration of right-mindedness. Tewahedo catechumenate cites Lk 8:35 as the canonical anchor for the catechumen's restored posture — at Christ's feet, clothed in the white baptismal garment, sound of mind.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LVI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace' (Lk 8:48), Cyril reads the second instance of the Lukan 'thy-faith-hath-saved-thee' formula (after Lk 7:50) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the woman's bold-touch-in-faith is the active-receptive cause of her healing: she did not need permission, the touch of faith drew Christ's power. Tewahedo theology of bold-faith cites Lk 8:48 as the canonical anchor of the doctrine that the believing approach to the consecrated species (the body and blood) is the parallel of the hemorrhaging woman's healing-touch; one approaches the Eucharist in the same posture.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's call to Jairus's daughter 'Maid, arise' (Lk 8:54), Cyril reads the imperative-command-as-resurrection-word as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christ's word effects what it says: the same authority that 'in the beginning was the Word' (Jn 1:1) speaks the dead to life with a single imperative. The doubled-raising of Lk 7 (Nain) + Lk 8 (Jairus's daughter) prepares the reader for Lk 24 (Christ's own resurrection): Christ raises others by his word, then is raised himself by the Father. Tewahedo Fasika theology cites Lk 8:54 + Jn 11:43 + Lk 24:46 as the canonical triple-witness of the word-effects-resurrection power that culminates in Christ's own raising.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Jn 11:43, Lk 24:46.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross DAILY, and follow me' (Lk 9:23), Cyril reads the distinctive Lukan 'daily' (kath' hēmeran) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christian discipleship is not a one-time martyrdom but a daily continuing renunciation: the cross is taken up every morning, not once at conversion. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 9:23 + the kath'-hēmeran daily-renewal pattern as the canonical anchor of the monastic morning-prayer renunciation: each day the bahǝtawi renews his vows, takes up his daily cross. The daily-eucharist tradition in some Tewahedo monasteries draws on the same Lukan pattern of daily Christ-following.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Luke's distinctive note about the Transfiguration conversation — '[Moses and Elias] spake of his decease (exodon) which he should accomplish at Jerusalem' (Lk 9:31) — Cyril reads the Greek exodon as the canonical Lukan double-entendre: Christ's death is his Exodus from this world AND the New-Exodus that liberates humanity from sin's bondage (the Moses-Exodus parallel made explicit). Moses, who led the first Exodus, now consults with the Greater-Moses who is about to lead the second. Tewahedo Buhe (Transfiguration) theology cites Lk 9:31 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the Transfiguration is the apocalypse of the coming Pascha — the same glory will return at the Resurrection.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Tewahedo liturgical witness: Buhe / Däbrä-Tabor.

entries.summary: On the Lukan turning-point 'when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem' (Lk 9:51), Cyril reads the set-his-face formula (estērisen to prosōpon — Hebraism: 'set the face') as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's deliberate-voluntary Passion: the Lord is not seized by hostile forces, he moves toward Jerusalem with intentional resolve. The verb 'received up' (analēmpseōs) embraces death + resurrection + ascension as a single integrated movement. Tewahedo theology of the voluntary Passion cites Lk 9:51 as the canonical Lukan anchor for the doctrine that Christ goes willingly to Calvary — the Lent-and-Holy-Week observance follows the Lukan travel-narrative geography.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God' (Lk 9:62), Cyril reads the plough-image as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the kingdom requires unbroken forward-orientation: the disciple resembles Elisha (1 Ki 19:19-21) who left the plough to follow Elijah without looking back. The image of the plough turning the soil prefigures the apostolic mission turning the soil of the nations for the seed of the gospel. Tewahedo monastic-formation cites Lk 9:62 + 1 Ki 19:19-21 as the canonical doubled-witness for the irreversibility of monastic profession: once the bahǝtawi has begun, he does not look back.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. 1 Ki 19:19-21.

entries.summary: On Christ's appointing 'other seventy [or seventy-two] also, and sent them two and two before his face' (Lk 10:1), Cyril reads the seventy(-two)-disciples as the canonical Lukan anchor of the ministry-beyond-the-apostolic-Twelve: the wider missionary commission corresponds typologically to Moses' seventy elders (Num 11:24-25) and (in the longer reading) to the seventy-two nations of the Table of Nations (Gen 10 LXX). The two-by-two pattern preserves the Deuteronomic two-witness rule (Deu 19:15) — apostolic witness is plural and corroborated. Tewahedo missionary theology cites Lk 10:1 + Num 11:24 + Deu 19:15 as the canonical triple-witness for the wider-than-apostolic missionary commission and the two-witness norm of evangelization.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Num 11:24-25, Deu 19:15.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven' (Lk 10:18), Cyril reads the seventy-two's return-with-joy + Christ's prophetic-vision as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the apostolic-missionary expansion enacts in time the eternally-decided defeat of Satan. The lightning-image draws on Is 14:12 (Lucifer fall) and is parallel to Rev 12:7-9. Tewahedo angelology, drawing on 1 Enoch 86 (Mäṣḥafä Hēnok's account of fallen stars), cites Lk 10:18 + 1 En 86 + Rev 12:7-9 as the canonical triple-witness of Satan's heavenly-fall — the same fall is the eschatological referent of every successful exorcism in apostolic mission.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Is 14:12, 1 En 86 (R.H. Charles, 1912 — PD), Rev 12:7-9.

entries.summary: On the Lukan 'In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit, and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth' (Lk 10:21), Cyril reads the doubly-emphatic 'rejoiced in spirit' (or, in the alternative reading, 'rejoiced in the Holy Spirit') as the canonical Lukan anchor of an explicit Trinitarian utterance in the public ministry: the Son addresses the Father in the joy of the Holy Spirit, voicing in time the eternal perichoresis of the divine persons. The verse is among the most-cited Lukan Trinitarian-cantilenas in Tewahedo Liturgy of the Hours. Tewahedo Trinitarian-doxology cites Lk 10:21 + Mt 28:19 + 2 Cor 13:14 as the canonical Lukan-NT triple-witness of explicit Trinitarian-prayer.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mt 28:19, 2 Cor 13:14.

entries.summary: On the lawyer's recital 'Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself' (Lk 10:27), Cyril reads the dominical-approved double-summary as the canonical Lukan anchor of the Greatest Commandment in its FOURFOLD heart/soul/strength/mind form (Luke alone among the Synoptics expands 'might' to 'strength + mind'). The four-faculty totality is taken up by the Tewahedo catechumenate as the framework for the four exercises of faith: heart (prayer) + soul (worship) + strength (ascetic labour) + mind (catechetical study). Tewahedo monastic spirituality cites Lk 10:27 + Deu 6:5 as the canonical fourfold-doubled-witness for the integral-formation pattern of the bahǝtawi.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Deu 6:5.

entries.summary: On the Lukan Lord's-Prayer petition 'And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us' (Lk 11:4), Cyril reads the forgive-as-forgiven-by-us clause as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that human forgiveness of debtors is the operative condition (not the meritorious cause) of receiving divine forgiveness. The clause's reciprocal grammar makes the Lord's Prayer the only canonical petitionary text that requires the petitioner to take an ethical action FIRST. Tewahedo penance-theology cites Lk 11:4 + Mt 6:12 + Mt 6:14-15 as the canonical triple-witness that priestly absolution presupposes the penitent's forgiveness of debtors; sacramental confession is incomplete without horizontal reconciliation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mt 6:12, Mt 6:14-15.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him' (Lk 11:13), Cyril reads the distinctive-Lukan substitution of 'Holy Spirit' (where Matthew has 'good things' at Mt 7:11) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the supreme petition of Christian prayer is the gift of the Spirit himself, not merely material or providential goods. Luke's pneumatological theology is integrated throughout: the Spirit is the Promise-of-the-Father (Lk 24:49 + Acts 1:4-5) and the gift to which all other gifts are subordinate. Tewahedo charismatic-prayer-theology cites Lk 11:13 as the canonical Lukan anchor for the doctrine that the Holy Spirit is the answer to every prayer 'in Jesus' name'.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mt 7:11, Lk 24:49, Acts 1:4-5.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'But if I with the finger of God cast out devils' (Lk 11:20), Cyril reads the distinctive-Lukan 'finger of God' (where Mt 12:28 has 'Spirit of God') as the canonical Lukan anchor that links Christ's exorcisms to the Exodus plague-narratives — the Egyptian magicians confessed 'this is the finger of God' (Exo 8:19). The Mosaic 'finger' = the Spirit, the same Spirit that wrote the Decalogue on stone tablets (Exo 31:18). Tewahedo christology cites Lk 11:20 + Exo 8:19 + Exo 31:18 + Mt 12:28 as the canonical fourfold-witness that the Mosaic-finger-of-God is identified with the Spirit-of-God operative in Christ's ministry; the same Spirit is the divine agent of liberation and of canon-formation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mt 12:28, Exo 8:19, Exo 31:18.

entries.summary: On the unnamed woman's exclamation 'Blessed is the womb that bare thee, and the paps which thou hast sucked' (Lk 11:27), Cyril reads the public Marian beatitude — uniquely Lukan among the Synoptics — as the canonical Lukan-public-anchor of the Theotokos doctrine: even mid-public-ministry, a Galilean crowd-woman utters spontaneous Marian-praise. Christ's response 'yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it' does NOT cancel her praise but transfers its principle: Mary's blessedness is not biological-only but also the FIRST exemplar of hearing-and-keeping (Lk 1:38). Tewahedo Wǝddase Maryam preserves Lk 11:27 alongside Lk 1:42 as the canonical doubled-Lukan public-Marian-beatitudes.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXXII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'unto him that blasphemeth against the Holy Ghost it shall not be forgiven' (Lk 12:10), Cyril reads the unpardonable-sin clause as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the sin against the Spirit is not a single verbal lapse but a settled-final refusal of the Spirit's offered forgiveness: one who rejects the agent of forgiveness cannot be forgiven. The unpardonability is structural-receptive, not capricious. Tewahedo penance-theology cites Lk 12:10 + Mk 3:29 as the canonical doubled-witness that the Spirit is the active-agent of every absolution; willful-final refusal of the Spirit closes the door from the human side. Pastoral wisdom in the Tewahedo confessional tradition: anyone WORRIED about having committed this sin has not committed it.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXXVI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mk 3:29.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom' (Lk 12:32), Cyril reads the doubled-tenderness (little flock + Father's good pleasure) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the Church's smallness is no obstacle to the Kingdom's gift: God's good pleasure (eudokia — the same word as 'good will toward men' in the angelic hymn Lk 2:14) does not measure recipients by their numbers. Tewahedo ecclesiology, mindful of the minority-position of the Ethiopian Tewahedo Church in the broader Christian world, cites Lk 12:32 as the canonical anchor of the doctrine that the small flock of right-believers (the Tewahedo 'right-believing' identity) receives the same kingdom as any larger communion.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily LXXXIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning' (Lk 12:35), Cyril reads the doubled-readiness-image (girded loins + burning lamps) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the vigil-of-the-Lord eschatological-posture: the Christian awaits the master's return in the same posture as the Passover-Israelite (loins girded per Exo 12:11) and the wise virgins (lamps burning per Mt 25:1-13). Tewahedo Holy-Saturday vigil-liturgy cites Lk 12:35 + Exo 12:11 + Mt 25:1-13 as the canonical triple-witness for the vigil-of-the-Lord posture: the all-night Pascha vigil is the liturgical-iconic realization of this canonical readiness.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XC (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Exo 12:11, Mt 25:1-13.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished!' (Lk 12:50), Cyril reads the future-passive-baptism (paraphrasably 'I am-to-be-baptized') as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christ's death-and-resurrection is itself the baptism-toward-which-his-earthly-baptism-pointed: the Jordan baptism prefigures, the Cross effects. The straitening-cry expresses the Word-in-flesh's deep human anticipation of the Passion. Tewahedo baptismal theology cites Lk 12:50 + Rom 6:3-4 ('baptized into his death') as the canonical doubled-witness that Christian baptism participates in Christ's own death-baptism; the catechumen is buried with Christ in the font.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XCII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Rom 6:3-4.

entries.summary: On the parable of the barren fig tree — 'Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down' (Lk 13:7) — Cyril reads the three-years-fruit-seeking + intercessor's-plea-for-one-more-year as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of patient divine longsuffering: God seeks fruit, the Son intercedes for delay, the Spirit's manure-and-digging (the means of grace) is given for one more year. The three years correspond to the public ministry; the digging-and-dunging is the apostolic-and-monastic intercession. Tewahedo intercessory theology cites Lk 13:7 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that priestly intercession can postpone (though not forever) the just judgment of fruitlessness.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XCIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able' (Lk 13:24), Cyril reads the strive (agōnizesthe) + many-shall-not-be-able as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that salvation requires sustained-effort, not merely benign assent: the verb (root of 'agony') is the same Paul uses for the apostolic struggle (1 Cor 9:25, 1 Tim 6:12). The 'many shall not be able' warns against presumption. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 13:24 + 1 Cor 9:25 as the canonical doubled-witness for the strenuous-character of Christian discipleship; the desert-fathers' ascetic 'agon' against the demons is the appropriation of this command.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XCVI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. 1 Cor 9:25, 1 Tim 6:12.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God' (Lk 13:29), Cyril reads the fourfold-compass-points eschatological-gathering as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the universal-Gentile inclusion in the eschatological-banquet: salvation flows from the East (where Cyril sees the dominant Mediterranean diaspora) but also the West, the North, and the South — explicitly including Ethiopia. Tewahedo missionary-eschatology cites Lk 13:29 as the canonical Lukan anchor for the doctrine that the southern-African (specifically Ethiopian) inclusion in the eschatological-Kingdom is canonically promised — the Acts 8 Ethiopian eunuch is the firstfruits of this fulfilment.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XCVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Acts 8:26-39 (Ethiopian eunuch's baptism).

entries.summary: On Christ's lament 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem... how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not!' (Lk 13:34), Cyril reads the doubly-vocative city-address + maternal-hen-image as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's divine-anguish over human refusal: the Word is Maker-Mother of Israel — the 'how often' acknowledges the prophetic outreach to Jerusalem across centuries (Christ identifies himself as the agent of that outreach). The maternal hen-and-chicks image preserves the Old-Testament eagle-wings imagery (Exo 19:4, Deu 32:11) in maternal-form. Tewahedo Marian theology cites Lk 13:34 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the maternal-Christ-image alongside Mary's own maternal-Theotokos role.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily XCVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Exo 19:4, Deu 32:11.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted' (Lk 14:11), Cyril reads the doubled-passive-formula (shall-be-abased + shall-be-exalted — the divine passive) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the great-reversal eschatological principle: God himself is the agent of both the abasement and the exaltation. The phrase recurs in Luke at 18:14 (Pharisee + Publican), making it a Lukan refrain. Tewahedo monastic spirituality cites Lk 14:11 + Lk 18:14 + Phil 2:8-9 (Christ's-own humiliation-and-exaltation) as the canonical triple-witness of the humility-precedes-exaltation pattern — the same pattern Christ embodies in the Incarnation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Phil 2:8-9.

entries.summary: On the parable of the Great Supper — 'A certain man made a great supper, and bade many' (Lk 14:16) — Cyril reads the supper-parable as the canonical Lukan anchor of the Eucharistic-eschatological-banquet image: the great supper is the messianic feast (anticipated at Lk 13:29 from-east-and-west) prepared by the Father, hosted by the Son, distributed by the Spirit's apostolic invitations. The original-invited (covenant-elect) excuse themselves; the streets-and-lanes poor are brought in. Tewahedo Eucharistic theology cites Lk 14:16 alongside the Marriage Supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9) as the canonical Lukan-Apocalyptic doubled-witness of the Eucharist as the present-eschatological-banquet: every Mass anticipates the Great Supper.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Rev 19:9.

entries.summary: On the master's command 'Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in' (Lk 14:23), Cyril reads the compel-them-to-come-in (anagkason eiselthein) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of evangelistic-persuasive-urgency: the apostolic invitation is not coy permission but earnest-pressing constraint. Cyril is emphatic that the constraint is moral-persuasive, never physical-coercive (Augustine's later use of this verse to justify coercion against the Donatists is not Cyril's reading). Tewahedo missionary-pastoral theology cites Lk 14:23 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that evangelistic urgency is genuine pressure of love, not state-religious coercion.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple' (Lk 14:33), Cyril reads the forsake-all-that-he-hath (panta apotassetai tois huparchousin) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of total-discipleship: the cost-of-discipleship parable (counting-the-tower + counting-the-battle) issues in this absolute. Cyril does not read 'forsake' as universal-divestment for every Christian but as the inner-detachment that some are called to embody outwardly in monastic profession. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 14:33 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the bahǝtawi's vow of poverty — the monastic outwardly enacts what every disciple inwardly possesses.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance' (Lk 15:7), Cyril reads the more-joy-over-one-sinner-repenting as the canonical Lukan anchor of the heaven-rejoices doctrine: the conversion of a single soul is not a private-individual event but a cosmic-angelic celebration. The 'more joy' is not comparative-quantitative but pastoral-emphatic — Cyril preserves the divine preference for the rescuing-pattern. Tewahedo missionary-spirituality cites Lk 15:7 + Lk 15:10 (joy in the presence of the angels) as the canonical doubled-witness of the doctrine that the angelic host participates joyfully in each conversion; the Tewahedo evangelistic-prayer tradition invokes the angels' rejoicing.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the parable of the lost coin — 'Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?' (Lk 15:8) — Cyril reads the maternal-housekeeping-image as the canonical Lukan anchor of a doctrine that complements the shepherd-image (Lk 15:4) and the father-image (Lk 15:11): God seeks the lost in three iconic ways — shepherd seeking on the hills, woman seeking in the house, father waiting at the door. The triple-image is Trinitarian-iconic-pedagogy. Tewahedo Trinitarian-iconography cites Lk 15:4-32 as the canonical Lukan iconographic triple-pattern of the Father-Son-Spirit's-shared-search-for-the-lost.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the parable's opening 'A certain man had two sons' (Lk 15:11), Cyril reads the two-sons frame as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the parable's THIRD pivot (after shepherd + housekeeper) gives the Father his speaking-part: the father whose first speech is the silent embrace at 15:20, whose second speech is the celebration-command, whose third is the explanation to the elder brother. The full-pericope (Lk 15:11-32) is Christ's most-extended-character-development parable; the father's character is most-fully-disclosed. Tewahedo pastoral theology cites Lk 15:11-32 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Father's threefold-speech-of-mercy — the priest who absolves speaks as the father in the parable speaks.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the father's final words to the elder brother 'It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found' (Lk 15:32), Cyril reads the doubled-formula (dead-and-alive + lost-and-found) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of conversion-as-resurrection: the prodigal's return is not merely moral-improvement but a passage from death to life. The same doubled-formula echoes Christian baptism (Rom 6:4 — dead with Christ, alive in Christ). Tewahedo baptismal-and-penance theology cites Lk 15:32 + Rom 6:4 as the canonical doubled-witness that every conversion is a participation in the death-and-resurrection of Christ; the Tewahedo penance-rite preserves the alive-again grammar in its absolution formula.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Rom 6:4.

entries.summary: On the master's commendation of the unjust steward — 'the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely' (Lk 16:8) — Cyril reads the lord-commended-the-unjust paradox as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that prudent-shrewdness in temporal matters should be matched by prudent-shrewdness in eternal matters: the steward is praised not for his dishonesty but for his foresight in securing his future. Tewahedo stewardship theology cites Lk 16:8 + Lk 16:9 ('make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness') as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of strategic-almsgiving — the prudent Christian uses temporal wealth to build eternal friendships (the recipients of the alms welcome the giver into eternal habitations).
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'No servant can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon' (Lk 16:13), Cyril reads the impossibility-formula (ou dynasthe — 'ye CANNOT') as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the metaphysical incompatibility of God and mammon as objects-of-ultimate-loyalty: the disjunction is not pastoral counsel but ontological fact. Cyril notes the personification of mammon (treated as a rival lord) anticipates later patristic identifications of mammon-greed as a demonic principality. Tewahedo asceticism cites Lk 16:13 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that monastic poverty is the only consistent answer to the impossibility-formula — the bahǝtawi physically forecloses the option of serving mammon.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the parable's opening 'There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day' (Lk 16:19), Cyril reads the unnamed-rich-man + named-Lazarus contrast as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the reversal-of-recognition: the rich man (anonymous in the parable, anonymous in heaven) has his fine-linen reversed to torment; the poor man Lazarus (named, known to God) has his sores reversed to glory. The parable is Christ's most-vivid teaching on the post-mortem intermediate state — the doctrine elaborated at 16:23 seed. Tewahedo intermediate-state theology cites Lk 16:19 + Lk 16:23 + Lk 23:43 (good thief) as the canonical Lukan triple-witness for the conscious-intermediate-state of departed souls.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the rich man's plea + Abraham's answer 'If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead' (Lk 16:31), Cyril reads Abraham's verdict as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the sufficiency-of-Scripture for salvation: even resurrection-witness will not persuade those who have hardened against the canonical word. The verse becomes load-bearing in the Lukan-Acts trajectory: the post-resurrection apostolic preaching cites the OT Scriptures as the basis of belief (Acts 17:11 — Bereans searched the Scriptures). Tewahedo bibliology cites Lk 16:31 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the canonical Scriptures are sufficient for salvation; private revelations and apparitions are accountable to that canonical word.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Acts 17:11.

entries.summary: On the apostles' petition 'Lord, increase our faith' (Lk 17:5), Cyril reads the prosthes-hēmin-pistin (add-to-us-faith) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that faith is a gift to be asked for, not a quality to be produced: the apostles do not say 'we will work harder' but 'Lord, give us more'. Christ's mustard-seed answer (Lk 17:6) does not rebuke the request but redirects it — faith's POWER is not in its quantity but in its OBJECT (God's omnipotence). Tewahedo faith-formation cites Lk 17:5 + Lk 17:6 as the canonical doubled-Lukan-witness that faith is request-receivable from God (not striven-produced by self) and small-but-real-faith is sufficient if its object is the true God.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do' (Lk 17:10), Cyril reads the unprofitable-servants-formula as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of grace-against-merit: even maximal Christian-virtuous-action puts the disciple no further than baseline-duty; salvation is never owed to the disciple. The Greek achreioi (unprofitable, but also 'without-superfluous-claim') captures the disposition of the just-debtor with no surplus. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 17:10 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the monk's perpetual-humility-formula — 'I am an unprofitable servant' is recited in the daily-office.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'the kingdom of God is within you' (Lk 17:21 — entos hymōn estin), Cyril reads the entos-hymōn (within-you or among-you) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the present-immanent-kingdom: in Christ's person and ministry, the kingdom has already arrived among the questioners — the Pharisees see-but-do-not-recognize it. Cyril allows both readings (within = interior reign of God in the believer; among = Christ-the-kingdom-present-among). The Greek is deliberately ambiguous. Tewahedo theology of the kingdom cites Lk 17:21 + Mk 1:15 ('the kingdom of God is at hand') as the canonical doubled-witness for the already-present (Christological) and the still-coming (eschatological) dimensions of the kingdom.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mk 1:15.

entries.summary: On Christ's terse warning 'Remember Lot's wife' (Lk 17:32), Cyril reads the imperative-of-memory (mnēmoneuete) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that disobedient-looking-back is a paradigmatic-fatal-sin: Lot's wife (Gen 19:26) is preserved in canonical-memory not as a personal-name but as a warning-icon. The eschatological context (Lk 17:31 — that day, the rooftop) makes the warning explicit: when the kingdom comes, no looking-back. Tewahedo eschatological-asceticism cites Lk 17:32 + Lk 9:62 (plough-no-looking-back) as the canonical doubled-Lukan-witness for the irreversibility-of-disciple-orientation — both verses use the same forward-orientation grammar.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Gen 19:26.

entries.summary: On Luke's editorial introduction to the unjust-judge parable — 'he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint' (Lk 18:1) — Cyril reads the dei-pantote-proseuchesthai (it-is-necessary-always-to-pray) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of ceaseless-prayer (later codified by Paul at 1 Th 5:17 — 'pray without ceasing'). The grammatical necessity (dei) puts ceaseless-prayer on the same canonical level as 'must-be-baptized' and 'must-suffer'. Tewahedo monastic-prayer-discipline cites Lk 18:1 + 1 Th 5:17 as the canonical doubled-witness for the seven-fold daily office (Mäshafä Sǝʾatat) — seven daily prayer-points are the canonical operationalization of 'always pray, never faint'.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. 1 Th 5:17.

entries.summary: On the Pharisee's self-praising prayer 'God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are' (Lk 18:11), Cyril reads the Pharisee's-prayer as the canonical Lukan anti-model: addressed-to-God-in-form but self-praising-in-content. The prepositional pros-heauton (with-himself / to-himself — preferred reading) makes the Pharisee's prayer self-directed even in posture. Tewahedo confessor's-prayer-formation cites Lk 18:11 + Lk 18:13 (the Publican's prayer — seed γ.4.3) as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness of the two-prayer-patterns: the wrong one (Pharisee, self-praise) and the right one (Publican, 'God be merciful to me a sinner' — the Jesus-Prayer of Tewahedo monastic-spirituality).
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's command 'Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God' (Lk 18:16), Cyril reads the doubled-imperative (suffer-them + forbid-them-not) as the canonical Lukan anchor of paedo-receptivity and (in the wider patristic tradition) infant-baptism: children are not deferred until adult-comprehension but received-now into the kingdom. The kingdom belongs not to children alone but to those characterized by child-like receptivity (Lk 18:17). Tewahedo baptismal theology — practising infant-baptism (often on the 40th day for boys, 80th day for girls per Lev 12 + Lk 2:22-24) — cites Lk 18:16 as the canonical Lukan-NT anchor for the practice.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Lev 12, Lk 2:22-24.

entries.summary: On Christ's command to the rich young ruler 'Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me' (Lk 18:22), Cyril reads the sell-all + follow-me as the canonical Lukan anchor of the monastic-vocation specifically (not universal divestment for every Christian — Cyril is careful here): some are called to total-divestment as a particular vocation, and the rich-young-ruler is identified as such a call-and-refusal narrative. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 18:22 + Acts 4:34-35 (early-Jerusalem communal-divestment) as the canonical doubled-witness for the monastic vocation; the cenobitic-Tewahedo monasteries preserve the apostolic-divestment pattern.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Acts 4:34-35.

entries.summary: On Christ's call to Zacchaeus 'make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house' (Lk 19:5), Cyril reads the dei-me (it-is-necessary-for-me) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's seeking-grace: the dominical 'I must lodge with thee' is a divine-imperative, not a guest's-request. Christ initiates the encounter; Zacchaeus's tree-climbing met halfway by Christ's calling-down. Tewahedo evangelism-theology cites Lk 19:5 + Lk 19:10 (Son of Man come to seek-and-save) as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness of the doctrine that Christ initiates the salvation-encounter; the priestly-pastor follows the dominical-pattern of seeking-the-Zacchaeuses.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXVI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's mission-statement at the Zacchaeus episode 'For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost' (Lk 19:10), Cyril reads the doubled-mission (seek + save) as the canonical Lukan summary-statement of the Incarnation's purpose: the Son of Man's earthly trajectory (already-emphasized at Lk 5:32 — come to call sinners) reaches its compact-definitive expression here. The verse becomes load-bearing for the patristic doctrine of the missio Dei — God's outgoing mission preceding any human response. Tewahedo missionary theology cites Lk 19:10 + Lk 5:32 as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness of the doctrine that Christian mission participates in the dominical-search-and-rescue mission; the Tewahedo apostolic-outreach to the Beta-Israel and surrounding peoples is the appropriation of this canonical pattern.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Lk 5:32.

entries.summary: On the triumphal-entry cry 'Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest' (Lk 19:38), Cyril reads the Lukan-distinctive 'peace in heaven' (where the Synoptic parallels say 'Hosanna in the highest') as the canonical Lukan anchor of the cosmic-reconciliation announcement: heaven-and-earth peace is the explicit content of Christ's triumphal-entry. The phrase echoes the angelic Christmas-hymn (Lk 2:14 — peace-on-earth) and now reverses: peace-on-earth then, peace-in-heaven now. Tewahedo Hosanna-procession (Hosanna feast — the Sunday before Pascha) cites Lk 19:38 alongside Lk 2:14 as the canonical Lukan-doubled-witness of the peace-of-the-incarnation completed at the Cross.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Lk 2:14. Tewahedo liturgical witness: Hosanna feast.

entries.summary: On Christ's cleansing of the Temple — 'It is written, My house is the house of prayer: but ye have made it a den of thieves' (Lk 19:46) — Cyril reads the citation of Isa 56:7 + Jer 7:11 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the consecrated-place is by-definition the house-of-prayer; commerce within the precinct DEFILES the consecration. Christ's action is canonical-prophetic, not anti-Temple in principle (Christ continues to teach there daily, Lk 19:47). Tewahedo church-discipline cites Lk 19:46 + Is 56:7 + Jer 7:11 as the canonical triple-witness that the church-building is by definition the house-of-prayer; commercial use of the precinct (vending, money-changing) is excluded by canonical prophet-and-dominical authority.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Is 56:7, Jer 7:11.

entries.summary: On the Temple-elders' challenge 'by what authority doest thou these things?' (Lk 20:1-2), Cyril reads the authority-question as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christ's authority is self-authenticating, not derived from human institutions: the Lord refuses to license his actions to the question-form because to do so would already concede that authority is delegable by the Sanhedrin. Christ's counter-question about John's baptism (Lk 20:4) traps the elders in their own institutional logic. Tewahedo ecclesial theology cites Lk 20:1-8 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the Church's authority traces to Christ directly, not through Imperial-Sanhedrin-style human delegation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the parable of the wicked husbandmen (Lk 20:9-16), Cyril reads the vineyard-tenants who reject the servants and finally kill the heir as the canonical Lukan anchor of the salvation-history-as-progressive-rejection: prophets sent, prophets killed; finally the Son sent, the Son killed; the vineyard given to others (Gentiles + Tewahedo). The 'heir' language is Christological: Christ's death is the prophetic-final rejection that opens the vineyard to the wider mission. Tewahedo missionary-theology cites Lk 20:9-16 + Mt 21:43 ('the kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof') as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the Gentile-Ethiopian inclusion in the vineyard is the consequence of the canonical-prophetic rejection of Christ at Calvary.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mt 21:43.

entries.summary: On Christ's citation 'The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner' (Lk 20:17, citing Ps 118:22), Cyril reads the stone-rejected-yet-cornerstone as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Christological-rejection-reversal: Christ is the rejected stone (by the Jerusalem builders) who becomes the foundation-cornerstone of the New-Covenant building (apostolic + Gentile-inclusion). The citation chain runs Ps 118:22 → Lk 20:17 → Acts 4:11 (Peter's apostolic preaching) → 1 Pet 2:6-8 (foundation theology). Tewahedo ecclesiology cites this canonical chain as the foundation of the doctrine that the Tewahedo Church is built on Christ-the-Cornerstone, not on the rejecting Jerusalem-builders' approval.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Ps 118:22, Acts 4:11, 1 Pet 2:6-8.

entries.summary: On the Sadducees' resurrection-denying scenario (the woman-with-seven-husbands at Lk 20:27-33), Cyril reads the Sadducees' rejection-of-resurrection as the canonical anti-pattern: those who deny the resurrection prove they neither know the Scriptures (the basis of resurrection-hope) nor the power of God (the agent of resurrection). The Sadducees' literalistic-marriage scenario fundamentally misunderstands that resurrection-life is transformed-life, not extended-marriage. Tewahedo eschatology cites Lk 20:27-40 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the resurrection is the trans-marital + trans-procreative life of the Kingdom, distinct from earthly marriage's covenantal exclusivity.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Neither can they die any more: for they are equal unto the angels; and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection' (Lk 20:36), Cyril reads the isaggelos (equal-to-angels) and the children-of-resurrection compound title as the canonical Lukan anchor of the resurrection-anthropology: the resurrected human is not made into an angel (against later Origenist confusion), but enjoys angelic immortality and angelic non-procreative communal-life. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 20:36 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the bahǝtawi's celibacy anticipates the resurrection-state in this life — eschatological-existence proleptically embodied.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him' (Lk 20:38), Cyril reads the all-live-unto-him (pantes gar autō zōsin — Luke's distinctive addition over Mark/Matthew) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the patriarchs whom God identifies himself with (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) are alive-to-God right now — not merely scheduled-for-future-resurrection. The intermediate-state of the righteous is conscious-life-with-God. Tewahedo intermediate-state-theology cites Lk 20:38 as the canonical Lukan anchor doubled with Lk 16:23 (Lazarus in Abraham's bosom) and Lk 23:43 (today thou shalt be with me in paradise) — the conscious-life-with-Christ of the departed righteous is canonically witnessed three-times in Luke alone.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's puzzle from Psalm 110 — 'David himself saith in the book of Psalms, The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand' (Lk 20:42, citing Ps 110:1) — Cyril reads the Psalm-110 citation as the canonical Lukan anchor of the Christological double-Lordship: David (the messiah's ancestor) addresses the messiah AS HIS LORD, which makes the messiah more than merely David's son. Ps 110:1 becomes the most-cited Old-Testament verse in the New Testament (~25 times) and the foundational text for Christ's session at the Father's right hand (Ascension theology). Tewahedo Christology cites Lk 20:42 + Ps 110:1 as the canonical Old-Testament-Christological double-Lordship anchor; the Tewahedo Anaphora preserves the right-hand-of-the-Father language verbatim.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXVI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Ps 110:1.

entries.summary: On Christ's prophecy 'there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down' (Lk 21:6), Cyril reads the Temple-destruction prophecy as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the canonical-end-of-the-Old-Covenant-cultus: the Temple as the chosen-place (Deu 12:5) is replaced by the eucharistic-altar in every local church. The destruction in 70 AD is the historical confirmation, but the spiritual transition is already accomplished in Christ. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Lk 21:6 + Heb 10 (sacrificial-system fulfilled in Christ's one offering) as the canonical doubled-witness for the New-Covenant transition; the tabot bearing the Christic-presence replaces the Temple as the dwelling of God.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Heb 10.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'when ye shall hear of wars and commotions, be not terrified... the end is not by and by' (Lk 21:9), Cyril reads the not-by-and-by (ouk eutheōs — 'not immediately') qualification as the canonical Lukan anchor against eschatological-panic: military-and-political upheaval does NOT mean the end is now. Cyril notes the eschatological discourses regularly correct panic — Christian eschatology is patient, not feverish. Tewahedo eschatological-spirituality cites Lk 21:9 + 2 Th 2:1-2 (Pauline corrective against 'the day of the Lord is at hand' panic) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of patient-eschatological-hope rather than panic-eschatology.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. 2 Th 2:1-2.

entries.summary: On Christ's promise 'I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist' (Lk 21:15), Cyril reads the doubled-gift (mouth-and-wisdom) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Spirit's-utterance-in-persecution: when the disciple is delivered up before kings, the Spirit speaks IN him. The doctrine flows into Stephen's defense before the Sanhedrin (Acts 6:10 — 'they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake'). Tewahedo confessor-theology cites Lk 21:15 + Acts 6:10 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of the Spirit-given confessor's-utterance; the Tewahedo martyrs (e.g. Ethiopian Christians under Imperial persecution) participate in this canonical promise.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Acts 6:10.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'But there shall not an hair of your head perish' (Lk 21:18), Cyril reads the hyperbolic-hair-promise in juxtaposition with the immediately-preceding 'some of you shall they cause to be put to death' (21:16) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the spiritual-preservation-through-bodily-death: the believer who dies for Christ does not perish (the hair-of-the-head is not lost) — the apparent perishing is preserved-life in the heavenly economy. Tewahedo martyr-theology cites Lk 21:18 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of resurrection-preservation: every hair of the Tewahedo martyrs (Saint Yared, the Nine Saints, Imperial-era confessors) is preserved with God.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled' (Lk 21:24), Cyril reads the times-of-the-Gentiles (kairoi ethnōn) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Gentile-inclusion-interval: between the canonical-rejection of Christ at Calvary and the eschatological-restoration there is an apostolic-missionary period during which the Gentile-Ethiopian-nations are brought into the fold. Tewahedo missionary-eschatology cites Lk 21:24 + Rom 11:25 ('blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in') as the canonical Lukan-Pauline doubled-witness for the doctrine of the Tewahedo-Gentile-times — the Tewahedo Church's mission contributes to the fulfilment of the times of the Gentiles.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXL (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Rom 11:25.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh' (Lk 21:28), Cyril reads the doubled-imperative (look-up + lift-up-your-heads) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of upward-eschatological-orientation: the Christian's posture in eschatological-troubled-times is not downcast fear but upward-confident expectation. The redemption (apolytrōsis) draws-near is in present-tense participial form — the deliverance is approaching, not merely imminent. Tewahedo liturgical-posture cites Lk 21:28 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of standing-with-uplifted-eyes during the Eucharistic anaphora — the liturgical-posture embodies the eschatological-anticipation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Watch ye therefore, and pray always, that ye may be accounted worthy to escape all these things that shall come to pass, and to stand before the Son of man' (Lk 21:36), Cyril reads the watch-and-pray-always + stand-before-the-Son-of-Man as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of eschatological-vigilance grounded in ceaseless-prayer (doubled with Lk 18:1 — 'always to pray, and not to faint'). The stand-before-the-Son-of-Man is the canonical Lukan formula for eschatological-judgment-readiness. Tewahedo monastic-vigil-prayer (the night-office tradition of the great monasteries) cites Lk 21:36 + Lk 18:1 as the canonical doubled-Lukan-anchor for the ceaseless-prayer + eschatological-vigilance discipline.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Lk 18:1.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer' (Lk 22:15), Cyril reads the Hebraic-redoubled-formula (epithymia epethymēsa) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's deliberate-eager-anticipation of the institutional Last Supper: not reluctant, not pressured, but deeply-desired. The Lord's eagerness for the canonical-eucharistic-institution dignifies every later celebration. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Lk 22:15 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's desire-for-the-eucharist; every Tewahedo Mass is participation in the Lord's own canonical-desire-fulfilment.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you' (Lk 22:20), Cyril reads the new-testament-in-my-blood as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the eucharistic-cup-as-new-covenant-blood: the Lord identifies the wine as the cup of the New-Covenant ratified by his impending blood-shedding. The pairing of the bread-body (Lk 22:19 — seed entry) and the cup-blood-covenant institutes the full eucharistic-form. Tewahedo Anaphora theology cites Lk 22:20 + 1 Cor 11:25 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of the cup as the new-covenant-blood; the Tewahedo Mass preserves Christ's covenant-blood institution language verbatim in every Anaphora.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. 1 Cor 11:25.

entries.summary: On the disciples' Last-Supper strife — 'there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest' (Lk 22:24) — Cyril reads the strife-at-the-Last-Supper as the canonical Lukan anti-anchor: the very moment of institution, when the Word made flesh is on the verge of his death, the disciples argue about greatness. Christ's response (22:26-27 — 'I am among you as he that serveth') makes priestly-service the inversion of secular-greatness. Tewahedo episcopal-formation cites Lk 22:24-27 + Jn 13:14 (foot-washing) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of the bishop-as-servant — the highest ecclesial office is the lowest service-vocation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Jn 13:14.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat' (Lk 22:31), Cyril reads the doubled-name (Simon, Simon) + the sifting-permission as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Satan's limited-permission-to-test (parallel to Job 1:6-12 + Lk 4:13 'the devil... departed from him for a season'): the testing is permitted, not unconstrained. The doubled-name-vocative is the same intimate-pastoral-form Christ uses with Martha (Lk 10:41), Saul (Acts 9:4), and at Gethsemane (Mt 26:38 — 'My soul is exceeding sorrowful'). Tewahedo pastoral theology cites Lk 22:31 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of pastoral-warning love: Christ warns Peter before the fall.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Job 1:6-12, Lk 4:13.

entries.summary: On Christ's 'But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren' (Lk 22:32), Cyril reads the doubled-promise (I-prayed-for-thee + strengthen-thy-brethren) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of dominical-intercession + apostolic-fraternity: Christ's High-Priestly intercession precedes the apostolic ministry; Peter's restoration is the model for fraternal-strengthening after each apostolic failure. Tewahedo pastoral-theology of confession cites Lk 22:32 as the canonical Lukan anchor for the priestly post-confession ministry — the restored confessor strengthens his brethren by sharing his repentance-and-restoration testimony.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's Gethsemane prayer 'Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done' (Lk 22:42), Cyril reads the not-my-will-but-thine as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's two-wills in the unity of the one-person: the human-will of Christ truly desires deliverance, the divine-will (shared with the Father) wills the salvific-Passion. The hypostatic-union does not absorb the human will but ratifies its perfect-obedient-subordination to the divine. Tewahedo Christology — Miaphysite-with-two-operations — cites Lk 22:42 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christ in his humanity prays the prayer the entire human race must learn to pray: 'not my will but thine'.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLVI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the Lukan-unique addition 'And there appeared an angel unto him from heaven, strengthening him' (Lk 22:43), Cyril reads the Gethsemane-angel-strengthening as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of angelic-ministry to Christ in his true-human extremity: the same angels that ministered to him after the Temptation (Mt 4:11) now minister at the Passion's edge. The Word made flesh receives angelic strengthening — not because the divinity needs it, but because the humanity legitimately does. Tewahedo angelology cites Lk 22:43 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of angelic-ministry to suffering Christians; the Tewahedo Angelic-Intercession tradition (the 'Mäshafä Mäla'ǝkt' supplications) draws on this canonical pattern.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLVI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mt 4:11.

entries.summary: On Christ's word to the arresting-officers 'this is your hour, and the power of darkness' (Lk 22:53), Cyril reads the doubled-phrase (your-hour + power-of-darkness) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Satan-permitted-darkness-hour: the Passion proceeds not because Christ is defeated but because the Father permits the hour of the powers-of-darkness. The exousia tou skotous (authority of darkness) is the same authority Christ acknowledges at his arrest as permitted but not victorious. Tewahedo Holy-Week theology cites Lk 22:53 + Col 1:13 (delivered from the power of darkness) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the Cross goes through the darkness-hour to the resurrection-light.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Col 1:13.

entries.summary: On Peter's Lukan-distinctive response after the cock-crow — 'And Peter went out, and wept bitterly' (Lk 22:62) — Cyril reads the eklausen pikrōs (wept bitterly) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of repentant-tears as the active-receptive expression of post-fall sorrow: tears are not despair but the moisture of returning-love. Peter's tears are the inverse of Judas's hanging (Mt 27:5); the same betrayal, different response. Tewahedo penitential theology cites Lk 22:62 + 2 Cor 7:10 (godly sorrow worketh repentance) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of repentant-tears; the Tewahedo monastic 'gift of tears' (charisma of compunction) is the spiritual descendant of Peter's Lukan tears.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. 2 Cor 7:10.

entries.summary: On the Jerusalem-mob's cry 'Crucify him, crucify him' (Lk 23:21), Cyril reads the doubled-imperative as the canonical Lukan anchor of the canonical-prophetic-rejection's voice: the cry that reverses the Hosanna of Lk 19:38 by the same population. Cyril is careful to distinguish the city-political mob from 'the Jewish people' as a whole (against any later anti-Judaic reading); the cry is the act of a Jerusalem-Caiaphas-orchestrated faction. Tewahedo pastoral theology cites Lk 23:21 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the same human voice can ascribe Hosanna-and-Crucify within a single week — the warning against fickle-religiosity.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXLIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On Christ's word to the Lukan-distinctive 'daughters of Jerusalem' — 'Weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children' (Lk 23:28) — Cyril reads the redirected-tears as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of properly-ordered-sorrow: the Christian does not pity the Crucified (he chose the Cross) but laments his/her own sin (whose burden he bears). The prophetic-Tewahedo lamentation tradition (the bēbet-äbiyot procession of Holy Week) preserves the redirected-sorrow pattern: the weeping is for our sins, not Christ's death. Tewahedo Holy-Week theology cites Lk 23:28 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of redirected-Holy-Week-lament.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CL (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the place-name 'Calvary' (Lk 23:33 — kranion 'place of a skull'), Cyril reads the Hebrew-Aramaic Golgotha as the canonical Lukan anchor of the typological-doctrine that the place of Christ's death is the symbolic place of Adam's skull: the Adamic-tradition (preserved in Tewahedo Synaxarium and Mäshafä-Adam) locates Adam's burial at Golgotha, making Christ's blood flow over the first father's bones. Tewahedo iconography cites Lk 23:33 + the Mäshafä-Adam tradition as the canonical doubled-witness for the depictive-tradition of the Adamic-skull at the foot of the Cross — the Cross stands over the head of the first father; the Second Adam restores what the First Adam lost.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Tewahedo apocryphal-tradition: Mäshafä Adam (Book of Adam).

entries.summary: On the cross-superscription 'THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS' (Lk 23:38 — in Greek, Latin, Hebrew per Jn 19:20), Cyril reads the trilingual-titulus as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the universal-kingship-of-Christ proclaimed at the Cross: Pilate's intended-mockery becomes (against his intent) the canonical proclamation of Christ's kingship in the three languages of the known world (Hebrew = covenantal, Greek = cultural, Latin = imperial). Tewahedo Solomonic-dynasty self-understanding cites Lk 23:38 + Jn 19:20 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the King of the Jews is also the King of all nations — the Ethiopian Solomonic-dynastic claim to Christ-the-King derives from this universal-trilingual-titulus.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Jn 19:20.

entries.summary: On the good-thief's plea 'Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom' (Lk 23:42), Cyril reads the dying-thief's confession as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of last-moment-saving-faith: a sinner with no time for catechesis, no baptism, no works — yet his confession ('Lord' + recognition of the kingdom) suffices. Christ's answer (Lk 23:43 — seed entry) is the canonical promise; this verse is the canonical confession. Tewahedo pastoral-theology of last-rites cites Lk 23:42 + Lk 23:43 as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness for the doctrine that the deathbed confession is salvifically-effective; the priest at the bedside follows the dominical pattern of the Christ-and-thief exchange.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the cosmic-darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour (Lk 23:44), Cyril reads the three-hour-darkness as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the cosmic-participation in the Passion: creation darkens because its Maker dies. The three hours echo Jonah's three days in the fish (Mt 12:40), the three days Moses was in the ark (Jub 47:5), and the three days Christ will be in the tomb. Tewahedo cosmic-Christology cites Lk 23:44 + Mt 27:51-52 (earth-quake, rocks rent, graves opened) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the natural-cosmic-order participates in the death of its Word-Maker; the Tewahedo Holy-Friday liturgy preserves the three-hour darkening observance.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Mt 27:51-52.

entries.summary: On the Temple-veil rent in twain at Christ's death (Lk 23:45), Cyril reads the schism-of-the-veil as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the opening-of-access to the Holy-of-Holies through Christ's flesh (Heb 10:19-20 — 'a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh'). The veil rent from top to bottom (Mt 27:51) signals God's-direction rather than human-direction of the action. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Lk 23:45 + Heb 10:19-20 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the iconographic-curtain in the Tewahedo sanctuary (which veils the maqdas) functions as both barrier-and-passage — the curtain that screens is also the curtain that opens at the Eucharistic moment.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Heb 10:19-20.

entries.summary: On Joseph of Arimathea's wrapping of Christ's body and burial 'in a sepulchre that was hewn in stone, wherein never man before was laid' (Lk 23:53), Cyril reads the new-unused-tomb as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the sanctified-tomb: just as the virgin-womb prepared the Word's entry into the world, the new-tomb (Joseph's own, never used) prepares his three-day rest. The pairing virgin-womb + new-tomb forms the canonical-bookend of the Incarnation. Tewahedo Marian-and-Easter theology cites Lk 23:53 + Lk 1:34-35 ('how shall this be, seeing I know not a man') as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of the sanctified-virginal-spaces that bound the Incarnation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLIV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Lk 1:34-35.

entries.summary: On the women's discovery 'upon the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came unto the sepulchre' (Lk 24:1), Cyril reads the first-day-of-the-week (mia tōn sabbatōn) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the resurrection's calendrical-establishment of the Lord's-Day: the resurrection inaugurates the new-creation week, and the first-day becomes the Christian sabbath (without abolishing the Saturday-Sabbath — Tewahedo preserves BOTH per Acts 20:7 + Heb 4:9). Tewahedo doubled-Sabbath-observance cites Lk 24:1 + Acts 20:7 + Jub 50:9 (Saturday-Sabbath as foretaste of the holy kingdom) as the canonical triple-witness for the Tewahedo Sänbatä-Krǝstiyan (Christian-Sabbath) on Sunday alongside the Saturday Sabbath.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Acts 20:7, Jub 50:9 (R.H. Charles, 1902 — PD).

entries.summary: On the angels' question to the women 'Why seek ye the living among the dead?' (Lk 24:5), Cyril reads the angelic-rhetorical-question as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the proper-place-of-the-living-Christ: the tomb is the wrong location for the living Lord. The angels redirect from tomb-search to risen-recognition. Tewahedo Easter (Fasika) liturgy cites Lk 24:5 + Lk 24:6 ('he is not here, but is risen') as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that Easter-worship is not tomb-pilgrimage but risen-Christ-recognition; the Tewahedo Pascha vigil uses the angelic-question as a refrain.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the angels' recital of Christ's pre-Passion prediction — 'the Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again' (Lk 24:7) — Cyril reads the dei (must-be) + third-day-rise as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the entire Passion + Resurrection sequence is divinely-necessary (the Lukan dei recurs at 9:22, 17:25, 22:37, 24:7, 24:26, 24:44 — six times the divine-necessity formula). The third-day-rise specifically fulfils Hos 6:2 + Jonah's three-days. Tewahedo Pascha theology cites Lk 24:7 + Hos 6:2 + Mt 12:40 as the canonical triple-witness of the divinely-necessary third-day-resurrection.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Hos 6:2, Mt 12:40.

entries.summary: On the Emmaus-road encounter (Lk 24:13-32), Cyril reads the unique-Lukan post-resurrection narrative as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the eucharistic-recognition pattern: word-of-Christ (expounded along the road, Lk 24:27) → breaking-of-bread (eyes opened, Lk 24:30-31 seed) → burning-hearts (in retrospect, Lk 24:32). The structure preserves the canonical Eucharistic shape: Liturgy of the Word + Liturgy of the Sacrament + Mystagogical reflection. Tewahedo Anaphora structure cites Lk 24:13-32 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the Eucharistic-recognition-shape; every Tewahedo Mass is an Emmaus-road journey.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the risen Christ's rebuke 'O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken' (Lk 24:25), Cyril reads the rebuke + 'all-that-the-prophets-have-spoken' as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the comprehensive-prophetic-witness to Christ: the Resurrection-Christ holds his disciples accountable to ALL the prophets, not selected proof-texts. The slow-of-heart-to-believe formula appears as a Lukan refrain (Lk 24:11 + 24:25 + 24:38). Tewahedo Bibliology cites Lk 24:25 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the unitary-prophetic-canon: the Old Testament prophets uniformly witness to Christ; selectivity or hesitance is rebuked.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the Emmaus-road exposition 'And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself' (Lk 24:27), Cyril reads the comprehensive-Christological-hermeneutic as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the entire Old Testament is Christologically interpretable: the Lord himself models the patristic-Christological hermeneutic on the resurrection road. Cyril's own commentaries (and the entire patristic exegetical tradition) appropriate this canonical-resurrection-pattern as their methodological foundation. Tewahedo Andǝmta hermeneutic cites Lk 24:27 as the canonical Lukan anchor for the multi-layered Christological reading of the Tewahedo canonical Scriptures.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.

entries.summary: On the Emmaus-disciples' retrospective 'Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?' (Lk 24:32), Cyril reads the burning-heart formula as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the affective-pneumatological response to Scripture-rightly-expounded: the heart-burn is the Spirit's-confirmation of the Christological exegesis. The same heart-burn recurs at Pentecost (Acts 2:3 — 'cloven tongues like as of fire'). Tewahedo monastic-mystical theology cites Lk 24:32 + Acts 2:3 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of the Spirit-given heart-burn at canonical-Scripture-encounter; the Tewahedo daily Mass preserves the Word-and-Sacrament heart-burning pattern.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLV (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Acts 2:3.

entries.summary: On the risen Christ's 'Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have' (Lk 24:39), Cyril reads the handle-me + flesh-and-bones formula as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the real-bodily-resurrection: not a ghost, not a mere appearance, but a transformed-yet-real body with flesh-and-bones. The verse is load-bearing against the docetic-spiritualizing tendencies that would later challenge the resurrection. Tewahedo Easter theology cites Lk 24:39 + Jn 20:27 ('reach hither thy finger') + 1 Cor 15:42-44 (resurrection body) as the canonical triple-witness for the real-bodily-resurrection doctrine; the Tewahedo Fasika Anaphora confesses 'we believe in the resurrection of the body'.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CLVI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Jn 20:27, 1 Cor 15:42-44.
